Under favorable conditions (e.g. a nutrient-rich anoxic habitat), they multiply rapidly and form colonies. There is no male/female or mating in the conventional sense. However, they could exchange genetic material through mechanisms like conjugation (a plasmid or DNA segment passing through a pilus from one cell to another) or transformation (uptake of free DNA). These processes allowed them to acquire new traits (like antibiotic resistance or new metabolic pathways) – a kind of parasexual reproduction that increases genetic diversity. Some anaerobic bacteria, especially Gram-positive spore-formers (like Clostridium), form endospores when conditions are harsh; while not reproduction (one cell turns into one spore), it’s a life cycle stage that ensures lineage survival and subsequent “germination” into reproducing cells. The invention of DNA genomes (replacing RNA) was fully in use – because of DNA’s superior stability, larger genomes could be maintained, enabling more complex metabolic capabilities. This means anaerobic bacteria could carry genes for various enzymes and regulatory systems, supporting versatility and setting the stage for future evolutionary leaps. Still, no true sexual reproduction (involving fusion of gametes) had evolved in these organisms.
Bacteria (Anaerobic).Integumentary System (Protection): Multi-layered cell envelope. Anaerobic bacteria wore a suit of armor in the form of their cell envelope, which serves the role of skin. The plasma membrane is the inner skin, containing the cytoplasm. Beyond that, the peptidoglycan cell wall provides a tough, porous mesh that protects and gives shape. Many anaerobes (particularly pathogenic ones) also secrete a capsule, a thick gelatinous layer of polysaccharides outside the cell wall. This capsule is analogous to a slimy skin coating: it helps retain moisture (important in fluctuating wet/dry conditions like soil surfaces), protects against phagocytic predators, and can mediate attachment to surfaces. For Gram-negative anaerobes, an outer membrane lies outside the peptidoglycan, containing lipopolysaccharides – this extra membrane is part of their integument, providing chemical protection and a permeability barrier. Together, these layers function like an integumentary system: controlling interaction with the environment, protecting against mechanical and chemical damage, and even camouflaging the bacterium from a host’s immune system in pathogenic cases. Although rudimentary compared to multicellular skin, the bacterial envelope with its layers (membrane, wall, capsule) was a highly effective protective interface with the world.
Bacteria (Anaerobic).Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Nonexistent. Anaerobic bacteria, being single-celled, have no lymphatic system. There is no body fluid to circulate or filter. If these bacteria lived in communities, any extracellular fluid is just the environment (water or substrate they inhabit). They lack any structure analogous to lymph vessels or nodes. Waste removal and immune defense occur at the cellular level (each cell dumps waste out, each cell defends itself). In biofilms (communities encased in slime), diffusion through the slime and movement of bulk fluid (when the biofilm is in water) handle distribution of nutrients and removal of wastes for the community, but there is still no dedicated lymph-like network. The lymphatic system concept simply doesn’t apply until organisms are composed of many cells with internal compartments.

DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Nervous System (Signal Response): No new nerves, but information storage boosted responses. The transition from an RNA/protein-based world to a DNA-based genetic system did not immediately create a nervous system, but it enabled greater complexity in regulatory networks. DNA’s stability allowed organisms to evolve more genes, including those for advanced receptors and signaling proteins. Over time, this supported more refined sensory apparatus (e.g. more kinds of chemotaxis, phototaxis proteins) because the genome could hold more information. So while organisms at the moment of DNA’s emergence still had only simple prokaryotic sensory systems, the foundation was laid for enhanced signal transduction. In essence, DNA allowed the “blueprints” for proto-nervous functions (like receptor proteins, ion channels, etc.) to be safely stored and passed on, setting the stage for future nervous system development in complex life.
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Circulatory System (Internal Transport): No circulatory system (unicellular context). The invention of DNA does not equate to the invention of multicellularity or organs. Early DNA-based organisms remained single-celled for a long time. Therefore, internal circulation was unchanged – diffusion on the microscale was sufficient. However, with DNA genomes, cells could grow slightly larger or develop internal compartments (like cyanobacteria developed thylakoids) which in turn necessitated some intracellular transport (e.g. vesicles or protein motors) to move molecules around efficiently. One could say that DNA-based complexity eventually led to cells with endomembranes that traffic molecules (like the internal shipping department of a cell). But at the point of DNA’s emergence, no true circulatory innovation had occurred. So there were still no blood vessels – just perhaps more efficient intracellular distribution as cell architecture grew in complexity.
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Higher metabolic complexity supported. The shift to DNA did not directly alter gas exchange (still by diffusion) but it allowed cells to encode far more enzymes and regulatory proteins. This means organisms could combine and regulate metabolic pathways more intricately. For instance, with more genes, cells could regulate anaerobic respiration in response to different electron acceptors, or evolve tolerance to small amounts of oxygen. In fact, DNA’s error-correction and larger coding capacity were prerequisites for the evolution of oxygenic photosynthesis and aerobic respiration down the line. Once oxygen appeared (via cyanobacteria), DNA-bearing life could adapt to use it. So while a DNA-based cell still just diffused O₂/CO₂ across its membrane, it had the genetic tools to eventually develop things like dedicated respiratory proteins (cytochromes, etc.) and manage reactive oxygen. In summary, breathing remained the same physically (diffusion), but genetically DNA allowed much more sophisticated control of respiratory metabolism.
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Encoded enzymes expand dietary breadth. The DNA revolution meant organisms could carry a lot more hereditary information – enabling them to produce diverse enzymes for nutrient acquisition. For example, genes for various hydrolases (to break down cellulose, starch, lipids) could all be maintained in the same genome, allowing a single species to digest multiple food sources. Early on, a DNA-based microbe might have a battery of enzymes to utilize different substrates – e.g. if glucose is absent, switch to lactose (lac operon is an example of regulated digestion made possible by DNA-encoded regulators and enzymes). Additionally, some genes could code for membrane transporters for numerous nutrients. In effect, DNA-based life could evolve metabolic versatility: the “digestive system” at the cellular level became richer, since large genomes could encode complete pathways to synthesize essential molecules (vitamins, amino acids) or break down complex chemicals. This innovation was entirely at the microscopic scale – no gut, but a genetically flexible metabolism that functions like a Swiss army knife of digestion.
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Better homeostasis genes. With DNA, cells could evolve and retain complex transport systems for waste management. For instance, multiple efflux pumps (proteins that eject toxic compounds) and sophisticated regulators for osmotic stress (like DNA-binding proteins that sense high salt and trigger production of osmoprotectants) became possible. DNA’s stability meant even multi-step stress response systems (requiring many genes working together) could be maintained in the genome. So while physically the cell still used its membrane to handle excretion, it now had genetic programs to respond to changing conditions: e.g. turning on a suite of genes to pump out excess acid or synthesize neutralizing agents if internal pH drops. Early DNA-based cells likely had improved repair enzymes for DNA itself, which indirectly improved survivability under stress (e.g. DNA repair proteins fixing UV damage meant cells could better handle sunlight). In short, the excretory/osmoregulatory functions remained membrane-centric, but DNA allowed these functions to be finely tuned and more resilient through complex gene networks.
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Genomic stability fosters new defenses. The DNA genome brought higher fidelity replication, which in turn allowed organisms to devote resources to elaborate defense mechanisms without losing them to mutation. For example, the CRISPR-Cas immune system is recorded in DNA – only with stable DNA could cells archive viral sequences reliably and pass that memory to progeny. DNA also allowed the evolution of the SOS response – a global DNA-damage response in bacteria where a single protein (LexA) represses a battery of DNA repair and protection genes and is inactivated when DNA damage is sensed, thereby inducing a suite of protective functions. This kind of coordinated response is only possible with a DNA regulatory network. Moreover, DNA-based life likely saw the emergence of toxin-antitoxin systems, molecular immune-like systems where genes encode both a toxin and its neutralizer, which can help cells cope with stress or post-segregational killing (a kind of internal immunity). All these innovations are “immune” in the broad sense of protecting the organism, and they rely on DNA’s coding capacity and regulatory potential. Thus, while a DNA cell still defended itself with enzymes and barriers like before, the breadth and reliability of immune strategies increased, guarded by the stable storage DNA provided.
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Cytoskeleton and membrane innovation coded by DNA. The existence of DNA didn’t create new structural elements overnight, but it permitted the accumulation of genes for structural proteins. For example, tubulin and actin homologues in prokaryotes (which became the eukaryotic cytoskeleton) could evolve and refine because DNA genomes could expand. Over time, cells could afford a larger set of structural proteins: beyond just a simple FtsZ ring and MreB, perhaps new filament systems or motor proteins started to appear (flagellar proteins are numerous – those genes can all co-exist thanks to large DNA genome). The “skeletal” systems of cells, like the peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis machinery, also became more complex and tightly regulated by DNA-encoded enzymes (multiple penicillin-binding proteins, autolysins, etc. for cell wall turnover). So, while the basic support (cell wall, primitive cytoskeleton) remained, DNA allowed enhancements: cells could grow bigger or change shape because they could produce more varieties of structural molecules and control them via gene regulation. In essence, the blueprint for more elaborate skeletal features was now safely stored and could gradually elaborate – eventually enabling, for instance, the development of eukaryotic cytoskeletal elements and even biomineralization in some lineages. But at this stage, it’s still a single-celled “skeleton” scenario, just with more genes to fortify and regulate it.
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Muscular System (Movement): Prerequisite for true motility complexity. Motility structures like the bacterial flagellum are made of dozens of proteins – the evolution of such complex nanomachines likely depended on the stable, large-genome environment that DNA provided. Thus, DNA-based life could evolve intricate motors and assembly systems for movement. Once evolved, those genes (e.g. all the proteins of the flagellar basal body, hook, filament, export apparatus) could be retained together. So DNA indirectly spurred “muscular” innovation at the micro scale: more sophisticated flagella, contractile pili (like Type IV pili for twitching motility), or secretion systems that have motility roles. Also, DNA genomes allowed regulation of motility – bacteria could turn motility genes on or off in response to signals, something orchestrated by global regulators (e.g. sigma factors, cyclic AMP, etc.). None of this is muscle tissue, but it is the genetic groundwork that one day leads to muscle. For now, organisms with DNA continued using flagella and pili, but those systems were optimized and diversified thanks to DNA. For instance, some bacteria evolved differentiated states (swarm cells vs. sessile cells) where they produce flagella only when needed, a level of control enabled by complex gene networks on DNA. In summary, DNA didn’t add a new motility mechanism immediately, but it ensured that the machinery of motility could become more elaborate and efficiently inherited, eventually opening pathways to entirely new motile structures in eukaryotes (cilia, etc.).
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Endocrine System (Regulation): Genome-based regulation and cell differentiation. The presence of DNA and its transcriptional regulation systems is essentially the birth of the modern regulatory regime in cells. Bacteria with DNA genomes have operons, promoters, and regulatory proteins that can turn sets of genes on or off in response to the environment – a primitive endocrine-like coordination. For instance, sporulation in some DNA-based bacteria (like Bacillus) is controlled by a cascade of sigma factors (transcription regulators) that act in sequence – resembling a hormonal cascade in that one molecular signal triggers another, and so on, ultimately leading to a developmental change (spore formation). DNA allowed the evolution of global regulators – proteins like CRP (cAMP receptor protein) in E. coli that respond to internal metabolites (cAMP) and coordinate multiple operons (sugar metabolism genes) at once. This is analogous to having an internal messenger (cAMP, in this case) that globally alters the cell’s state – similar to an endocrine hormone affecting multiple tissues, except here it’s one cell’s multiple pathways. Also, with DNA came plasmids and mobile elements that could carry regulatory circuits between cells, enriching regulatory diversity. So while still no hormones are secreted into a bloodstream (no bloodstream exists), intracellular signaling and gene regulation reached a new level of sophistication. Cells could mount stress responses (heat shock response turning on chaperone proteins), stationary phase responses, etc., all programmed in DNA. This is effectively an internal “management system” for the cell’s physiology – the evolutionary predecessor to hormone signaling pathways in multicellular life.
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Reproductive System (Replication): High-fidelity genetic reproduction. The emergence of DNA as the genetic material was a monumental reproductive innovation. DNA’s double-stranded structure allowed proofreading and error correction during replication, drastically reducing mutation rates. Consequently, organisms could maintain larger genomes – a prerequisite for evolving greater complexity. Reproductively, cells now passed on DNA to offspring, and because DNA is more stable chemically than RNA, information was preserved across generations with fewer losses. This means traits and adaptations could accumulate over time (whereas in an RNA genome world, too high an error rate would erase large genomes). Also, DNA-based cells evolved dedicated apparatus for replication and segregation (like the origin of replication, DNA polymerase complexes, etc.), making cell division more reliable. In sexual terms, DNA set the stage for sex: it enabled processes like recombination. Early on, bacteria with DNA could exchange pieces of DNA (as noted, via conjugation or transformation), and the universality of DNA meant that even unrelated organisms could share genes – massively accelerating evolution through lateral gene transfer. Much later, the existence of a stable DNA genome made meiosis (sexual reproduction) feasible, since crossing over and chromosomal segregation require stable, complementary strands. In sum, DNA itself doesn’t equate to sexual reproduction – life remained mostly asexual in this phase – but it laid the groundwork for genetic recombination. The immediate effect was clonal reproduction with high fidelity and the capacity for a much larger set of traits to be inherited. This opened the door for the complex life cycles and sexual processes that would evolve in eukaryotes.
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Integumentary System (Protection): More durable “skin” components and novel surface molecules. Transition to DNA-based life didn’t drastically change the physical makeup of cell membranes or walls at first (those were set by chemistry and ancestry), but it did allow the evolution of new membrane proteins and structural polymers. For instance, cells could evolve glycoproteins, S-layer proteins with different properties, or enzymes to modify their lipid A or capsule polysaccharides, all encoded in DNA. This led to a richer integumentary diversity: some bacteria gained the ability to form extracellular slime layers, sheaths, or even mineral coatings (e.g., some precipitate iron or sulfur on their surfaces). DNA encoding also meant repair systems for the cell envelope could be more complex (e.g., multiple enzymes patching peptidoglycan, etc.), making the “skin” more robust. In effect, cells now had a stable blueprint to refine their protective layers: genes for UV-protective pigments (like carotenoids in the membrane) could accumulate, genes for efflux pumps to remove harmful substances added chemical protection, and so on. While in a single cell we still call this ensemble the cell envelope, it serves analogous functions to an integument: containing the organism and shielding it from the outside. DNA-based coding meant if a mutation produced a better capsule or a novel surface protein that helped evade predators, it could be retained and spread. Over evolutionary time, this enabled the development of complex cell coverings (e.g., the multiple-layered envelopes of Gram-negative bacteria, or the waxy coat of mycobacteria). But in the immediate sense, organisms at the dawn of DNA looked similar externally to their RNA-world predecessors – just with the potential to evolve much tougher and specialized integuments thanks to the stable genome.
DNA (Emergence of DNA-based life).Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: None. The innovation of DNA had no direct impact on multicellularity or the need for a lymphatic system. All organisms were still unicellular (or simple colonies) at this point. There was no internal fluid separate from the environment that required circulation or filtering. Thus, no lymphatic vessels or nodes existed. Any intercellular communication was through direct contact or diffusion in the environment, not via an internal fluid network. The management of internal vs. external remained at the single-cell level. Only when organisms become multicellular and develop circulatory systems (to move nutrients) does the concept of a lymphatic system (to return leaked fluid and provide immune surveillance) become relevant. DNA did enable multicellularity later by allowing larger genomes (hence instructions for cell adhesion, communication, differentiation), but until those multicellular bodies evolved, there was simply no lymphatic function to speak of.

Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Nervous System (Signal Response): Primitive sensory and response systems. Cyanobacteria, though still bacteria, exhibit more complex behaviors suited to their photosynthetic lifestyle. They have photoreceptors to sense light quantity and quality – for example, Synechocystis has a phototaxis system with a UV/blue light sensor that directs movement. Indeed, photosynthetic cyanobacteria show phototaxis, moving towards light using a chemotaxis-like signaling pathway and type IV pili for crawling. This is a rudimentary vision system: a pigmented “eyespot” area in some filamentous cyanobacteria can help them distinguish light direction. Additionally, cyanobacteria possess circadian clocks at the molecular level (Kai proteins) to track day-night cycles and adjust metabolism – an internal timing signal akin to a very primitive nervous regulation. They also sense nutrients (like nitrogen or phosphate) and communicate internally to respond (e.g. initiating heterocyst differentiation when nitrogen is low). In summary, while they have no neurons, cyanobacteria coordinate environmental information and cellular response via integrated signaling networks, effectively a step up in sensory complexity relative to earlier microbes.
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Circulatory System (Internal Transport): No blood, but some internal exchange in filaments. Individual cyanobacterial cells rely on diffusion, as before, for moving molecules around internally. However, many cyanobacteria form multicellular filaments or colonies, and within these, there is a degree of internal transport. For instance, some filamentous forms (like Anabaena) differentiate heterocysts (nitrogen-fixing cells) that share nitrogen compounds with neighboring photosynthetic cells, which in turn share sugars – this exchange happens through small pores between cells, somewhat like a crude circulatory exchange of nutrients within the filament. It’s not a dedicated circulatory system with a pumping mechanism, but cell-to-cell transfer through junctions does occur, distributing vital nutrients along the chain. In general, though, cyanobacteria have no specialized vessels or fluids; each cell of a colony still largely absorbs what it needs from the environment. In large layered colonies (biofilms or stromatolites), the diffusion of nutrients and signals between layers could be seen as a precursor to internal transport, but it remains passive.
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Oxygenic photosynthesis and aerobic respiration. Cyanobacteria revolutionized respiration by producing oxygen. They perform oxygenic photosynthesis, using sunlight to split water, releasing O₂ as a byproduct. During daylight, they take in CO₂ and light, and their internal thylakoid membranes carry out photosynthesis, generating sugar and oxygen. At night, they can switch to aerobic respiration (they consume the stored sugars and oxygen to produce energy). Thus, they have both “lungs” and “breath” in a manner of speaking: in light they act like plants (producing O₂), in the dark like animals (consuming O₂). All gas exchange is done across the cell membrane – there are no organs – but because many cyanobacteria are small or filamentous, every cell has access to water to diffuse CO₂ in and O₂ out. The accumulation of oxygen by cyanobacteria in Earth’s oceans and atmosphere (~2.4 billion years ago) profoundly changed the planet, eventually enabling aerobic respiration in other organisms. Internally, cyanobacteria have specialized micro-compartments (carboxysomes) to concentrate CO₂ for efficient photosynthesis, which is an innovation to improve gas usage. In terms of a respiratory system, they lack anything like gills; diffusion suffices, but they are noteworthy as the first to supply atmospheric oxygen, linking the “respiratory” needs of the entire biosphere to their activity.
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Self-feeding (autotrophy) with some versatility. Cyanobacteria are predominantly autotrophic, meaning their “digestive system” is photosynthesis. Their cells contain chlorophyll a and accessory pigments (phycobilins) that capture sunlight; they use CO₂ from the water and build sugars. Thus, they produce their own food internally (glucose) which then feeds into their metabolic pathways. They don’t ingest particles or organisms (no phagocytosis in bacteria), but they do absorb inorganic nutrients: nitrates, phosphates, iron, etc., from the environment – these are their “vitamins and minerals.” Some cyanobacteria can also fix atmospheric nitrogen (N₂) into ammonia using specialized cells called heterocysts (thick-walled cells that create an anaerobic interior for the nitrogenase enzyme). In a sense, heterocysts act as a digestive specialization – providing the “fertilizer” (ammonia) that the rest of the filament can use to build proteins. In certain conditions, some cyanobacteria can switch to mixotrophy – for example, they might uptake small organic acids or sugars if available, supplementing photosynthesis. But primarily, their capability to perform oxygenic photosynthesis was their major nutritional innovation – using light and water to generate biomass, essentially the first “plants” on Earth in terms of energy and carbon intake. There is no gut, just a highly efficient cellular factory converting light into food.
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Excreting oxygen and maintaining balance. The most notable “waste” cyanobacteria produce is oxygen, which they freely release into the water. What is waste to them became vital to aerobic life. They also excrete other metabolites; for example, excess fixed nitrogen (if too much) might be released as ammonium, or they may secrete mucus (polysaccharides) which carries away some waste by binding metals or toxins. Osmoregulation in freshwater species is crucial – many cyanobacteria live in freshwater ponds, so to avoid bursting from water influx, they rely on their cell wall and possibly contractile vacuoles in some (though classical contractile vacuoles are more common in eukaryotic algae; cyanobacteria mostly use other means). Primarily, ion pumps help maintain osmotic balance, and the cell wall prevents lysis by counteracting turgor pressure. Some cyanobacteria form akinetes (dormant spores) that accumulate polyphosphate or cyanophycin granules; these could be seen as storing excess nutrients (phosphate, nitrogen) and thus managing waste/nutrient excess by sequestration. Additionally, many cyanobacteria control their buoyancy with gas vesicles – protein-shelled bubbles inside the cell; while not for excretion, these allow them to move vertically for optimal light/nutrient conditions (by adjusting gas content they float or sink). If conditions become too oxygen-rich (which can be damaging), cyanobacteria can modulate photosynthesis or use mechanisms like Mehler reaction (pseudo-cyclic electron flow) to dissipate excess O₂. Overall, waste removal (like CO₂ release at night from respiration, O₂ release in day) is passive, but these cells evolved structures (thylakoids, cell walls, vesicles) to manage the byproducts and conditions of their metabolic activity, maintaining internal stability while dramatically changing their external environment.
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Fortified against predators and oxidative stress. Cyanobacteria often form gelatinous sheaths or mucilage layers around their cells or colonies – a bit like a slimy skin that can inhibit protozoan predators from easily ingesting them and also protect against UV radiation. They also produce various bioactive compounds; some produce toxins (like microcystin in certain species) that deter grazing by zooplankton – an early form of chemical defense. Importantly, because they generate oxygen (which can form toxic reactive oxygen species), cyanobacteria have a strong complement of antioxidant enzymes: superoxide dismutase and catalase are present to neutralize superoxide radicals and hydrogen peroxide, and peroxidases to deal with peroxides. These enzymes are essentially a cellular immune system against oxidative damage – without them, the oxygen they produce would harm or kill them. Cyanobacteria also can absorb high UV through pigments (their sunscreen-like pigments, e.g. scytonemin, protect them from intense sunlight in shallow waters). In terms of pathogen defense, cyanophages (viruses infecting cyanobacteria) do attack them, and cyanobacteria use CRISPR-Cas systems as well for adaptive immunity against phages. So they share the molecular immune strategies of other bacteria, but additionally have unique defenses suited to a photosynthetic lifestyle: UV-protective and antioxidant measures. As multicellular communities (some form thick mats), if one layer is attacked or dies, others can survive – a communal resilience. But there is no immune organ or circulating immune cells; each cyanobacterial cell must fend for itself using chemical and enzymatic defenses, aided by the shelter of colonies or filaments.
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Cell wall and mucilaginous sheath. Like other bacteria, cyanobacteria have a peptidoglycan cell wall that gives them shape and strength. In fact, the peptidoglycan layer in cyanobacteria is intermediate in thickness between typical Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (they are Gram-negative in architecture, with an outer membrane). This wall is critical to withstand the osmotic pressures of their often freshwater habitats. Many cyanobacteria secrete a thick gelatinous sheath around the filaments or colonies – this extracellular polysaccharide matrix holds cells together in colonies (like in stromatolites) and provides structural integrity to the community, akin to a jelly-like skeleton. In some colonial forms, this sheath can be quite substantial, giving the colony a defined form (e.g., spherical colonies of Nostoc have a firm mucous ball structure). Some cyanobacteria even form rock-like structures (stromatolites) in concert with minerals – layer upon layer of cells and calcium carbonate deposition that creates a sort of reef; while the mineral part is not produced by the cells intentionally, their presence causes precipitation, effectively encasing them in a stony support. Internally, cyanobacteria don’t have the microtubules or actin cytoskeleton of eukaryotes, but they do have internal membranes (thylakoids) that help organize the cell’s interior. So the skeletal role in cyanobacteria is played by the cell wall (giving each cell rigidity) and the colonial sheath or biofilm matrix (giving the group form and anchoring them). These are primitive exoskeletal features, ensuring the cyanobacteria maintain their shape, whether it’s filaments waving in water or slimy mats carpeting a rock.
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Muscular System (Movement): Gliding motility and buoyancy – movement without muscles. Cyanobacteria lack flagella (most are non-flagellated), but many can move. Filamentous cyanobacteria often show gliding motility: they can creep along surfaces, possibly by secreting slime and using tiny motors in their cell wall to ratchet along that slime. Some oscillate or bend towards light (hence names like Oscillatoria). Unicellular cyanobacteria like Synechocystis can move on moist surfaces using type IV pili, pulling themselves along (similar to how some bacteria twitch). Additionally, planktonic cyanobacteria like Microcystis regulate their depth using gas vesicles – by making or collapsing these internal gas bubbles, they rise or sink to find the right light levels, which is a form of movement in the water column. These motions are slow and lack the force of flagellar swimming, but they suffice to reposition the cells for optimal light and nutrients. Some filamentous forms (e.g., Anabaena) can also adjust positioning within colonies to some degree. In terms of analogies, their gliding is like a snail’s movement (very slow and slime-assisted) on a microscopic level. There are no muscle fibers or cilia, but surface proteins and polysaccharide extrusion generate movement. When conditions are adverse, cyanobacteria can also form akinetes (resting spores) that simply wait out bad times – not movement, but a strategy to disperse through time rather than space. Overall, cyanobacteria demonstrate that you can have directed movement (especially toward light, as noted under nervous/sensory) without any muscles, using just cellular structures and physics (pili pulling, or buoyant lifting). This allowed them to seek light (phototaxis) and form extensive blooms at the water surface.
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Endocrine System (Regulation): Internal chemical coordination and community signaling. While cyanobacteria are unicellular/colonial, they show signs of internal regulation that parallels hormonal control. For example, in Anabaena filaments, when nitrogen is scarce, a fraction of cells differentiate into heterocysts. This patterning is controlled by a gradient of a small peptide (PatS) that diffuses from heterocysts to neighbor cells, inhibiting them from also becoming heterocysts – effectively a morphogen-like signal ensuring proper spacing of these specialized cells. That’s analogous to hormonal or developmental signaling in higher organisms, albeit on a simpler scale. Cyanobacteria also produce and secrete quorum-sensing molecules to coordinate biofilm formation and toxin production in blooms. Internally, each cyanobacterial cell uses signaling networks (two-component systems, second messengers like cyclic AMP or cyclic di-GMP) to adjust to changes – for instance, switching between day and night metabolism is tightly regulated by their circadian clock proteins and transcriptional regulators (a bit like an internal hormonal cycle keyed to light). They don’t have glands or bloodstream, but in a filamentous cyanobacterium, the movement of regulators or small signals from cell to cell acts like an endocrine system for the filament, ensuring cells specialize or act in unison when needed. Also, during stress, they may release allelochemicals that signal other organisms or their own kind. In sum, cyanobacteria introduced cellular differentiation and chemical communication in a community context, which are hallmarks of endocrine control (just in a very nascent form).
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Reproductive System (Replication): Alternation of growth and dormancy – no true sex. Cyanobacteria generally reproduce asexually by cell division. A filament grows by division of cells along its length; a colony expands as cells divide and secrete more matrix. Some cyanobacteria exhibit rudimentary lifecycle changes: they can form akinetes (dormant thick-walled spores) when conditions are unfavorable, and these akinetes later germinate into new filaments when conditions improve, which is a survival/reproductive strategy. But there is no sexual reproduction (no fusion of gametes) in cyanobacteria – they do not undergo meiosis. Genetic recombination can occur via horizontal gene transfer (viruses or direct uptake of DNA), which can introduce genetic variation similarly to sex. The real innovation in some cyanobacteria is cell differentiation as part of reproduction: heterocysts for nitrogen fixation (not exactly reproduction, but division of labor), akinetes for dormancy, and hormogonia (small motile filaments that break off from the main filament to disperse). Hormogonia formation is a dispersal strategy – a piece of a filament (just a few cells) differentiates into a motile form and glides away to colonize a new spot, then grows into a new filament. This is analogous to reproductive propagation of a colony. It’s not sexual, but it’s a step towards multicellular life cycles where different cell types and stages are involved. The presence of DNA allowed complex gene regulation for these stages. In summary, cyanobacteria’s reproduction remained asexual (binary fission, fragmentation), but with specialized stages (spores, motile fragments) that improved survival and spreading. They set the stage for later oxygen-dependent organisms to evolve true sex by oxygenating the planet and contributing to the DNA toolbox; however, within cyanobacteria themselves, reproduction was about making more identical cells and sometimes packaging or spacing them out for maximal success.
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Integumentary System (Protection): Thick cell walls, sheaths, and UV shields – a proto-skin. The integument of cyanobacteria is essentially their multi-layer cell envelope: a plasma membrane inside, a peptidoglycan cell wall for structure, and often an outer membrane (typical of Gram-negatives) plus an external polysaccharide sheath. Many also have protective pigments in their outer layers. For example, some species secrete sunscreen-like compounds (such as scytonemin, a pigment that sits in the sheath and absorbs UV light). This helps them survive intense sunlight in shallow waters or deserts, functioning like a skin pigment in higher organisms. The gelatinous sheath not only gives structural cohesion but also prevents desiccation by holding water, much like how terrestrial plant integuments prevent water loss (though cyanobacteria are mostly aquatic or in moist soils). In colonial forms, the outermost layer of the community can sacrifice itself, shielding inner cells from UV or grazing – analogous to a skin layer protecting inner tissues. Some cyanobacteria in mats form a stratified structure: a top layer of heavily pigmented cells absorbs harmful radiation and too much light, allowing cells beneath to photosynthesize optimally – this is a cooperative integumentary function at the colony level. In essence, cyanobacteria developed a robust outermost layer (cell wall + sheath + pigments) that acts as a skin: it isolates the cell from external fluctuations, prevents mechanical and radiation damage, and mediates interaction with the environment (e.g., by selectively allowing nutrients to diffuse in through the gelatinous matrix). They do not have an epidermis or cuticle in the plant sense, but these bacterial “skin” features were the precursors to those in multicellular photoautotrophs.
Cyanobacteria (Oxygenic Photosynthesizer.Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Absent – external water serves this role. Cyanobacteria, even when in multicellular filaments or colonies, do not have an internal fluid transport system separate from the environment. There is no lymphatic system; the surrounding water and the water-filled mucilage around cells handle distribution of substances. In a cyanobacterial mat, water flows between cells and layers, removing waste and bringing nutrients; if we stretch the analogy, the ocean or pond is the lymphatic fluid that bathes their community. They do have small pores between some cells in filaments, but these are for nutrient exchange, not for circulating an immune fluid. Also, cyanobacteria don’t have specialized immune cells to move around – each cell deals with immune challenges on its own. So, no lymphatic vessels or nodes exist. If a cyanobacterium is part of a lichen or microbial community, sometimes there are common channels in the biofilm, but that’s more like shared plumbing than a true lymphatic system. The evolution of a lymphatic system required complex multicellular organisms with circulatory systems, which is far beyond cyanobacteria.

Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Nervous System (Signal Response): Sensory systems tuned to oxygen and more. Aerobic bacteria typically possess all the sensory capabilities of anaerobes (chemotaxis, etc.) and then some specialized ones. For instance, many have an aerotaxis system – they can sense oxygen concentration via sensors (like the Aer receptor in E. coli) and swim toward an optimal O₂ level. This is crucial: too little oxygen and they starve for energy; too much could be harmful (if they lack defenses). So they navigate gradients of oxygen, which is a new environmental cue earlier life didn’t handle. Additionally, aerobic bacteria often live in dynamic environments (soil, host organisms), so they have complex two-component systems sensing everything from nutrients to signals from hosts. Pathogenic aerobic bacteria can sense host signals (like adrenaline, temperature) and turn on virulence genes – a primitive integration of sensory input to alter behavior akin to a neural-like response (though molecular). Some soil aerobes like Myxobacteria even coordinate in “wolf-pack” hunting of other microbes via chemical signaling, indicating group sensory-response behavior. In summary, no nerves, but networks of sensory proteins (histidine kinases, chemoreceptors) that monitor oxygen, redox state, quorum signals, etc., give these bacteria a responsive edge. They essentially have expanded “input channels” (e.g., dedicated O₂ sensors, oxidative stress sensors) feeding into regulatory circuits that orchestrate responses (motility, enzyme production), functioning as a diffuse neural-like system wholly at the cellular level.
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Still none, but multicellularity experiments begin. Individual aerobic bacteria don’t need circulatory systems – they’re single cells. But interestingly, some aerobic bacteria started forming complex multicellular structures. For example, Myxobacteria (aerobic soil bacteria) aggregate by the thousands to form fruiting bodies when starving. Inside these fruiting bodies, cells differentiate into spores at the top. While there’s no circulatory system in a myxobacterial fruiting body, there is a primitive interior/exterior – cells on the interior get nutrients from those on the outside that may lyse. Similarly, Streptomyces bacteria grow as filaments (hyphae) in the soil, forming a network (mycelium) with branches that share cytoplasm; they even have septal pores allowing nutrient flow along the filament. This begins to resemble a circulatory function: nutrients can move within the colony through filamentous connections. Also, biofilms formed by aerobic bacteria (like plaque on teeth or slime on rocks) often have water channels that run through the biofilm, distributing nutrients to interior cells – an analog to blood vessels in a very loose sense. These are not genetically determined vessels, but emergent structures. So, while no true circulatory system evolved in bacteria, the cooperative structures of some aerobic bacteria foreshadow the need for internal distribution in larger assemblages. The vast majority of aerobic bacteria, however, remain unicellular or simple filaments and rely on diffusion from the environment (which is greatly enhanced by the presence of oxygen circulating in air or water).
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Oxygen breathing and high-energy yield. Aerobic bacteria use oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor in respiration, allowing them to extract far more energy (ATP) from nutrients than anaerobes. They developed complete electron transport chains in their inner membrane with cytochromes that hand off electrons to O₂, forming water. Gas exchange in bacteria is still by diffusion through the cell envelope – O₂ diffuses in, CO₂ diffuses out – but aerobes often have adaptations to maximize this. For example, some have internal membranes (like Nitrosomonas bacteria have invaginated membranes to increase surface area for nitrification, an oxygen-requiring process). Others, like Azotobacter, increase their respiration rate to consume O₂ rapidly and create a low-O₂ environment internally so they can fix nitrogen (a balancing act – they intentionally respirate quickly as a form of oxygen control). The presence of oxygen allowed bacteria to live in new habitats (surface of waters, on land) and to evolve into bigger cells since energy was abundant. Some giant bacteria (like Thiomargarita, though anaerobic in parts, and Epulopiscium, an aerobic giant in fish guts) can exist, but they still rely on diffusion of O₂; they survive by having low metabolic needs or internal structures to circulate fluids. In general, aerobic bacteria “breathe” by diffusion, but they often position themselves in oxygen-rich environments (near air-water interfaces, in our lungs, etc.). The efficiency of aerobic metabolism also meant less waste per ATP – aerobes fully oxidize organic carbon to CO₂ and H₂O, which probably simplified waste management. Overall, introducing oxygen as their “fuel combuster” was the key respiratory innovation, not a new organ but a new gas and set of enzymes. Over time, some aerobes became obligate (cannot survive without O₂), whereas others remained facultative (could switch between aerobic respiration and fermentation). This flexibility is controlled by sensors (like an oxygen-sensing repressor that switches metabolism genes on/off). So, in terms of respiratory systems: aerobes didn’t develop lungs, they developed cytochrome oxidases and efficient respiratory pathways, and behavior to seek out oxygen.
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Versatile and often extracellular digestion. Many aerobic bacteria became decomposers in ecosystems – armed with enzymes to digest complex organic matter that anaerobes left behind. With the oxidative power of oxygen, they could break down tough molecules like lignin or recalcitrant polymers. Aerobic soil bacteria (e.g., Streptomyces) secrete a cocktail of enzymes into the environment (proteases, cellulases, chitinases) to digest dead organisms, then absorb the resulting monomers. Some aerobic bacteria are predators on other bacteria – they release enzymes or even drills (like Bdellovibrio bores into Gram-negative bacteria and devours them from inside-out). Pathogenic aerobes often secrete toxins and enzymes to break host tissues (for nutrition). So we see an expansion in “digestive” strategies: outside-the-cell digestion is common, followed by absorption of nutrients. Additionally, oxygen allows complete oxidation of nutrients internally (via Krebs cycle), so aerobes can thrive on smaller concentrations of food – they “burn” it fully. Certain aerobes also developed storage inclusions (like PHB granules or glycogen) to bank nutrients when in excess, for use when scarce – a metabolic strategy akin to an organism storing fat. Overall, though they remain single-celled, aerobic bacteria exhibit a more aggressive and varied approach to obtaining nutrients: they can scavenge or actively decompose a wide range of organic substrates. There is no “stomach,” but in a colony of bacteria on say a leaf, the collective secretion of digestive enzymes and subsequent absorption by the community functions like an external gut. Moreover, aerobes in symbiosis (like gut bacteria in animals) contribute to digestion by breaking down compounds the host cannot, effectively acting as part of a digestive system for larger organisms. But from the bacteria’s perspective, they are simply feeding by absorption after enzymatic breakdown, as has been the mode since prokaryotes began – just now with O₂, the menu of what can be digested and the energy yield from it is much larger.
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Active expulsion and detoxification. Aerobic metabolism generates reactive oxygen species (ROS) as byproducts (superoxide, peroxide). Aerobic bacteria thus required robust detox systems – producing enzymes like superoxide dismutase, catalase, and peroxidases to neutralize ROS. These enzymes are like an excretory system for toxic byproducts of metabolism, converting them into harmless substances (oxygen and water). In terms of waste, aerobes breathe out CO₂ which diffuses away; nitrogen waste often is excreted as ammonium or other soluble forms. Because they often fully oxidize their food, the end products (CO₂, H₂O) are readily lost by diffusion, meaning less problematic waste accumulation than fermenters (which accumulate acids or alcohol). However, living in oxygen means dealing with potential toxins like heavy metals in oxidative states; many aerobes have efflux pumps that actively pump out toxic metal ions or antibiotics (the latter being either waste of other microbes or signals – aerobic soil bacteria frequently encounter antibiotics in microbial warfare and evolved pumps to expel them). They also have membrane transporters to export excess metabolites – for instance, if a metabolic intermediate builds up, some bacteria can secrete it. Another adaptation in some aerobic bacteria is the microcompartment or organelle-like structures to isolate certain metabolic processes that produce dangerous intermediates (e.g., Nitrosomonas have carboxysomes for CO₂ fixation and annamox bacteria have an “annamoxosome” to handle toxic hydrazine). While these are more metabolic, they aid in containing and neutralizing waste internally. Osmoregulation remains vital; many aerobic bacteria inhabit fluctuating environments (like soil drying/wetting), so they accumulate osmoprotectant molecules or expel ions to maintain balance. Some can form cysts when desiccated, reducing metabolic waste production to near zero until water returns. Summarily, aerobic bacteria excel at waste management via enzymatic neutralization and active export. They pump out what they don’t need and break down harmful compounds internally before they can do damage. The fundamental excretory organ is still the cell membrane and the suite of proteins embedded in it that transport wastes out. If conditions overwhelm these systems (e.g., too much waste or salt), the bacteria will either move (if motile) to a better locale, form a resistant state, or die. But as a group, aerobic bacteria are quite hardy in waste management, contributing to them being successful in diverse, sometimes polluted environments (indeed, many are used in bioremediation to degrade pollutants).
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Enhanced innate and competitive defenses. Aerobic bacteria often live in competitive, oxygen-rich niches where both microbes and host organisms (if pathogenic) exert pressures. As a result, they have evolved potent defense/offense mechanisms. Many soil-dwelling aerobic bacteria in the genus Streptomyces and others produce antibiotics – chemical weapons that inhibit competitors. These antibiotics also double as a defense: by killing or suppressing nearby microbes (including fungi and other bacteria), they reduce competition for nutrients. The producing bacterium is immune to its own antibiotic thanks to specific resistance genes (a form of self-immunity). Pathogenic aerobes, on the other hand, evolved ways to evade host immune systems: e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis has a waxy cell envelope that resists destruction by macrophages (analogous to armor against the host’s immune “attacks”). Many aerobic bacteria have biofilm formation ability – by living in a biofilm, they embed themselves in a protective matrix that antibiotics or immune cells have trouble penetrating. This communal defense can be likened to an “immune system” of the colony, where the matrix and the outer layer of cells sacrificially protect inner cells. At the molecular level, all the earlier-mentioned systems (restriction enzymes, CRISPR) are found in many aerobes, providing defense against phages. Actually, with oxygen present, the biosphere saw a proliferation of phages (viruses) and plasmids; aerobes often carry multiple toxin-antitoxin modules on their plasmids that ensure plasmid maintenance and can induce dormancy under stress – sort of a programmed self-defense against severe conditions (rather than external threats). Also, stress responses in aerobes (heat shock, oxidative stress response) are well-developed, allowing them to survive hostile conditions like spikes in temperature or oxygen radical exposure, which is a resilience mechanism analogous to immune stress responses in higher organisms. In summary, aerobic bacteria’s “immune system” is a combination of chemical warfare (antibiotics, siderophores to sequester iron away from others), physical barriers (biofilms, capsules), and genetic systems (restriction-modification, CRISPR, DNA repair). They still lack anything like immune cells or adaptive immunity beyond CRISPR, but as single cells they are arguably better defended than their anaerobic predecessors because they had to be, in the cutthroat oxygenated world.
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Cell walls, capsules, and multicellular structures. Aerobic bacteria keep the proven design of a peptidoglycan cell wall for shape and support. Some, like Gram-positive aerobes (e.g., Bacillus), have very thick walls that allow them to live in drier, more variable environments, including forming endospores with additional protective layers. Many aerobic bacteria also secrete extracellular polysaccharides to form a capsule or biofilm matrix; when these bacteria aggregate, the matrix can serve as a shared exoskeleton, holding colonies together on a surface (like dental plaque has a scaffolding of polymers that bacteria adhere to). Additionally, certain aerobic bacteria develop multicellular fruiting bodies or hyphae – these come with structural differentiation. Streptomyces (an aerobic actinobacterium) forms a mycelium in soil – a network of filaments that behave much like fungal mycelium. This network provides support and penetration into organic material; it even produces aerial hyphae that stand upright and produce spores, demonstrating significant structural specialization (the aerial hyphae are supported by turgor and a rigid cell wall, acting like bristles). Myxobacteria form stalked fruiting bodies where many cells pile up into a column – the bottom of the column (stalk) comprises dead or metabolically sacrificed cells that form a rigid support for the spores at the top. Those stalk cells often undergo changes like forming a thick cell wall, making the structure stiff. These instances show incipient “skeletal” functions in bacterial groups: some cells or secreted materials form a supporting framework for others. Still, in a single bacterium, the cell wall remains the main skeletal element maintaining shape. For motile aerobes, the flagellar structure (basal body anchored in the wall) and the chemoreceptor arrays (which cluster at cell poles, often attached to the inner membrane and perhaps peptidoglycan) might be considered internal scaffolds that organize cell function. Flagella especially require a firm anchor – which the cell wall provides – showing the synergy between structure and function. In essence, the skeletal system in aerobic bacteria ranges from the simple rigid cell wall of solitary cells to the communal frameworks of biofilms and fruiting bodies, enabling them to conquer a variety of niches (from free-swimming in water to crusty growths on rocks to fuzzy colonies in soil).
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Muscular System (Movement): Swift and directed movement. Many aerobic bacteria are highly motile – think of Pseudomonas or Bacillus species with several flagella allowing them to swim rapidly toward nutrients or away from harm. With abundant ATP from aerobic respiration, these bacteria can power strong flagellar motors; some are among the fastest bacteria in terms of body lengths per second. Swarming motility is a phenomenon in some aerobic bacteria (like Bacillus subtilis, Proteus mirabilis) where they differentiate into elongated, hyper-flagellated swarm cells and move across surfaces in coordinated packs – a bit like multicellular migration. This is an advanced “muscular” behavior: groups of bacteria pushing collectively, aided by flagella and slime, to travel and colonize new territory. Another example: Myxobacteria (aerobic) glide on surfaces and do so cooperatively, even displaying rippling patterns as they move in waves – this coordination is driven by cell-cell contact and signals, akin to how muscle cells coordinate contraction (though in myxobacteria it’s each cell moving itself, but with alignment to neighbors). Aerobic conditions also allowed larger bacteria with unusual motility: e.g., Spirochetes have internal flagella (axial filaments) that let them corkscrew through viscous media; pathogens like Treponema and Borrelia use this to move through host tissues. In essence, the “muscular” repertoire of bacteria expanded – flagella got refined, pili-based twitching became common for crawling on surfaces (especially in biofilm-forming aerobes), and collective movement emerged. These are all protein-based motility systems functioning at microscopic scale, but they parallel muscular functions by generating force and directional movement. No muscle fibers or actin-myosin complexes yet – those come with eukaryotes – but flagellar rotation and pilus retraction in large groups can achieve feats analogous to muscular movement (for instance, bacterial swarms can overcome surface tension and spread across agar, a kind of strength in numbers). Summarily, aerobic bacteria are exemplars of efficient, adaptable locomotion in the microbial world, achieving impressive navigational feats (chemotaxis in 3D gradients, swarming across solid surfaces) with their evolved motility organelles.
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Endocrine System (Regulation): Chemical signaling for multicellular coordination. In oxygen-rich environments, bacteria often found themselves in dense communities and had to coordinate behaviors – this led to elaborate quorum sensing systems. Many aerobic bacteria produce quorum sensing molecules (like AHLs in Gram-negatives, peptides in Gram-positives) that accumulate and, upon reaching a threshold concentration, trigger a suite of changes: biofilm formation, virulence factor production, bioluminescence (in Vibrio bacteria), sporulation, etc. This is strikingly analogous to hormonal regulation in that a secreted molecule alters developmental state or behavior of the whole population once it hits a critical level. For example, Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses quorum sensing to regulate biofilm maturation and production of enzymes – one can liken the quorum signal to a hormone that says “we have a crowd now, behave like a community.” In Bacillus subtilis, different subpopulations communicate during biofilm formation and sporulation; they even have a cannibalism toxin system where, under stress, some cells produce a toxin that kills some siblings – releasing nutrients to delay sporulation in the survivors. This toxin production is regulated by signaling peptides and corresponds to a coordinated developmental decision (again akin to hormonal regulation of tissue fate, albeit in a bacterial context). Internally, aerobic bacteria have complex networks of transcription factors (e.g., Fur for iron metabolism, SoxRS for oxidative stress, etc.) that act like an endocrine web inside the cell – sensing small molecules (like iron, or superoxide) and globally adjusting gene expression. Notably, Caulobacter crescentus (an aerobic aquatic bacterium) undergoes a cell cycle with different cell types (a motile “swarmer” and a sessile “stalked” cell) each division; this differentiation is tightly regulated by internal signaling pathways (second messengers like cyclic di-GMP) which are reminiscent of how hormones regulate life-cycle transitions in higher organisms (though all within one cell’s lifetime here). So, while still far from having organs or hormones traveling through a bloodstream, aerobic bacteria make extensive use of chemical signals for both intercellular communication and intracellular regulation – effectively serving the role of hormones to coordinate behavior, development, and group dynamics. These signaling systems were a stepping stone to the more complex endocrine systems seen in multicellular life.
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Reproductive System (Replication): No sexual reproduction, but gene exchange persists; some life-cycle complexity. Aerobic bacteria remain asexual in reproduction – a single cell divides into two. However, the presence of oxygen often correlates with environments where gene exchange is rampant (soil, surfaces, hosts). Conjugation (bacterial “mating”) was notably characterized in aerobic bacteria (E. coli experiments, etc.), where plasmids carrying genes (like the F plasmid) transfer between cells via a pilus. This is not sexual reproduction in the eukaryotic sense (no formation of a zygote; it’s one-way DNA donation), but it creates partial genetic mixing. Additionally, transduction (virus-mediated gene transfer) and natural transformation (uptake of free DNA) are common among aerobes – for instance, Acinetobacter can take up DNA from its environment (which could be considered akin to a form of gene uptake “eating genes” from dead cells). All these lead to genetic recombination and variability. On the multicellular front, certain aerobic bacteria exhibit life-cycle stages: we discussed how Myxobacteria form fruiting bodies – that’s a reproductive cycle culminating in spores (which are dormant until conditions improve). Bacillus and Clostridium (facultative or aerobic) form endospores – again a developmental process: one cell divides asymmetrically into a mother cell and a spore, the mother cell sacrifices itself to encase the spore. This is a form of cell differentiation and propagation of the species (spores surviving harsh times to germinate later). While not sexual, it’s a complex reproduction-related process requiring tight regulation and coordination (like an embryo formation in simplistic terms). So, aerobic bacteria have begun to diversify their reproductive strategies: simple binary fission for regular growth, but spores for survival, and exchange of genetic material horizontally for innovation. True sexual cycles with meiosis and gametes still do not exist in bacteria. The ability to use oxygen didn’t directly trigger sex; however, the oxidative environment likely increased DNA damage (via ROS) and perhaps promoted mechanisms like recombinational repair (some bacteria take up DNA to repair their own, etc.), which is tangentially related to the origin of sexual recombination in the distant sense. For now, reproduction is mainly about making clones (fast and efficient) and sometimes specialized resting stages – with remarkable sophistication in timing and structure for some species, but no males or females or fertilization events.
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Integumentary System (Protection): Rugged cell envelopes and community “skins.” Aerobic bacteria often confront more variable environments (presence of oxidants, desiccation, immune systems of hosts), so their integuments are often especially reinforced. Many have capsules – thick, gummy polysaccharide layers – that not only help in evading host immunity but also in preventing drying out and buffering external changes. For example, Bacillus anthracis (which is aerobic) has a proteinaceous capsule that protects it from phagocytosis. Soil bacteria like Azotobacter secrete copious slime to encyst themselves in a protective covering when needed. Some aquatic aerobes have surface layers (S-layers) of protein that act like chain mail. Pathogens may have lipopolysaccharide in their outer membrane that confers resistance to bile salts and complements – this can be seen as a chemical shield. In biofilms, the outer layer of the biofilm (produced by aerobic bacteria in many cases) acts as a shared integument – it can absorb damage (like antibiotics or shear forces) and keep the community intact. The production of pigments by many aerobic bacteria not only serves immune evasion (some pigments scavenge ROS from host defenses) but also protects against UV light – these pigments often deposit in the cell envelope, giving coloration (e.g., Serratia marcescens produces a red pigment prodigiosin, Micrococcus luteus a yellow carotenoid). These are analogous to skin pigmentation protecting against UV. In some cases, aerobic bacteria orchestrate multicellular protective structures: Myxobacteria fruiting bodies have an outer layer of cells that die to form a sturdy casing for the spores inside – essentially a differentiated “integument” of dead cells covering the survivors. So, from the perspective of systems, we see an integumentary trend: multiple layers (membrane, wall, capsule, biofilm matrix) to defend and contain the bacteria. This is still microscopic – not a true skin with multiple cell types – but in function, it serves similarly. For instance, an encapsulated bacterium in a host is somewhat analogous to an organism with thick skin and mucus coat resisting external assault. In sum, aerobic bacteria retained the fundamental integument of prokaryotes (membrane + wall) but augmented it with additional coatings (capsules, S-layers), pigments, and communal matrices, making them exceptionally well-protected and giving a hint of specialized “outer tissues” (though not true tissues) that later multicellular life would refine.
Aerobic Bacteria (O₂-utilizing).Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: None internally. Even when aerobic bacteria form complex colonies or fruiting bodies, they lack a lymphatic system. There is no internal fluid circulation separate from external flow. If in a host, they may end up in the host’s lymphatic system (as pathogens moving through lymph), but within themselves, no such thing exists. They also do not produce mobile cells that patrol for infection (each bacterium is its own immune defender). The concept of a lymphatic system – a network to return interstitial fluid and participate in immunity – only arises with multiple-cell layered organisms with a circulatory system. Aerobic bacterial communities rely on diffusion through their biofilm matrix to distribute nutrients and remove waste; if an immune threat (like a phage) attacks part of the colony, those cells might die but neighbors can survive – there’s no dedicated immune fluid to relocate “immune factors” like in higher animals. So, as before, no lymphatic vessels, no lymph nodes. The external water or host fluids remain the medium that carries things around for bacteria. Even in pseudo-multicellular arrangements like Streptomyces filaments, movement of fluid is either through the environment or simple streaming in the hyphae – not an independent lymph system. In conclusion, despite aerobes reaching new heights of single-cell complexity and forming primitive multicellular assemblies, a true lymphatic system is still absent; that awaited the advent of large multicellular organisms with closed circulatory systems (where leaking of plasma created a need for lymphatics).

Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Nervous System (Signal Response): Internalized signaling and beginning of excitability. The first eukaryote (an archaeal host merged with a bacterium turned mitochondrion) had no nerves, but it did develop far more elaborate internal communication. With a nucleus separating transcription from translation, regulation became more complex (mRNAs must be transported out, etc.). Early eukaryotes evolved calcium signaling: they sequester Ca²⁺ in organelles and release it as a second messenger, coordinating activities like muscle contraction (in later eukaryotes) or secretion. Even a single protozoan uses Ca²⁺ signals for processes like changing flagellar beat or triggering exocytosis of trichocysts (in ciliates). We also see the first membrane potentials: all cells have ionic gradients, but many protists can generate action potentials across their membrane (for instance, Paramecium fires a Ca²⁺-based action potential to reverse its cilia beating when it hits an obstacle). This is analogous to a very primitive nervous impulse. Moreover, within the eukaryotic cell, vesicle trafficking is guided by molecular signals (Rab GTPases, etc.), ensuring that internal communication directs proteins to correct organelles. So, while there is still no multi-cell nervous system, the single eukaryotic cell carries out rapid and complex signaling internally (and can respond to environmental stimuli in a more integrated way). If it was motile, it likely had a sophisticated chemotaxis and phototaxis ability orchestrated by networks of signaling proteins and ion channels. Thus, the “nervous system” at this stage is the intricate web of signaling pathways inside one cell – a leap beyond prokaryotes in scale – and the ability to generate electric responses to stimuli, foreshadowing true neurons.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Intracellular transport and compartmentalization (proto-circulation). The ancestral unicellular eukaryote was much larger than typical bacteria and filled with organelles. Diffusion alone is not enough for efficient internal transport in such a big cell, so it evolved a cytoskeleton with motor proteins (like kinesin and dynein) that ferry vesicles and organelles along microtubule “tracks”. This means, for example, nutrients taken in at the cell membrane could be packaged into vesicles and actively carried to lysosomes for digestion, or waste vesicles carried to the membrane for exocytosis. This is analogous to an internal circulation system: vesicular traffic moves substances around in a directed way, similar to how a bloodstream moves cargo in a body (albeit without a pumping heart – the motors provide the motive force). The cytoskeleton also enables cytoplasmic streaming (especially seen in large cells like algae or fungi): an active flow of cytoplasm that distributes metabolites. So within this single cell, there was a micro-transport network ensuring all parts of the cell got what they needed. Of course, there is still no circulatory system in the multicellular sense – there’s just one cell – but this cell likely could not survive by diffusion alone given its complexity, and thus internal transport processes were key. When it comes to sharing resources between cells, since we’re only at one cell, that’s moot; but this eukaryote is the precursor to multicellular lineages where circulatory systems will evolve. As a cell with mitochondria, it also had to distribute those mitochondria around – which it does via cytoskeletal movement, ensuring energy supply is circulated. In essence, the eukaryotic cell evolved an active internal distribution network – a critical stepping stone to the eventual invention of circulatory systems in multicellular organisms.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Efficient aerobic powerhouse. With mitochondria integrated, this eukaryote enjoyed vastly higher ATP production. Mitochondria carry out oxidative phosphorylation internally, so the cell no longer relies on its surface area for respiration as much – each mitochondrion is like a microscopic “lung” consuming O₂ and making energy. Gas exchange for the cell as a whole still occurs by diffusion across its outer membrane (and possibly across internalized membranes if it’s large), but because mitochondria are so efficient, the cell could afford to grow larger and have a higher metabolism without running out of energy. O₂ uptake likely increased – these cells would be avid consumers of oxygen given the mitochondria. Many such eukaryotes lived in O₂-rich environments (like shallow waters post-Great Oxidation). Internally, they needed to get oxygen to each mitochondrion; in very large single cells, cytoplasmic streaming helps move dissolved gases, but also mitochondria can move toward areas of higher O₂ if needed. The key respiratory innovation was that respiration became compartmentalized in mitochondria, freeing the rest of the cell to specialize. Because mitochondria generate ROS (reactive oxygen species), the cell also evolved better antioxidant defenses (some of which might be inherited from the mitochondrial symbiont). So catalase, SOD, etc., are present in the cell cytoplasm and mitochondria to protect against oxidative damage. In summary, the “respiratory system” is now an organelle: mitochondria serving as internal respiration units, analogous to tiny distributed lungs, dramatically boosting energy extractionucl.ac.uk. Gas exchange per se is still via diffusion through the cell’s surface, which suffices for single cells. (Interestingly, some large protozoans have cytoplasmic hemoglobin-like molecules to bind oxygen – a foreshadowing of blood pigments – to facilitate intracellular oxygen transport; for instance, some ciliates and algae have molecules to store O₂ for dark periods.) But broadly, acquiring mitochondria was like getting a high-performance furnace with internal pipelines – respiration became an internal affair within organelles, enabling cellular complexity and higher ATP budgets.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Phagocytosis – the first “mouth.” One of the hallmark capabilities of early mitochondriate eukaryotes was phagocytosis – the ability to engulf solid particles or whole other cells by extending the cell membrane around them and internalizing them into a vesicle (phagosome). This was a profound leap in “digestive” strategy. It means our single eukaryotic cell could actively hunt and eat bacteria or detritus, rather than only absorbing pre-digested molecules. Once ingested into a phagosome, the cell could fuse it with a lysosome (an organelle containing digestive enzymes) to form a phagolysosome where the prey is broken down – essentially an intracellular stomach. This required many innovations: a flexible cytoskeleton (actin) to deform the membrane, receptors to recognize food particles, and an array of digestive enzymes (proteases, nucleases, lipases) packaged in lysosomes. Because of phagocytosis, the eukaryote could access nutrients unreachable to smaller cells, fueling its larger size and supporting the costly mitochondria-containing structure. Some early eukaryotes might have still also harbored the ability to absorb dissolved nutrients across the membrane (like their ancestors), but phagocytosis gave them an edge in nutrient-poor environments by consuming biomass directly. Additionally, this eukaryote likely had a complete endomembrane system (ER and Golgi), which produces enzymes and processes food vacuoles. The Golgi apparatus can be likened to a digestive gland producing lysosomal enzymes, and the lysosomes to small “intestines” in the cell. All digestion occurs within membrane-bound compartments, preventing uncontrolled degradation of the cell itself. Once nutrients are broken down, they are transported out of the lysosome into the cytosol where mitochondria can use them. Waste material (indigestible bits) can be expelled by exocytosis (the phagolysosome fuses back to the membrane and dumps residual debris out) – akin to defecation on a cellular level. So, in summation, the first mitochondriate eukaryote had a true digestive system at the cellular scale: a mouth (phagocytic membrane), a stomach (phagolysosome), digestive secretions (lysosomal enzymes), and elimination (exocytosis). This predatory ability is what likely allowed the ancestral proto-eukaryote to capture the bacterial endosymbiont in the first place (leading to mitochondria), and thereafter, it remained a key feature of many protists. (Some descendants later became purely autotrophic or osmotrophic and lost phagocytosis, but phagocytosis was likely present in LECA – the Last Eukaryotic Common Ancestor.)
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Organelle-based waste management. In the first eukaryotic cells, excretion became more structured. Contractile vacuoles likely evolved in freshwater protozoa to pump out excess water (to counteract osmotic influx). These vacuoles fill with water and then merge with the membrane to expel it, functioning like a simple kidney. The presence of a cytoskeleton and motor proteins allowed the cell to position the contractile vacuole and control its filling/expulsion cycle. Meanwhile, metabolic waste (CO₂, ammonia) can diffuse out or be transported out by membrane proteins, as in bacteria. However, eukaryotes often convert ammonia (which is toxic) to less toxic forms or sequester it in vacuoles until release. Some protists have microbodies (peroxisomes) dedicated to certain wasteful or harmful byproducts – e.g., peroxisomes break down fatty acids and toxins, generating hydrogen peroxide which they then decompose with catalase. This compartmentalization keeps dangerous reactions away from the rest of the cell. Osmoregulation in general was improved: beyond contractile vacuoles, eukaryotes maintain ion pumps on their plasma membrane (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPases in later eukaryotes) to regulate salt balance. The nuclear membrane also segregates transcription and translation, which indirectly helps manage macromolecular waste (e.g., improperly made mRNAs can be degraded in the nucleus, etc.). If this first eukaryote was a heterotroph, after digesting prey in lysosomes, it would expel indigestible remnants by exocytosis – a clear excretory process. The cell might also have stored certain waste in residual bodies if immediate expulsion wasn’t possible. All of this is analogous to having rudimentary excretory organs: contractile vacuole as a kidney/bladder for water, lysosome as a digestive waste processor, and peroxisome as a liver for detoxification. Notably, the separation of metabolic processes into organelles reduced interference and allowed specialized handling of byproducts. For example, mitochondria release CO₂ internally which diffuses out – if the cell is large, it may even have cytoplasmic circulatory flow to get that CO₂ to the surface. Summarily, early eukaryotes had a much more controlled internal environment than prokaryotes. They could actively pump and package wastes for removal, and thus maintain homeostasis in varying conditions. This protist-level excretory system was critical for managing a complex, high-turnover metabolism.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Innate immunity goes cellular – predation as defense. The advent of phagocytosis not only served nutrition but also is essentially an immune mechanism: eukaryotes could engulf and destroy would-be pathogens. Early single-celled eukaryotes rarely got “infected” by others (though there were viruses and possibly some intracellular bacterial parasites), but their phagocytic capability set the stage for the evolution of dedicated immune cells in multicellular life. Meanwhile, within one cell, having mitochondria and many organelles required quality control: eukaryotes evolved autophagy, a process where they sequester damaged organelles or protein aggregates in a double-membrane autophagosome and then fuse it with lysosomes to degrade the contents. This is like an immune system for the cell’s interior – removing “self” debris and potentially invasive particles. In terms of molecular immunity, eukaryotes lost CRISPR (that’s prokaryote-specific), but they gained the RNA interference (RNAi) pathway: small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) and associated proteins that can target and slice foreign RNA (like viral RNA). RNAi likely evolved as a defense against viruses and transposons – it’s present in many protists.
