So our first mitochondriate eukaryote probably had some form of RNAi, given how conserved it is, thus providing an adaptive-like immune mechanism (not based on memory of specific sequences except those encountered and processed during infection) that silences invader genes. Another cellular immune aspect is the presence of peroxisomes and oxidative enzymes: eukaryotes can produce reactive oxygen or nitrogen species in controlled ways to kill engulfed prey or microbes (this is exactly what later macrophages do – a direct extension of single-cell protist predation). Also, eukaryotic cells have stress responses to infection – e.g. interferon response in multicellular context has roots in single-cell responses to dsRNA. Summing up: the unicellular eukaryote’s immune system was cellular digestion and molecular silencing. It could physically eat intruders and chemically dismantle foreign nucleic acids. DNA repair and checkpoint mechanisms also improved, preventing the cell from propagating if DNA was damaged (which is like an immune response to internal errors). While it had no separate immune cells or lymphatic support, every early eukaryotic cell was its own immune system, armed with an array of defensive tools far beyond those of prokaryotes.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Endoskeleton and dynamic shape. The first eukaryote had a fully developed cytoskeleton with microtubules, microfilaments (actin), and likely intermediate filaments (though those might have developed a bit later, they are present in most eukaryotes). This internal network provided not just transport (as above) but also mechanical support. Microtubules formed organizing centers (the centrosome with centrioles) to orchestrate cell division (mitotic spindle) – ensuring chromosomes were segregated properly. That mitotic spindle is an internal scaffold that temporarily becomes the “skeleton” during cell division, physically pulling chromosomes apart. Actin filaments underlie the plasma membrane in the cell cortex, allowing the cell to maintain or change shape, and to form structures like filopodia or lamellipodia for movement or engulfment. These filaments, along with myosin motors, can contract – a primitive muscle-like function used in processes like cytokinesis (contractile ring pinching the cell in two). The eukaryotic cell often lacks a rigid cell wall (many early ones, especially the ones that could phagocytose, would have had just a flexible membrane without a wall – more like animal cells). Without a wall, the cytoskeleton was solely responsible for structural integrity and shape – it’s an endo-skeleton in a literal sense. Some early eukaryotes (especially if we consider the ancestor of plants/fungi) might later evolve cell walls, but the initial one likely did not (as phagocytosis and cell motility were crucial). Instead, it may have secreted an extracellular matrix or glycocalyx for protection, but not a solid wall. This gave it plasticity: it could be amoeboid or have various shapes. Microtubules also formed structures like flagella and cilia – the eukaryotic flagellum is a bundle of microtubules (axoneme) powered by dynein motors, encased in the cell membrane. LECA (last common ancestor of eukaryotes) is thought to have had one or two flagella (and associated basal bodies/centrioles)ucl.ac.ukucl.ac.uk. The flagellum requires mechanical support of the microtubules and exact architecture (9+2 arrangement), which is a skeletal structure at the cellular level allowing movement. Summarily, the eukaryote’s skeletal system was multi-faceted: an internal framework (microtubules/actin) that maintained cell shape, enabled division, and built motile appendages, and possibly a lack of external wall which meant the cell itself could be thought of as “soft-bodied” with an inside skeleton. This is analogous to how animals have internal skeletons and no rigid outer shells – these cells were more like tiny animals in that sense, versus the “exoskeleton” cell wall of bacteria. With this internal skeleton, the cell could achieve feats of strength and shape change that were impossible for prokaryotes – for example, extend pseudopods to crawl, or engulf large prey, or simply maintain a large cellular size without collapsing. It’s the precursor to the true skeletal systems in multicellular organisms, which in many cases simply scale up the principles of tension (actin) and compression (microtubules/bones) that even this single cell used.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Muscular System (Movement): True motility organelles (flagella, cilia, pseudopods). The mitochondriate eukaryote is the first cell with eukaryotic flagella (undulipodia) – which are fundamentally different from bacterial flagella. These are long, whip-like extensions of the cell containing an array of microtubules. By whipping back and forth, they can push or pull the cell through fluid. If our ancestral eukaryote had a flagellum, it could swim actively – an enormous advantage for finding food or mates (when sex later evolved). Cilia are essentially shorter flagella, but in unicellular eukaryotes with many of them (like a hypothetical ciliated ancestor or later ciliates), they act like hundreds of tiny oars for very precise and versatile movement, including the ability to rotate, translate, and even generate feeding currents. In addition, these cells could move via amoeboid motion: using actin and myosin to flow their cytoplasm and extend parts of the cell (pseudopodia) to crawl on surfaces or capture food. Amoeboid movement is actually quite fast on surfaces and allows navigation in complex environments (like slithering between grains of sediment). Thus, this cell effectively had muscle-like proteins (actin-myosin) working at the cell cortex to deform the cell for movement. It’s no coincidence that the proteins used (tubulin, dynein, actin, myosin) are the evolutionary precursors of muscle fibers and motors in multicellular creatures. The coordination of flagellar beating involves calcium and other signals, similarly to how muscle contraction is regulated – albeit at a single-cell level. Moreover, these cells could have chemo- and phototaxis that directs their movement: for instance, a photosynthetic flagellate (if it later acquired chloroplasts) will use an eyespot to steer toward light (as mentioned with eyespots) – that coupling of sensor to motor is akin to a neuromuscular reflex (though done with simple biochemical pathways). In sum, by having flagella and actin-powered shape change, the eukaryote possessed a dedicated locomotor toolkit – a true muscular analog. It could swim faster and navigate more complexly than any bacterium (though bacteria are faster in body lengths/sec, the eukaryote’s absolute speed and directional control in many cases surpass what tiny bacteria can do, especially in viscous conditions where flagellar size helps). This was critical for predation (chasing prey) and dispersal. So, the muscular system at this stage is intracellular and mechanical: microtubule motors for flagellar bending, actin-myosin for contraction, both energy-intensive but supported by abundant ATP from mitochondria. This synergy of energy supply and motility machinery allowed these cells to be the first true predators and explorers at the microscopic scale.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Endocrine System (Regulation): Hormone-like cell signaling and cell cycle control. Inside this first eukaryotic cell, regulation took on new levels. It had a nucleus with a cell cycle (phases G1, S, G2, M) controlled by cyclin and cyclin-dependent kinases – chemicals that rise and fall in concentration to trigger DNA replication or mitosis. These cyclins are analogous to hormones in that they are produced and degraded in a timed fashion and influence the cell’s “developmental” progression (here, the cycle). Additionally, if the cell engaged in any form of sexual reproduction (let’s assume not yet – sex is considered to have evolved later, but some evidence suggests LECA might have had meiosis), then it would have signaling pathways to induce mating or meiosis. Many protists release pheromone-like signals to find partners or to trigger mating reactions. Even in asexual protists, environmental sensing triggers (like starvation leading to cyst formation) involve signaling cascades that could be seen as endocrine-like: e.g. accumulation of a stress molecule inside triggers expression of cyst-specific genes. For example, Dictyostelium (a social amoeba) uses cAMP as a signal to aggregate – cells release cAMP pulses that attract others; that’s a clear chemical messenger coordinating behavior among cells (though Dictyostelium is multicellular in that stage, it shows how single cells use messengers to act in concert). For our single-cell eukaryote, the analog would be perhaps quorum sensing among eukaryotes or cues to encyst or divide. Eukaryotes also invented steroid and lipid signaling internally: they produce molecules like diacylglycerol, IP3, calcium, cAMP as second messengers to amplify signals from receptors (e.g., detecting a nutrient might lead to a signaling cascade that causes the cell to grow faster – much like a hormone telling a tissue to grow). Also, protein kinases in eukaryotes diversified greatly – allowing integration of many pathways (nutrient sensing, energy status sensing by AMPK, etc.). All these signaling molecules and kinases serve similar roles to hormones and hormone receptors: coordinating the physiology of the cell in response to internal and external cues. If this cell were in an environment with others of its kind, they might coordinate via sex pheromones or aggregation signals (as some extant protists do). So, broadly speaking, the eukaryote had a primitive endocrine system at the intracellular level and potential beginnings of intercellular signaling. It’s the prototype that in multicellular forms will become actual hormones traveling between cells. For now, chemicals did not travel far – perhaps from one part of the cell to another (nucleus to cytoplasm) or in the environment to a neighboring cell. But this was enough to yield regulated responses akin to endocrine control: entry into dormancy, mating type switching, growth and division cycles, etc., all managed by chemical regulators.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Reproductive System (Replication): Asexual reproduction with mitosis, plus introduction of sex. The first eukaryotes reproduced predominantly by mitotic cell division – a much more complex process than binary fission. Mitosis ensured each daughter cell got an identical set of chromosomes from the separated nucleus. This process involved many “reproductive system” innovations: a mitotic spindle of microtubules, kinetochores on chromosomes, nuclear envelope breakdown and reformation, etc. It’s as if the cell built a whole apparatus (spindle = equivalent of a uterus?) to orchestrate proper division. The result was two daughter cells, akin to binary fission’s outcome but through a distinct mechanism. Now, crucially, eukaryotes also introduced sexual reproduction (meiosis and syngamy). While it’s debated exactly when sex arose, evidence suggests that LECA already had the genes for meiosis, meaning the ability to undergo a reduction division and form gamete-like cells that could fuse. If so, that implies our mitochondriate ancestor either had or soon evolved a sexual cycle. This would involve halving its chromosome number (meiosis), likely forming four haploid cells from one diploid, then those haploids could fuse in pairs to restore diploidy. The innovations here are staggering: pairing of homologous chromosomes, recombination (crossing over) between them (fostering genetic diversity), and cell fusion (where two cells’ membranes and nuclei merge). These events created true gametes (even if not named so then) and fertilization. Initially, gametes might have been isogamous (same size), just two cells of compatible type fusing. Sex allowed the mixing of genetic material between different lineages, speeding up evolution and clearing deleterious mutations via recombination. In terms of a “reproductive system,” this single-celled organism now had two modes: clonal reproduction via mitosis (analogous to vegetative propagation) and sexual reproduction via meiosis-fertilization. The sexual process required cellular differentiation (gametes vs. somatic phase) and timing (likely tied to stress or cell density). Regulatory pathways (possibly involving the aforementioned endocrine-like signals) would trigger meiosis or mating. This is the primordial version of having gonads and gametes – except all within one cell’s capabilities. We can think of the nucleus undergoing a switch to a meiotic program (like an ovary/testis generating gametes) and the cell then acting as a gamete that finds another to fuse with. Once multicellularity evolves, these processes become segregated into specialized cells, but at this stage, the one cell did it all. So, the early eukaryote’s reproductive system was the most advanced on Earth to date: it included both mitosis for growth and meiosis/fusion for sex, ensuring both the continuity of its lineage and the variability for adaptation. This dual capability is one of eukaryotes’ defining features. It’s worth noting some protists may have temporarily lost sex and just do mitosis, but the capacity was there from very early on.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Integumentary System (Protection): Flexible cell covering, extracellular matrix. Unlike its prokaryotic precursors, the first eukaryotic cell likely did not have a rigid cell wall (assuming it was phagocytic and motile). Instead, it was bounded by a plasma membrane supported by the cortical cytoskeleton. This gave it animal-cell-like properties: it was pliable and could change shape. As a result, it also became more vulnerable, but to compensate, eukaryotes developed other protective measures. One is the glycocalyx – a layer of carbohydrate-rich molecules on the cell surface (glycoproteins, glycolipids) which can protect the cell and help in recognition. Another is secreting an extracellular matrix (ECM) or capsule-like material. Many protists secrete mucilage or have a pellicle (in euglenoids, a pellicle of interlocking protein strips under the membrane provides both flexibility and support). Some early eukaryotes might have had scales or lorica (tiny mineral or organic scales on their surface) as additional armor; for instance, certain extant algae encase themselves in tiny silica scales (this likely came later, but shows the trend that eukaryotes often elaborate external coverings). If our ancestral eukaryote lived in water, UV radiation could damage it, so it may have retained pigmentation or developed melanin-like compounds to absorb harmful rays (some unicellular eukaryotes synthesize melanin in their cell wall or cyst walls). Over time, different lineages did different things: ancestors of plants/fungi reinstated a cell wall (cellulose or chitin) to protect and support, whereas the lineage leading to animals kept the soft membrane and instead relies on an ECM of collagen and other fibers for structural support when multicellular. But at the single-cell stage, likely a soft outer membrane with dynamic actin support was the main integument, allowing phagocytosis. This was partly offset by the presence of internal organelles handling threats (like lysosomes digesting invaders) and by behaviors (moving out of harm’s way). Some early eukaryotes might have harbored symbionts or pigments for protection, too. When we consider immune aspects: if an invader like a bacterium got past the membrane, the lysosome would handle it – which is an “integumentary” defense synergy with the immune function. The cell’s surface also had receptors and could shed and renew them, somewhat analogous to how skin sheds cells to remove attached pathogens. To summarize, the eukaryote’s integument was multi-component and dynamic: a fluid plasma membrane (with cholesterol now, which adds stability and flexibility) protected by a fuzz of carbohydrates (glycocalyx), sometimes supported by proteinaceous pellicles or scales, and capable of rapid repair (thanks to membrane flow and vesicle fusion). This is a very flexible protective strategy – it can seal wounds in the membrane quickly by exocytosis (handy if the membrane is punctured). As eukaryotes grew larger or formed colonies, some secreted slimy or hard coverings (e.g., algal colonies embedded in gelatin, or forams building calcium carbonate shells) – the first step toward specialized integument (like shells or skin in multicells). In the first single cell, though, the integument was essentially the cell membrane plus any immediately associated structures, which is the foundation from which all complex integuments (shells, skin, cuticle) in multicellular life would evolve.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria (First Eukar.Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: None (single cell). Still, as a lone cell, there was no concept of an internal body fluid separate from the environment – so no lymphatic system. All fluid was either cytosol (inside the cell) or outside water. If this eukaryote lived in a colony (some protists can form temporary colonies), the space between cells was just the environment or some shared gelatinous matrix; there were no dedicated vessels to move fluid. Lymphatic systems proper begin to appear in animals that have circulatory systems – their absence continues in all single-celled and most colonial microbes. However, one could stretch an analogy: the contractile vacuole in freshwater protists removes excess water (like lymphatics remove excess tissue fluid). But it’s an intracellular organelle, not a body-wide vessel network. So effectively, no lymphatic system existed in a single-celled eukaryote. Each cell managed its own internal fluid and dumped excess directly out. Immune functions (like engulfing invaders) were handled by the cell itself, not by mobile immune cells in a lymph. When multicellularity eventually arose in eukaryotes, circulatory systems evolved in some, and only then did lymphatics come into being to complement blood circulation. Our protozoan ancestor is far from that stage – it relies on direct exchange with its environment for all fluid balance and on internal mechanisms for immune defense. Hence, it does not require or possess any lymphatic vessels or nodes.

Eukaryote with Mitochondria & Chloroplas.Nervous System (Signal Response): Light sensing organelles – primitive vision. Once a eukaryotic cell acquired chloroplasts (from engulfing a cyanobacterium), it became imperative for it to seek light for photosynthesis. Many photosynthetic protists (like algae) developed a dedicated eyespot (stigma) as part of a light-sensing system. For example, a motile green alga has an eyespot – a pigmented organelle in or near the chloroplast – that shades a photoreceptor, so as the cell rotates, it can detect the direction of light and then the flagella steering is adjusted accordingly. This coupling of a photoreceptor signal to flagellar motor response is essentially a prototype of vision and neural response: the photoreceptor (often a rhodopsin-like molecule) triggers an electrical or chemical signal that influences the flagellar beating. Thus, the cell can swim toward optimal light (positive phototaxis) or away if it’s too intense (negative phototaxis). This is much more advanced than earlier light responses because it’s directional (requiring integration of signals as the cell rotates) and because it controls a locomotory organelle. We see here a sensory “organ” (eyespot) that is not just molecular but morphological. Aside from light, chloroplast-bearing eukaryotes also sense nutrients (they still need minerals like nitrate, phosphate) and may show chemotaxis for those when needed (though if fully autotrophic and motile, light is the main factor). Multicellular coordination isn’t relevant yet (still one cell), but within itself, this alga must coordinate chloroplast function with the rest of the cell’s needs – for instance, some have blue-light receptors that adjust the position of chloroplasts inside the cell to avoid photodamage or optimize light capture. All these signals – from eyespot to flagella, from chloroplast status to nucleus (e.g., chloroplast-to-nucleus retrograde signaling controlling gene expression) – needed integration. The cell likely had calcium signaling and other second messengers linking these sensory inputs to motor outputs. In effect, with both mitochondria and chloroplasts, the cell’s internal communication grew even more complex: it now regulated two types of energy organelles and responded to two environments (light vs. dark, nutrients in both). One could argue it’s developing separate “sensory modalities” (light for phototaxis, chemicals for chemotaxis) and integrating them – a task akin to a rudimentary nervous processing, albeit all inside one cell. Summarily, the nervous analog in this first alga was an integration of photoreception and other cues to modulate movement and internal metabolism. This was as close to a neuron as a single cell could get, using membrane potentials and signaling pathways to make “decisions” like moving toward light only when also low on internal sugar (thus needing photosynthesis).
Eukaryote with Mitochondria & Chloroplas.Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Cell-to-cell transport in simple multicellular forms. The first photosynthetic eukaryote might have been unicellular (like a single-celled alga), but soon these cells gave rise to colonial or simple multicellular algae. For instance, some green algae form small colonies where cells adhere in a matrix (e.g., Volvox forms spherical colonies with somatic and reproductive cells). In such colonial organisms, circulation of nutrients starts to be an issue – Volvox solves it by having cytoplasmic bridges between cells so that some nutrient sharing can occur, and the rolling motion of the colony helps move fluid around the cells on the inside. If we consider the step where a single alga became a multicellular seaweed (e.g., red or green algae later), those developed some crude internal transport: cell-to-cell connections (plasmodesmata in algae/plants) and differentiation between cells that gather nutrients (photosynthetic surface cells) and those that distribute or store them. Red algae, for example, have pit plugs connecting cells – while primarily structural, they allow some exchange. However, focusing on the first cell with chloroplast, it’s likely solitary or simple filamentous. Within the one cell, the same cytoskeletal transport exists as before (moving proteins, messenger RNAs, and metabolites around). The chloroplast itself often has to move inside the cell to optimize light capture or avoid excess light – this is achieved by the cytoskeleton towing chloroplasts within the cell, which is like an internal distribution of organelles to where they’re needed (kind of like moving “organs” within a body for best function, albeit on a small scale). Some large unicellular algae (like Acetabularia, a single-celled giant) rely on extensive cytoplasmic streaming to move nutrients from the chloroplast-rich cap to other parts – a clear circulatory function inside one cell. But our first chloroplast-bearing eukaryote was probably not that large. If it had flagella, the beating of flagella also creates water currents around the cell that help bring in CO₂ and nutrients and remove O₂ and waste – an external circulation analog. To sum up, no dedicated circulatory system yet, but in colonial forms, nascent intercellular transport appears (shared cytoplasm), and inside the cell, streaming and directed vesicle/organelle traffic continue to serve the role of distributing materials. Once algae became larger and multicellular, they indeed evolved more specialized transport (e.g., sieve elements in giant kelps for nutrient translocation, though that’s analogous to phloem rather than heart/blood). But at the stage of a single photosynthetic protist or simple colony, diffusion and cytoskeletal movement were enough to meet transport needs due to relatively small size and aquatic environment.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria & Chloroplas.Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Dual respiration and photosynthesis. This cell was capable of both releasing O₂ (from photosynthesis in chloroplasts) and consuming O₂ (in mitochondria). By day, it captured light and produced organic molecules and oxygen; by night, it respired those organics to stay alive. We have here the need for coordination between chloroplasts and mitochondria. Typically, such cells produce excess oxygen in light – much of which diffuses out (helping oxygenate the environment further). They also fix CO₂ into sugars. At night, they take in O₂ and release CO₂ via mitochondria. Gas exchange for the cell as a whole remained through the cell membrane by diffusion. However, an interesting twist is that oxygen produced in the chloroplasts can be directly used by mitochondria – reducing the need to take it from outside during daylight, and CO₂ produced by mitochondria can be re-fixed by chloroplasts when light is available. Some modern algae even time their processes so that during the day, mitochondria might run minimally (since the cell can get ATP from photosynthesis or at least has plenty of immediate energy), whereas at night, mitochondria ramp up using stored photosynthate. The integrated metabolism meant the cell had to avoid harmful conflicts: e.g., avoiding excessive oxygen radicals when both organelles are active (which they mitigate with antioxidants). Possibly, the chloroplast contributed its carbon-concentrating mechanisms to help gather CO₂ (many algae have Rubisco in pyrenoids within the chloroplast and use dissolved inorganic carbon pumps – effectively an internal “lung” improving CO₂ uptake for photosynthesis). So within one cell, the chloroplast membrane and associated pumps might concentrate CO₂ near Rubisco, while the mitochondria ensure O₂ is not building up too high (consuming some of it). In strong light, if sugar production exceeds what the cell needs, the cell can convert sugars to starch and store it (often within the chloroplast). At night, it will break that down for respiration – analogous to how animal livers store glycogen for later use. And any metabolic “exhaust” (like NH₃ from protein metabolism) can actually be re-used by chloroplasts to make new amino acids if there is enough energy. Also noteworthy: with chloroplasts, the cell could endure periods of scarcity of external food by making its own, which is a huge advantage and changed how it interacted with its environment (less dependent on finding prey, more on finding light). Summarily, respiration and photosynthesis were balanced in this cell. It was self-sustaining in daylight and only needed external minerals. Over evolutionary time, this balance would lead to diurnal cycles and maybe even division tied to day-night. But physically, still no lungs or gills – gas exchange by diffusion sufficed at the cellular level. Only when photosynthetic organisms became multicellular and large (like terrestrial plants) did they need specialized structures (stomata, etc.) for gas diffusion deep inside tissues. Our single cell didn’t have that constraint – as long as it could mix its cytoplasm or move in the water, all its parts got gas.
Eukaryote with Mitochondria & Chloroplas.Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Autotroph with supplemental feeding. The cell’s chloroplast allowed it to make organic carbon from CO₂ and light, so its primary “diet” became sunlight and inorganic nutrients (much like a plant). Its digestive system shifted: the chloroplast itself is like an internal “gut” that converts raw environmental inputs (sunlight, CO₂, water) into usable energy (sugars). It even has its own small genome and enzymes, but the host nucleus controls much of it. The cell likely retained the ability to feed heterotrophically as well – many algae can also uptake dissolved nutrients or even phagocytose if they are not strictly wall-encased. For instance, some algae are mixotrophic: in low light they might eat bacteria for energy. So this first photosynthetic eukaryote may have been capable of phagocytosis too (the ancestor had it, and unless it lost it immediately, it could still snack on other microbes to get nutrients like nitrogen or to get energy in dark conditions). Over time, some lineages specializing in autotrophy lost phagocytosis and developed cell walls (like plants did), but some kept both modes. Having chloroplasts, the cell had to acquire more inorganic nutrients: notably, nitrogen and phosphorus for building biomass. It would uptake nitrate or ammonia and phosphate via membrane transporters – essentially “digesting” inorganic matter. The assimilation of nitrate to amino groups requires energy and enzymes (in plants this happens in roots and leaves; in a unicell, it happens in the cytosol or chloroplast). So, the cell’s “digestion” included enzymatic pathways to incorporate these nutrients into organic molecules. Possibly, symbiosis can be considered: if the chloroplast endosymbiont came from a cyanobacterium, initially there might have been a period where the host and symbiont exchanged metabolites – a sort of internal digestion where the host provided some nutrients and the symbiont provided sugars until it became fully integrated as an organelle. This is analogous to having an endosymbiotic gut microbe aiding digestion, a theme that repeats in animals. Also, any inability to directly digest cellulose (for example, if it ate a plant fiber) might be circumvented by storing such vacuoles until finding light and making own energy. In short, the chloroplast made the cell predominantly self-feeding (autotrophic), reducing the emphasis on external digestion of organic matter. Instead, its “digestive organs” were chloroplasts capturing carbon and lysosomes still present for processing whatever it ingests or recycling internal components. One could say photosynthesis shifted the “digestive paradigm” from consuming others to producing food internally. This is akin to how herbivores rely on plants (here the cell is the plant). The cell also had to avoid digesting its chloroplast (since originally it was a captured bacterium). Mechanisms evolved to suppress the normal phagosome-lysosome fusion for that symbiont – effectively a special status for the chloroplast inside. That’s like evolving a protected organ that won’t be broken down – an adjustment in the cell’s internal digestive rules to accommodate a beneficial part. Thus, the cell’s overall nutrient acquisition strategy became twofold: photosynthesis for carbon/energy, absorption or phagocytosis for everything else. This dual approach often persists (e.g., many algae can both photosynthesize and ingest dissolved organics).
Eukaryote with Mitochondria & Chloroplas.Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Contractile vacuole and metabolic waste handling. A photosynthetic eukaryote in freshwater would still need a contractile vacuole to expel water (if it’s marine, less so). It also now has to deal with storing starch and lipids from photosynthesis – not wastes, but storage products. Excess oxygen produced in bright light could be a problem (can cause photorespiration or ROS) – many algae mitigate this by the photorespiratory pathway (glycolate pathway in peroxisomes) which helps recycle some of the byproducts of oxygenic photosynthesis. They essentially evolved a peroxisome-based mini-excretory system to handle the toxic metabolite glycolate that results when Rubisco grabs oxygen instead of CO₂. So, peroxisomes work with mitochondria and chloroplasts in a photorespiratory cycle to detoxify and recover carbon – an internal waste management for a photosynthetic cell. In general, waste products of metabolism (CO₂, O₂, ammonia) diffuse out or are reused. If the cell fixes nitrogen (some algae still had that ability if they kept some cyanobacterial capabilities, though typically primary endosymbiosis led to loss of that in the chloroplast – except some like glaucophytes? But likely not), ammonia would be a waste of nitrogen fixation. More commonly, ammonia is a waste of protein breakdown, which the cell can likely excrete or refix into amino acids if energy is abundant (especially with photosynthesis, there is plenty of ATP to drive ammonium assimilation via glutamine synthetase). Thus the cell probably excretes very little – it tends to recycle internal wastes into new building blocks given the energy available. On the osmotic side, accumulating sugars can cause water influx; often algae convert excess sugars to osmolytes that they can tolerate or store as starch to avoid osmotic issues. For salt balance, if in freshwater, contractile vacuole pumps out water constantly; in saltwater, they actively pump out sodium if too much enters or synthesize compatible solutes to balance osmotic pressure. Because they have both chloroplasts and mitochondria, they have to coordinate waste between them: oxygen and CO₂ shuttle, as mentioned. Many protists, photosynthetic included, will encyst (form a dormant cyst) in harsh conditions. Encystment is like excretion on a large scale – they shed everything they don’t need, round up, secrete a protective wall, and reduce metabolism, often purging excess water and halting waste output until conditions improve. It’s a survival excretion of activity. When forming a cyst, a cell might dump certain vacuoles or undergo autophagy to reduce volume. Summarily, the excretory needs in a photosynthetic eukaryote remain similar to other protists

Fungi (early aquatic forms).Nervous System (Signal Response): Absent: No internal digestive tract; nutrients obtained by external enzyme digestion and absorption (New: first multicellular lineage with extracellular digestion)organismalbio.biosci.gatech.edu.
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Absent: No heart or vessels; nutrient transport via diffusion and cytoplasmic streaming in hyphae.
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Absent: No specialized respiratory organs; gas exchange by diffusion through cell surfaces.
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Absent: No nervous system or neurons.
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Absent: No muscle tissues; movement only by growth of hyphae.
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Partial: No internal skeleton; rigid chitinous cell walls provide structural support (New: chitin cell wall as exoskeletal support)organismalbio.biosci.gatech.edu.
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Absent: No specialized excretory organs; wastes diffuse out or are expelled with growth.
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Muscular System (Movement): Absent: No distinct endocrine organs; coordinates functions with simple chemical signals (no hormone glands).
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Reproduction via spores (both sexual and asexual); produces gametes and spores in life cycle. (Spores are durable new reproductive units for dispersal on land.)
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Reproductive System (Replication): Absent: No true immune system; relies on chemical defenses (e.g. antibiotics) against microbes (no immune cells).
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Integumentary System (Protection): Present: Tough cell wall protects cells from environment and predators (acts as an external protective layer); in multicellular fungi, fruiting body surfaces protect developing spores.
Fungi (early aquatic forms).Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Partial: No sense organs, but can detect environmental cues (chemicals, humidity, light) and respond (e.g. grow toward resources). No neurons – responses are at the cellular level.

Green Algae (aquatic).Nervous System (Signal Response): Absent: No internal digestive system (autotrophic: makes food via photosynthesis). No ingestion—absorbs nutrients and light.
Green Algae (aquatic).Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Absent: No circulatory system; simple diffusion moves nutrients and gases through the small algal body.
Green Algae (aquatic).Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Absent: No specialized respiration; gases (CO₂/O₂) diffuse across cell surfaces in water.
Green Algae (aquatic).Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Absent: No muscle tissue; motility (if present) via flagella in motile cells, not true muscles.
Green Algae (aquatic).Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Partial: No internal skeleton; cells have cellulose cell walls for shape/support (a rigid wall acting as structural support).
Green Algae (aquatic).Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Absent: No excretory organs; metabolic wastes (e.g. O₂ from photosynthesis) diffuse into the environment.
Green Algae (aquatic).Muscular System (Movement): Absent: No endocrine organs; growth and reproduction are regulated by simple chemical signals (no defined hormonal system).
Green Algae (aquatic).Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Reproduction can be sexual (fusion of gametes) or asexual (spores, fragmentation). Many green algae produce motile gametes and zygospores.
Green Algae (aquatic).Reproductive System (Replication): Absent: No immune system; they rely on cell walls and chemical compounds for protection (e.g. some produce anti-herbivory or antimicrobial chemicals).
Green Algae (aquatic).Integumentary System (Protection): Present: Cellulose cell wall provides a protective outer layer and prevents osmotic lysis (New: tough cellulose walls distinct from animal cells).
Green Algae (aquatic).Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Partial: No nervous system, but certain algae have light-sensitive organelles (eyespot) to sense light direction. Motile unicellular green algae (e.g. Chlamydomonas) use an eyespot and flagella to swim toward light (New: primitive photoreceptive organelle for phototaxis).

Sponges (Porifera).Nervous System (Signal Response): Partial: No true digestive organs or gut cavity (Absent in terms of organ system); feed by filtering water – choanocyte cells capture food and digest it intracellularly. Nutrients distributed by cell-to-cell transfer. (New: first multicellular filter-feeding mechanism, but no digestive tract).
Sponges (Porifera).Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Absent: No circulatory system (no blood or heart); water flow through sponge body carries food and oxygen and removes wastes. Nutrient distribution by water currents and cell diffusion.
Sponges (Porifera).Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Absent: No distinct respiratory system; each cell exchanges gases directly with water (constant water flow provides O₂ and removes CO₂).
Sponges (Porifera).Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Absent: No nervous system or neurons. Sponges show no coordinated neural activity.
Sponges (Porifera).Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Absent: No true muscle cells; they have only rudimentary contractile cells (e.g. around the osculum) that can slowly change sponge shape, but no muscle tissue for active movement.
Sponges (Porifera).Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Present: Internal skeletal elements present – sponges have mineral spicules (silica or calcium carbonate) and spongin fibers providing structural support. The mesohyl (gel matrix) acts as an endoskeleton. (New: first skeletal support in animals via spicules).
Sponges (Porifera).Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Absent: No specialized excretory organs; waste (ammonia) diffuses out into the water flow.
Sponges (Porifera).Muscular System (Movement): Absent: No endocrine glands; cell activities coordinated by local chemical signals (no hormones or endocrine tissues).
Sponges (Porifera).Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Can reproduce sexually and asexually. They are often hermaphroditic; produce sperm and eggs (though no true gonads – gametes arise from choanocytes or amoebocytes). Also regenerate or bud (asexual). (New: first animal gametes, though primitive).
Sponges (Porifera).Reproductive System (Replication): Partial: No complex immune system; sponges have primitive innate immunity. They recognize self vs. non-self – e.g. they reject grafts from other species. “Grey cells” in sponges can phagocytose invaders and secrete toxins to quarantine infections.
Sponges (Porifera).Integumentary System (Protection): Partial: Outer layer of flat cells (pinacoderm) acts as a simple protective “skin.” It is one cell thick with slight sealing between cells (not a true epidermis with basement membrane except in one subgroup). Spicules often protrude, deterring predators.
Sponges (Porifera).Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Absent: No organized sensory system or neurons. Sponges respond to stimuli in rudimentary ways (e.g. closing pores to harsh chemicals or touch) via local cell reactions, but have no nerve cells or sense organs.

Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Nervous System (Signal Response): Absent: Same external digestion strategy as aquatic fungi (secreting enzymes to break down organic matter externallyorganismalbio.biosci.gatech.edu). New adaptations: able to decompose terrestrial materials (e.g. plant cellulose/lignin by some fungi) and form symbiotic mycorrhizal associations to aid nutrient uptake – but still no internal digestive tract.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Absent: No circulatory system; multicellular filamentous body (mycelium) distributes nutrients by hyphal networks and cytoplasmic streaming.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Absent: No specialized respiratory structures; gas exchange by diffusion across hyphae. Terrestrial adaptation: must grow in moist environments or have structures to retain water for gas exchange.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Absent: No muscle cells; growth and turgor-driven hyphal extension allow movement into new areas (but no contractile tissues).
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Partial: No internal skeleton, but terrestrial fungi developed more robust structural support in tissues: thick chitinous cell walls and turgor pressure allow upright structures like mushroom fruiting bodies. Some fungi form large above-ground sporocarps (mushrooms), supported by fibrous hyphae – still a non-muscular, hydrostatic support.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Absent: No discrete excretory organs; wastes (e.g. excess nitrogen) diffuse or are stored in vacuoles.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Muscular System (Movement): Absent: No endocrine organs; growth and reproduction are triggered by environmental cues (e.g. light, temperature) and regulated by chemical signals (e.g. pheromones for mating) but no hormone glands.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Reproduce via spores adapted for land. New: Air-dispersed spores with tough walls (e.g. sporopollenin-like coats) to resist desiccation. Many land fungi evolved complex fruiting bodies (e.g. mushrooms, sporangia) to launch spores into the air. Also often capable of asexual spore production for rapid colonization.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Reproductive System (Replication): Absent: No immune system; fungi rely on passive defenses – e.g. cell walls and production of antibiotics/toxins to inhibit competitors and pathogens. (No immune cells or adaptive immunity.)
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Integumentary System (Protection): Present: Chitinous cell wall forms a protective integument, now often with additional coatings (hydrophobic proteins or pigments like melanin) to prevent desiccation and UV damage on land. New: Waxy or pigmented spore coats and hyphal surfaces to survive air exposure.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Partial: No nerves, but terrestrial fungi can sense gravity and light. For example, mushroom stems grow upward (negative gravitropism) and some fungi orient spore release to light gaps. They respond to environmental stimuli (light triggers spore release, chemicals trigger growth direction), but solely through cellular pathways (no specialized sense organs).
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Nervous System: Inherited: No nerves, just mycelial network signaling as in aquatic fungi. Innovated: Greater mycelial network integration with plant partners – on land, fungi formed mycorrhizal networks connecting plant roots, effectively allowing signal exchange (nutrient and chemical cues) between plants via the fungus. The fungal mycelium can rapidly transmit signals (e.g. warning neighboring plants of pest attack through chemical cues), acting somewhat like a “nervous system” for plant communities. Still no neurons, but the scale of network signaling increased in soil ecosystems.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Respiratory System: Inherited: Diffusion of gases across filament surfaces (as in aquatic fungi). Innovated: Adaptations to air exposure: terrestrial fungi often grow within moist soil or host tissues, ensuring their hyphae stay hydrated for gas exchange. Some have rhizomorphs (thick cords) that contain air channels to transport O₂ into low-oxygen environments (like waterlogged wood). Although fungi have no lungs or gills, the architecture of fruiting bodies (e.g. gills under a mushroom cap) maximizes surface area so that spores get oxygen and dry air for dispersal. The development of internal air spaces in large structures is a terrestrial innovation to facilitate respiration and spore release.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Digestive System: Inherited: External digestion and nutrient absorption as in aquatic fungi. Innovated: Ability to decompose tough terrestrial substrates: land fungi evolved enzymes like cellulases and ligninases to break down plant cell walls and wood – a major innovation enabling them to exploit abundant plant litter. They also formed symbiotic digestive partnerships (e.g. helping herbivores digest cellulose in guts, or forming lichens with algae to share nutrients). Additionally, mycorrhizal fungi feed by exchanging minerals for sugars with plants, effectively diversifying their “digestive” strategy from pure decay to mutualism.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Circulatory System: Inherited: No circulatory system; cytoplasmic streaming in hyphae still moves nutrients. Innovated: Development of long-distance mycelial cords (rhizomorphs) that act like “fungal veins,” carrying water and nutrients over meters of soil or wood. These cords have differentiated core and outer layers and can rapidly translocate resources (e.g. moving water from moist areas to dry areas in a forest soil). Such transport efficiency is crucial on land where nutrients and water are patchily distributed. It’s not a closed circulatory system with a pump, but it allows a fungus to function as a integrated organism across large distances.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Reproductive System: Inherited: Spore production (sexual and asexual) as primary reproduction, as in aquatic fungi. Innovated: Airborne spore dispersal – terrestrial fungi produce enormous quantities of dry spores that are released into the air (often from elevated structures like mushroom caps) to spread to new locations. They evolved ballistic spore discharge mechanisms (e.g. puffballs expelling spores in a cloud, or fungi that shoot spores using turgor pressure). Terrestrial fungi also often lost the ancestral motile gamete stage (no need for flagellated spores in soil). Additionally, many can reproduce asexually prolifically (molds spreading via conidia), ensuring colonization of ephemeral substrates.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Muscular System: Inherited: No muscles; growth and turgor changes continue to drive movement. Innovated: Terrestrial fungi show growth movements like tropisms – e.g. Pilobolus fungus can aim its spore shooters toward light (which often indicates open air for spores to travel), meaning it senses light direction and grows a stalk that rapidly launches spores toward that light. Also, some parasitic fungi can forcibly eject spores or even “zombie-ant” fungi direct their ant hosts to optimal positions – not a muscle system per se, but an evolved control over host behavior as a means of movement/dispersal. Overall, terrestrial fungi rely on strategic growth and turgor-powered motion (like mushrooms expanding overnight or spores being shot) as their form of movement.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Skeletal System: Inherited: Chitinous cell walls for structure, as in aquatic fungi. Innovated: Multicellular fruiting bodies (mushrooms, brackets) with supportive tissues – e.g. densely packed hyphae form a stem and cap that can stand upright. Fungal cell walls on land often contain melanin or other polymers that add rigidity and protect from UV. Terrestrial fungi also produce sclerotia (hardened masses of hyphae) that act as tough survival structures in soil. In symbiosis, some fungi contribute to plant skeletal support by entwining with roots (forming mycorrhizae that help anchor plants). While fungi themselves remain mostly “soft,” the formation of large, self-supporting sporocarps is a significant skeletal innovation on land.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Immune System: Inherited: Innate chemical defenses (antibiotics, etc.) as in earlier fungi. Innovated: Enhanced competitive and defensive chemistry: soil fungi secrete a wide array of antimicrobials to outcompete soil bacteria and other fungi. Many also evolved resistance to plant defense chemicals (allowing pathogenic fungi to infect plants). In terms of immunity, fungi on land encountered many new predators (like nematodes, insects) – some responded by evolving predatory structures (e.g. nematode-trapping loops) and producing toxins to deter fungivores. Additionally, mycorrhizal fungi can trigger plant immune responses systemically (helping plants resist disease), effectively extending a form of immune function to their plant partners.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Endocrine System: Inherited: Diffuse production of signals (no glands). Innovated: Terrestrial fungi use complex pheromone systems to orchestrate mating (e.g. mating type factors ensure hyphae only fuse with a compatible type). They also respond to environmental hormones – for instance, ethylene from ripe fruit can stimulate fruiting in some fungi. The optic gland analogue in fungi doesn’t exist, but they do have something akin to hormonal control: e.g. in mushroom-forming fungi, certain cells (in the cap) release hormones that trigger spore maturation synchronously. Essentially, fungi expanded their chemical communication repertoire to include triggers from the environment (day-night cycles, plant hormones) to time their life cycle events on land.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Excretory System: Inherited: Diffusion and environmental dumping of waste. Innovated: Terrestrial fungi must often conserve water, so they can’t flush wastes freely. Many package waste products into fruiting bodies – for example, mushrooms often accumulate heavy metals or metabolic byproducts, removing them from the active mycelium. When the mushroom is shed or eaten by an animal, the waste is removed from the fungus. Also, in symbiotic fungi, some waste (like CO₂) is actually useful to plant partners and is transferred to them. Fungi essentially continue to rely on diffusion, but their lifecycle (producing disposable structures) and partnerships help manage waste in a terrestrial context.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Integumentary System: Inherited: Single-celled covering (hyphal surface) as before. Innovated: Many terrestrial fungi developed hydrophobic cell wall coatings (proteins/hydrophobins) on their hyphae and spores to prevent desiccation. The surface of mushrooms is often water-repellent, protecting the spores until release. Some have a rind of thick-walled cells on structures like sclerotia or fruitbody surfaces, analogous to a skin. Fungi also frequently cover themselves in mucilage or slime (e.g. slime molds, though not true fungi, share this trait) to retain moisture. In short, fungi on land evolved a kind of integument: waterproof outer layers on their mycelium and spore structures to survive air exposure.
Fungi on Land (early terrestrial fungi).Sensory System: Inherited: Sensitivity to environment (chemotaxis, phototaxis) as in ancestors. Innovated: Land fungi became finely attuned to light, gravity, and humidity. For instance, mushroom fruiting bodies orient upward (negative gravitropism) so spores drop out under gravity – they have gravity-sensing mechanisms. Many fungi require specific light cues to form fruitbodies (ensuring spores release in optimal conditions), indicating developed photoreceptors. They also sense host-derived signals: pathogenic fungi can detect plant chemicals and grow toward them. Overall, terrestrial fungi have improved “senses” for environmental conditions – not via organs, but via specialized cells and receptors that detect light (blue-light receptors), volatile chemicals, moisture levels, and even surface touch (thigmotropism, e.g. rust fungi orienting growth by feeling stomata openings on leaves).

Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Nervous System (Signal Response): Present: Digestive system with mouth, pharynx, stomach and a branching canal system. Digestion is partly extracellular in the gastrovascular canals. They have two small anal pores at the aboral end that expel waste (though most undigested material is regurgitated via the mouth). New: First instance of a separate exit for waste (incipient through-gut), unlike cnidarians’ single opening.
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Absent: No dedicated circulatory system. The extensive gastrovascular canal system distributes nutrients and doubles as a circulatory system (no heart or blood vessels). Nutrient transport is via ciliary water movement in canals, not a separate blood flow.
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Absent: No specialized respiratory organs; gas exchange occurs by diffusion through the body surface and gastrovascular canals. Thin body walls and continuous internal water circulation suffice for O₂/CO₂ exchange.
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Present: A diffuse nerve net is present, coordinating muscle and ciliary beat. Ctenophores possess an apical organ at the aboral pole containing a gravity sensor (statocyst) that helps control balance and orientation. This apical organ acts like a primitive brain center to coordinate swimming. (New: One of the earliest nervous systems, with a specialized balance organ for locomotion control.)
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Present: True muscle cells (smooth muscle fibers) are present within the mesoglea (mesenchymal “muscles”). These muscles allow the mouth to contract and body to undulate. Ctenophores can swim by coordinated ciliary comb rows, but also use muscle for activities like swallowing prey. (New: muscle tissue derived from mesoderm-like layer – first musculature in lineage, enabling active feeding motions.)
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Absent: No rigid skeleton; body is supported by a gelatinous mesoglea that maintains shape. The mesoglea plus internal fluid act as a hydrostatic skeleton. (Ctenophores do not have spicules or mineral support; their support is purely soft and elastic.)
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Absent: No distinct excretory organs; nitrogenous wastes diffuse out through body surfaces or exit via the anal pores with digestive wastes. Osmoregulation occurs at the cellular level.
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Muscular System (Movement): Absent: No identified endocrine glands; however, ctenophores likely use neuropeptides for internal signaling (e.g. to induce spawning). There is no organized hormonal system comparable to higher animals.
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Nearly all are hermaphrodites. They have gonads in the meridional canals that release eggs and sperm through pores in the epidermis. Fertilization is typically external in the water column. They can produce many eggs, and some show continuous reproduction. (New: dedicated gonadal tissue lining canals, unlike sponges/cnidarians which had diffuse gamete origin.)
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Reproductive System (Replication): Absent: No complex immune system; ctenophores rely on barrier defenses (their mucus) and cellular phagocytosis. No specialized immune cells or memory. Innate immunity is limited to generic responses (if any known).
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Integumentary System (Protection): Present: Body is covered by a delicate epidermis. It secretes mucus that protects the surface and aids in trapping prey on tentacles. The integument is soft and lacks any hard covering. (No shells or cuticle; very vulnerable to drying, hence strictly aquatic.)
Comb Jellies (Ctenophores).Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Present: Statocyst at the aboral end for gravity perception – a new sensory innovation for orientation. Also have scattered sensory cells: ciliated cells on tentacles detect prey contact (mechanoreception), and some species have rudimentary photoreceptors (ctenophores can be bioluminescent and may sense light/dark). Overall, sensory systems are present but simple, serving to orient the animal and trigger feeding responses.

Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Nervous System (Signal Response): Present: An internal digestive tract existed. It’s likely this early bilaterian had a gut cavity with a mouth (and possibly an anus). Many evidence suggest a through-gut evolved around this stage (New: one-way digestive system with separate mouth and anal opening). At minimum, a mouth leading to an intestine was present for extracellular digestion of food.
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Partial: No fully developed circulatory system in the earliest bilaterians. If the ancestor was small and flat, it had no heart and relied on diffusion. Larger descendants evolved a primitive hemocoel or pseudocoel fluid for transport. (Some bilaterians later evolved closed circulatory vessels, but the first bilaterian likely lacked them.)
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Absent: No specialized respiratory structures initially; gas exchange by diffusion through the skin or gut. The small, thin body of early bilaterians allowed oxygen to reach cells without gills. (Gills or lungs evolved later in larger, more complex bilaterians.)
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Present: Centralized nervous system with anterior concentration of neurons (brain or cerebral ganglion) and longitudinal nerve cords running along the body. This represents cephalization: a head with sensory organs and a brain, and a pair of nerve cords (ventral in protostomes, dorsal in deuterostomes). (New: first true brain and directional nerve cords for coordinated movement).
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Present: Well-developed muscle layers (longitudinal and circular muscles) derived from mesoderm. These muscles allowed the bilaterian ancestor to move its body purposefully (e.g. crawl or swim). The presence of mesoderm was a key innovation providing robust musculature for locomotion and burrowing.
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Partial: No hard skeleton yet; support was via a hydrostatic skeleton. The bilaterian likely had a fluid-filled body cavity (coelom or pseudocoel) that muscles could push against to maintain shape and aid movement. (New: a true coelom evolved in bilateria, enabling efficient hydrostatic support and organ space.) No bones or shell were present at this stage.
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Present: Primitive excretory organs appeared. Most likely protonephridia (flame-cell systems) evolved to remove metabolic waste and control water balance – an innovation in bilaterians. Flame cells filtered body fluids and expelled waste through excretory pores. (New: first dedicated excretory system to regulate internal environment).
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Muscular System (Movement): Partial: Endocrine signaling in a basic form. The bilaterian ancestor had no discrete endocrine glands, but it did use chemical messengers (e.g. neurosecretory cells in the brain releasing hormones) to regulate functions like growth and reproduction. (True endocrine organs like thyroids or adrenal glands evolved later in specific lineages.)
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Sexual reproduction with separate gonads likely. The ancestor probably had ovaries/testes to produce gametes. Eggs and sperm were released for external fertilization in water (assumed aquatic habitat). A larval stage was likely present (e.g. a trochophore-like larva in protostome lineages). New: distinct gonadal tissue (as opposed to random cells) and a life cycle including a free-swimming larva for dispersal.
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Reproductive System (Replication): Present: Innate immune defenses present. Early bilaterians possessed wandering phagocytic cells and antimicrobial peptides to fight infections – a generalized innate immune system similar to that in modern invertebrates. (Adaptive immunity did not exist yet.) So, they could encapsulate parasites or bacteria, but had no lymphocytes or immune memory.
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Integumentary System (Protection): Present: True epidermis (outer skin layer) covered the body. This integument was likely a single-cell-layer epidermis with intercellular junctions and often cilia on its surface (for locomotion or feeding currents). It provided a protective barrier against the environment. Some may have secreted a thin cuticle or mucus over the epidermis for additional protection or to prevent desiccation (in those that later invaded land).
Bilateria (Ancestor of Protostomes & Deu.Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Present: Definitive sensory organs at the anterior end. The bilaterian ancestor had primitive eyes or eyespots (for light sensing), chemoreceptors (to smell/taste water for food), and mechanoreceptors (touch). For example, pigment cup eyes or ocelli may have been present. (New: paired sensory structures on a head, processed by a brain, allowing directed movement toward or away from stimuli.)

Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Nervous System (Signal Response): Present: Complete digestive tract (mouth and anus) present. As a protostome, the mouth formed first in development. Food entered a mouth, was processed in a gut, and waste exited an anus. This one-way digestion allowed more efficient nutrient absorption than a single opening. (Some extant primitive protostomes like flatworms have secondarily lost the anus, but the protostome common ancestor likely had one.)
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Partial: The earliest protostome was likely a small worm-like animal without a fully developed circulatory system. There was no closed blood vessel network. Nutrient transport occurred in a hemocoel (open body cavity) or by diffusion. A simple contractile heart tube may have been absent or just beginning to evolve. (Open circulation with hemolymph evolved in larger protostomes later.)
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Absent: No specialized respiratory organs initially. Oxygen absorbed through the skin or gut. In water, the small protostome ancestor didn’t need gills. (Gills appear later in larger aquatic protostomes like mollusks; terrestrial protostomes like insects evolved tracheal systems much later.)
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Present: Ventral nerve cords and an anterior brain (ganglionic mass) were present – a hallmark of protostomes. The nervous system likely consisted of a ring around the esophagus and one or more longitudinal nerve cords running along the belly side. This let the animal coordinate movement and respond quickly. (New: protostome-specific pattern – brain encircling the foregut and paired ventral nerve cords).
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Present: Well-developed muscles for locomotion. The ancestral protostome likely had layers of body-wall muscle (longitudinal and circular) allowing it to crawl or swim. These muscles, working against a fluid-filled body cavity, enabled peristalsis or undulatory movement. Early protostomes could actively search for food using this musculature.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Partial: No rigid skeleton; body supported by fluid pressure (hydrostatic skeleton). The protostome ancestor was soft-bodied. Some may have had a collagenous cuticle providing slight external support, but no bones or hard exoskeleton yet. (The evolution of hard exoskeletons occurred in specific protostome lines later – e.g. the cuticle in ecdysozoans.)
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Present: Excretory structures existed to eliminate waste. Protostomes pioneered protonephridia (flame cell systems) or early metanephridia to filter metabolic waste from the body cavity. For instance, a network of flame cells likely managed excretion/osmoregulation in the ancestral protostome, as seen in modern flatworms.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Muscular System (Movement): Present: Primitive endocrine signaling present. Neurosecretory cells in the protostome brain could secrete hormones (e.g. to regulate reproduction or molting in later groups). For example, protostomes later evolved hormones like ecdysone for molting (in arthropods) – indicating the protostome lineage had the capacity for hormone regulation. (No dedicated endocrine organs in the earliest form, just scattered hormone-secreting cells.)
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Sexual reproduction with gonads. The ancestral protostome likely had separate sexes (male and female) releasing eggs and sperm into the water for external fertilization. A trochophore-type larva may have been part of the life cycle (as seen in marine protostomes like mollusks and annelids). Some protostomes later became hermaphroditic, but the baseline is two sexes. (New: trochophore larva stage in many protostomes – an innovation for dispersal in this lineage.)
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Reproductive System (Replication): Present: Innate immune defenses present (as in all bilaterians). Early protostomes would have cells capable of phagocytosing invaders and producing antimicrobial molecules. For example, even primitive worms produce lysozymes to break down bacteria. No adaptive immunity, but a basic cellular defense system protected them from infection.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Integumentary System (Protection): Present: Soft epidermis often covered by a thin cuticle. The protostome ancestor likely had a ciliated epidermis (especially if the larval stage was ciliated). This integument provided protection and helped in movement (cilia for swimming in larvae or small forms). In some, a delicate cuticle (collagen-based) covered the epidermis, offering slight protection and shape – a precursor to the thicker molted cuticles of ecdysozoan protostomes.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Present: Cephalization in protostomes meant distinct sensory head structures. The earliest protostome probably bore simple eyespots to detect light, anterior chemoreceptors to find food, and mechanoreceptors (e.g. sensory bristles) to feel the environment. These sensors, linked to the brain and ventral nerve cords, allowed the animal to navigate toward food or away from danger.

Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Nervous System (Signal Response): Present: Complete digestive tract with separate mouth and anus (a defining trait of deuterostomes: the blastopore in the embryo became the anus, a new mouth opening formed). Thus, the earliest deuterostome had one-way digestion: food in at the mouth, waste out the anus. This was already established in their bilaterian ancestor, but deuterostomes retained and refined it.
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Partial: A simple circulatory system existed. The ancestral deuterostome was likely worm-like (similar to modern acorn worms) with an open circulatory system: a dorsal contractile vessel (“heart”) that pushed fluid through sinuses. Hemichordates (acorn worms) have a heart–glomerulus organ that pumps blood and filters it. So the ancestor probably had a rudimentary heart and some blood vessels, but not a fully closed circulatory network.
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Present: Pharyngeal gill slits in the throat were present – a key deuterostome innovation. The earliest deuterostome used gill slits to filter-feed and breathe. Water entering the mouth exited through these gill openings, exchanging gases in the process. (New: pharyngeal slit breathing apparatus, absent in protostomes). These slits later gave rise to gills in fish and remain as embryonic features in all chordates.
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Present: Nervous system present, with some centralization. In deuterostomes, the nerve cord tends to be positioned dorsally. The ancestor probably had a dorsal nerve strand (as seen in hemichordates’ collar cord) along with a simpler diffuse network elsewhere. There may not have been a well-defined brain – perhaps a nerve ring or plexus in the collar region. But a trend toward a dorsal central nerve was beginning (New: beginning of dorsal neural centralization, which becomes a hollow dorsal nerve cord in chordates).
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Present: Muscular system present for movement. The ancestral deuterostome likely had body-wall musculature allowing it to burrow or swim. For example, acorn worms use longitudinal muscles to burrow and muscle fibers to pump water through their pharynx. Thus, longitudinal and circular muscles enabled peristaltic movement and feeding currents.
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Partial: No hard skeleton initially. Support was hydrostatic via coelomic cavities. However, this lineage showed novel support structures: hemichordates have a stiff stomochord rod in the proboscis (a precursor-like structure to a notochord) and echinoderms later evolved calcite endoskeletons. In the earliest form, the body was soft; a gelatinous rod (stomochord) in the proboscis of hemichordates and fluid-filled coeloms gave some support. (The true notochord and calcified skeleton appeared in the split-off chordates and echinoderms, respectively.)
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Present: Excretory system present. A unique glomerulus-kidney in the proboscis of hemichordates suggests the ancestor had a similar organ. This glomerulus filtered waste from blood into the proboscis coelom, from which it exited the body. Thus, an early kidney-like organ existed (New: novel excretory mechanism different from protostome nephridia). In echinoderms, specialized excretory organs were lost (waste diffuses out), but the common ancestor likely could filter blood waste.
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Muscular System (Movement): Present: Endocrine system (basic). While no dedicated glands like thyroid or pituitary yet, the deuterostome ancestor had cells that released signaling molecules. Notably, an endostyle (iodine-concentrating organ in the pharynx, homologous to the thyroid) evolved in chordates; hemichordates have a similar structure in the pharynx. So hormonal regulation of metabolism (iodine use) was starting. Other hormones likely regulated larval development and metamorphosis (as seen in modern echinoderm larvae).
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Sexual reproduction with gonads. The ancestral deuterostome was dioecious (separate sexes) – e.g., extant hemichordates have males and females with gonads lining the trunk. Gametes were shed into the water through gill slits or gonopores (external fertilization). A ciliated larval stage (dipleurula-type larva) was part of the life cycle for dispersal. This larva is the precursor to both echinoderm larvae and chordate (tunicate) larvae.
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Reproductive System (Replication): Present: Innate immune system present. Deuterostomes had coelomic cells to fight infection – for instance, echinoderms have amoeboid coelomocytes that engulf pathogens, and hemichordates likely do as well. Antimicrobial enzymes and proteins were part of their immune defense. (No adaptive immunity at this stage, as that appears later in vertebrate chordates.)
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Integumentary System (Protection): Present: Epidermis (with cilia in larvae and maybe adults) covered the body, providing protection. The skin was likely thin and ciliated, secreting mucus. In hemichordates, a ciliated epidermis and mucus help in feeding and protection. No armor or scales yet – the surface was soft. Some echinoderm ancestors may have had soft spicules (lost or transformed into hard plates later in echinoderms).
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Present: Basic sensory structures. The ancestral deuterostome larva had an apical sensory organ with an ocellus (light sensor) and a statocyst (gravity sensor) – features still seen in echinoderm larvae. The adult hemichordate has ciliary feeders that also sense chemicals. So, this lineage had light-sensitive and gravity-sensitive cells and chemoreceptors in the anterior. They lacked image-forming eyes or complex ears, but they could detect light vs dark and up vs down.

Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Nervous System (Signal Response): Present: Complete gut with mouth and anus. Both hemichordates (e.g. acorn worms) and echinoderms have through-guts. The common ancestor likely was a deposit or filter feeder: a muscular pharynx in hemichordates ingests food and a simple intestine processes it. Echinoderm ancestors had a mouth and stomach (as modern sea stars do). No new digestive innovation beyond the one-way gut, but specialization differed: hemichordates used a pharyngeal filter system, echinoderms later evolved various feeding modes (e.g. eversible stomach in sea stars).
Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Present: An open circulatory system. Hemichordates have a heart and some vessels but largely open sinuses; echinoderms have a reduced hemal system. The ancestor had a dorsal heart-like organ pumping fluid. New (in echinoderms): the water vascular system, a network of hydraulic canals used for movement and feeding, which also transports coelomic fluid. (This water vascular system is unique to echinoderms and evolved after the split – hemichordates lack it.) So the Ambulacraria ancestor had blood circulation and, in the echinoderm line, this co-opted into a hydraulic locomotory system.
Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Present: Pharyngeal gill slits were present (inherited from the deuterostome ancestor) in the hemichordate branch for respiration and filter feeding. The Ambulacraria common ancestor likely had gill slits in the pharynx (since acorn worms do) that allowed water exit and gas exchange. Echinoderms, however, lost these slits as they adopted other breathing structures: e.g. starfish use skin gills (papulae) and sea cucumbers have respiratory trees. Thus, the ancestor used gill slits for breathing (New: deuterostome-style pharyngeal respiration), but the echinoderm lineage later innovated different respiratory organs after losing slits.
Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Present: Diffuse nervous system. In echinoderms, instead of a brain, there is a nerve ring around the mouth and radial nerves down each arm. Hemichordates have a nervous system with both a dorsal and ventral nerve cord (but also not strongly centralized). The Ambulacraria ancestor likely lacked a well-defined head brain; it had a nerve net and cords. Coordination in echinoderms became decentralized (ring and radial nerves) – a unique change. The ancestor had sensory nerves in the anterior (for hemichordate proboscis) and a net elsewhere. (No highly centralized CNS – that path was taken by chordates instead.)
Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Present: Muscles present for movement. Hemichordates have longitudinal and circular muscles (e.g. to burrow and swallow sediment). Echinoderms have muscle fibers in their tube feet and around their mouth parts (and in sea stars, to move arms). The common ancestor had body-wall muscles and likely contractile elements in the feeding apparatus (pharynx). When echinoderms later evolved calcified skeletons, they still retained muscle to move tube feet and spines. So musculature was present, though echinoderms rely on hydraulics plus muscle.
Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Present: Endoskeleton in echinoderms; hydrostatic in hemichordates. Here the lineage split in skeletal innovation. Hemichordates remained soft-bodied (no hard skeleton, just a hydrostatic proboscis and sometimes a fibrous support rod). Echinoderms evolved a calcite endoskeleton – plates and spines under the skin (New innovation: calcified endoskeletal plates that provide support and protection, unique to echinoderms). The Ambulacraria ancestor might have begun depositing calcium in the skin as microscopic ossicles. Thus, by the time of true echinoderms, there was a well-formed mesodermal skeleton of ossicles, whereas hemichordates continued without any hard parts.
Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Partial: Excretory system was minimal. Hemichordates possess a glomerulus (a network that filters waste in the proboscis), indicating the ancestor had some excretory ability. Echinoderms have no distinct excretory organ; they excrete ammonia by diffusion through tube feet and papulae. The common ancestor probably had the hemichordate-style glomerulus-kidney, but echinoderms lost it as they adapted to diffusive excretion. So excretion was present in one branch, absent in the other.
