Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Muscular System (Movement): Present: Endocrine-like coordination existed. Echinoderms and hemichordates both use chemical signals (neurosecretory hormones) for processes like spawning and metamorphosis. For instance, echinoderm larvae metamorphosis is hormonally controlled, and adult echinoderms can regenerate limbs influenced by hormonal cues. Hemichordates produce iodine-binding mucus in the pharynx (related to thyroid function). While no discrete endocrine glands are obvious in these animals, hormone-like substances regulate their physiology (e.g. seasonal spawning in echinoderms is triggered by neurohormones).
Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Sexual reproduction with gonads. Both echinoderms and hemichordates are usually dioecious. The Ambulacraria ancestor had gonads (hemichordates have gonad sacs along their trunk; echinoderms typically have gonads in each arm or body segment). Gametes were released into water for external fertilization. Development passed through a ciliated larval stage (the dipleurula larva, which in echinoderms becomes bipinnaria, etc., and in hemichordates is the tornaria larva). Some echinoderms later gained a remarkable ability to also reproduce asexually by splitting, but sexual gonadal reproduction was the primary mode.
Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Reproductive System (Replication): Present: Innate immunity. Echinoderms have active immune cells (coelomocytes) that engulf pathogens and help wound healing – the starfish immune response is notably strong (they can even resist grafts). Hemichordates likely have immune cells in their coelomic cavities as well. The ancestor’s coelomic fluid contained ameboid cells for defense. There is no adaptive immune system (that appears only in vertebrate chordates), but Ambulacrarians show advanced innate responses (e.g. starfish can isolate infections by cellular encapsulation).
Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Integumentary System (Protection): Present: The skin (integument) in this ancestor was ciliated and mucus-coated (especially in hemichordates). Echinoderms developed a unique integument: an epidermis over their calcite ossicles, often bearing spines and pincer-like pedicellariae as defensive structures (New: echinoderm spines and pedicellaria for protection and cleanliness). The Ambulacraria ancestor had a simple ciliated epidermis. As echinoderms evolved, their integument incorporated armor (spines, plates) beneath it. Hemichordates kept a soft, unarmored skin that secretes mucus (for trapping food and deterring microbes).
Ambulacraria (Echinoderm & Hemichordate.Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Present: Sensory and perception were present but not highly centralized. Hemichordates have ciliary receptors in the proboscis to taste and feel mud, and possibly light-sensing cells (their larvae have an eyespot). Echinoderms, despite lacking a brain, have quite a few sensory cells: for example, starfish have simple eye spots at the tips of their arms that detect light/dark, and their tube feet are sensitive to chemicals and touch. The Ambulacraria ancestor likely had a larval apical organ with sensory function and, as an adult, diffuse sensory cells in the skin (for touch and chemical detection). New in echinoderms: development of distributed “eyes” (e.g. sea stars’ arm-tip ocelli) and sensory tube feet, showing that even without a head they evolved ways to perceive the environment.

Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Nervous System (Signal Response): Present: Complete digestive system with regional specialization. Chordates inherited the one-way gut and elaborated it. The early chordate (imagine something like a lancelet/amphioxus) had a mouth, pharynx with pharyngeal slits to filter-feed, an esophagus, intestine, and anus. The pharynx was a large filtering basket (in cephalochordates and tunicates) – it both fed the organism and did gas exchange. The post-pharyngeal gut was simpler but present.
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Present: Closed circulatory system with a ventral heart-like pump and dorsal and ventral blood vessels – a chordate innovation. For example, amphioxus has a closed system (contractile vessels instead of a true heart) and vertebrate chordates developed a multichambered heart. Blood flowed in vessels: forward along a ventral aorta and back along a dorsal aorta in early chordatesallinonehighschool.com. (New: completely closed blood vessels for more efficient oxygen transport, unlike the open systems of ancestors). The blood in early chordates lacked specialized blood cells (vertebrates later added red blood cells with hemoglobin).
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Present: Pharyngeal gill slits used for respiration (as well as feeding). In the chordate ancestor, these slits were lined with vascularized tissue for gas exchange. Water drawn in the mouth exited the pharyngeal slits, releasing CO₂ and absorbing O₂. Cephalochordates and tunicates use many gill slits for breathing. As chordates diversified, these slits became true gills in fish (with gill arches and filaments – an enhanced respiratory organ). Thus, the chordate kept deuterostome gill slits and later amplified them. Additionally, chordates introduced a post-anal tail, which in aquatic forms helped in swimming and also increased surface area for minor cutaneous respiration.
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Present: Dorsal, hollow nerve cord running the length of the body, with an anterior expansion (primitive brain). This is a defining chordate traitbrainly.com. In early chordates like amphioxus, the nerve cord is a dorsal tube with a slight brain at the front. This contrasts with the ventral nerve cord of protostomes. (New: dorsal nerve tube for integrating sensory input and motor output). Chordates also show segmentation in the nerve cord via repeated nerves to muscle segments (like amphioxus’ metameric nerves). The nervous system was more centralized than in prior groups, enabling faster and more complex movements.
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Present: Segmented muscles (myomeres) along the body wall – another chordate hallmarkquizlet.comquizlet.com. The early chordate had a series of chevron-shaped muscle blocks from head to tail, attached to the notochord. These muscles, when contracting in waves, bend the flexible notochord to produce swimming motions (lateral undulations). (New: post-anal tail with segmented musculature for propulsion). This musculature and tail allowed the chordate ancestor to be an active swimmer, unlike the largely sessile or slow ancestors.
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Present: Notochord – a stiff, flexible rod made of large cells with fluid vacuoles, running along the body lengthbrainly.com. This was a revolutionary endoskeletal support in chordates (New innovation: axial internal skeleton). The notochord provided something firm for muscles to pull against, enabling powerful swimming while still being bendable. In early chordates like lancelets, the notochord extends tip-to-tip, supporting the entire body. Additionally, chordates later evolved cartilage and bone (in vertebrates) building on this support system – but the proto-chordate itself had just the notochord as its skeleton.
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Present: Excretory system with segmental nephridia or kidneys. The chordate ancestor refined excretion – for instance, amphioxus has segmented protonephridial tubules called nephridia that filter blood filtrate from the coelom and dump urine into the atrium. In vertebrates, this system became the glomerular kidney. So a chordate innovation was a more efficient, segmented excretory system. (New: in vertebrate descendants, a multi-stage kidney – but even the basal chordate had units to cleanse the blood.)
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Muscular System (Movement): Present: Endocrine system beginning to specialize. Chordates possess an endostyle in the pharynx (in lancelets and tunicates) – a groove that secretes iodinated compounds (mucus to trap food, but also binds iodine). The endostyle is homologous to the thyroid gland in vertebratescourses.lumenlearning.com. Thus, chordates introduced a distinct organ for metabolic regulation (iodine metabolism) – New: the origins of a thyroid endocrine organ. Additionally, early chordates had other hormone-secreting cells (for example, neural hormonal control of gamete release, etc.). The stage was set for a full endocrine system (pituitary, etc.) in vertebrates.
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Sexual reproduction with gonads. The chordate ancestor (e.g. amphioxus) has many paired gonads along its body that release gametes into the atrium and out through an opening for external fertilization. Tunicates have reproductive organs (often hermaphroditic) that release gametes into water or even retain eggs for internal fertilization in some cases. In any case, chordates had distinct ovaries and testes. New: Some chordates (the lineage leading to vertebrates) evolved internal fertilization and protective embryonic structures (e.g. amniotic egg much later), but the early chordate stuck to external spawning and a free-swimming larval stage.
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Reproductive System (Replication): Present: Immune system present, primarily innate. Early chordates had phagocytic cells and immune surveillance. Notably, the chordate lineage is where adaptive immunity eventually appears – jawed vertebrates later evolved lymphocytes and antibodies. However, basal chordates (amphioxus, tunicates) do not have adaptive immunity; tunicates do have a primitive self/non-self recognition system and amphioxus has many innate immune genes. So the chordate ancestor’s immune system was similar to invertebrates’ (innate), with the potential that in the vertebrate branch, new innovations (adaptive immune cells) would evolve. (Jawless fish even have a unique adaptive-like system with VLRs, but that’s later.)
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Integumentary System (Protection): Present: A multi-layered integument starts to appear in chordates. The epidermis of an amphioxus is a single-cell layer, but vertebrates will develop a stratified epidermis. Early chordates were mostly aquatic, so their integument was not keratinized; instead, it was covered in mucus (for protection and to streamline water flow). Tunicates have a special integument: a tunic made of a cellulose-like polysaccharide – an unusual trait in chordates (essentially an exoskeletal coat around the body of urochordates). In cephalochordates and early vertebrates, the integument is just skin. So, while skin is present, New: chordates are the only animals to use a cellulose-like biopolymer (tunicates) in an integument, and vertebrates later develop scales, feathers, etc., from the integument.
Chordate (early chordates, e.g. urochord.Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Present: Highly developed sensory systems. Even the simplest chordates show advanced sensory capabilities. For example, lancelets have a small pigmented eye spot (ocellus) at the front of the nerve cord to detect light, as well as chemosensory organs (anterior nerve organ to sample water) and touch receptors along the body. Tunicate larvae have a clear sensory head: an eyespot that senses light and an otolith (gravity sensor) for orientation, allowing the tadpole larva to navigate before settling. (New: Chordates set the stage for complex sensory organs – image-forming eyes, inner ears, lateral lines – which appear in vertebrates). In the proto-chordate, we see the precursors: a dorsal eye spot linked to the brain, a balancing organ, and various mechanoreceptors. These innovations mark a significant increase in sensory complexity compared to earlier animalsquizlet.com.

Mollusks (early protostome branch).Nervous System (Signal Response): Present: Complete digestive system with specialized organs. Mollusks typically have a mouth with a radula (a toothed, rasping tongue) to scrape or cut food (New innovation: the radula, unique to mollusks, for mechanical breakdown of food)allinonehighschool.com. The digestive tract is regionally specialized – e.g. esophagus, stomach with digestive glands, intestine – reflecting a more complex processing of food.
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Present: Open circulatory system in most (except cephalopods). A heart (often 3-chambered) pumps hemolymph through arteries into open sinuses bathing organsallinonehighschool.com. Blood returns to the heart via veins or ostia. This system is adequate for slower-moving mollusks (snails, clams). New: a true heart is present (first well-developed heart among these lineages). Cephalopod mollusks later evolved a closed circulatory system for high activity, but the earliest mollusk had the simpler open circuit. Ex: a snail has a heart and open hemocoel.
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Present: Gills (ctenidia) for aquatic mollusks. Located in the mantle cavity, these filamentous or plate-like gills facilitate gas exchange between water and bloodbio.libretexts.org. New: dedicated respiratory organs (gills) appear, which is a step beyond diffusion. Terrestrial mollusks (land snails) later modified the mantle cavity into a lung (a vascularized air space). Thus, mollusks innovated diverse respiratory strategies: aquatic gills and a primitive lung in land species.
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Present: Nervous system consisting of paired ganglia and nerve cords. Mollusks typically have a set of ganglia: cerebral (brain) ganglia in the head, plus pleural, pedal, and visceral ganglia connected by nerve cords. The early mollusk (e.g. a primitive snail) had a ring of neural tissue around the esophagus and two pairs of nerve cords running to the foot and visceral mass. Cephalization varies – it is moderate in snails, extreme in cephalopods (which evolved a large brain and camera eyes). New: mollusks show significant advancement in neural organization – in cephalopods, the most advanced mollusks, we see the largest brains of any invertebrates (an evolutionary later development).
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Present: Muscular system well-developed, especially the muscular foot used for locomotionallinonehighschool.com. Mollusks evolved a large ventral foot (e.g. for crawling in snails, digging in clams, or as arms/tentacles in cephalopods – modified foot) as a new locomotor structure. The mantle also has muscle to control the mantle cavity and siphons. Overall, mollusks possess smooth and striated muscles for movement, feeding (radula control), and in some, jet propulsion (cephalopod mantle muscles).
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Present: Exoskeleton (shell) in most mollusks, secreted by the mantle. Mollusks typically have a hard calcareous shell made of calcium carbonate. This shell (single, coiled in snails; two hinged valves in bivalves; internal or missing in some) protects the animal (New innovation: first major calcium carbonate external shell in soft-bodied animals for protection). Even shell-less mollusks (like slugs, octopus) have either lost it or retain internal remnants. The shell also serves as skeletal support for muscle attachment.
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Present: Excretory system with nephridia (often called “kidneys” in mollusks). These metanephridia filter waste from the blood/coelomic fluid and release urine into the mantle cavity. Mollusks typically have one or two kidneys. This was an advancement over flame cells, allowing handling of larger volumes and reabsorption. In aquatic mollusks, waste is flushed out with water flow; terrestrial snails excrete uric acid to conserve water.
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Muscular System (Movement): Present: Endocrine system (diffuse). Mollusks produce hormones that regulate reproduction, growth, and metabolism, though they don’t have discrete endocrine glands like vertebrates. E.g., gastropods have neuroendocrine cells in their brain that control egg laying; bivalves secrete hormones for gonad development. A notable endocrine innovation in mollusks is the hormonal control of metamorphosis in those with larvae, and in cephalopods, hormonal triggers for lifecycle events (like reproduction and death). So while mollusks lack a centralized endocrine organ, they have an internal chemical regulation system.
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Sexual reproduction (almost exclusively; only a few do parthenogenesis). Most mollusks have separate sexes (dioecious), though many snails are hermaphroditic. Gonads are well-defined – e.g., snails have an ovotestis (in hermaphrodites) or separate ovary/testis. Fertilization can be external (broadcast spawning in many bivalves) or internal (snails, cephalopods). Mollusks often have a trochophore larva (and a veliger larva in many gastropods and bivalves), indicating their protostome heritage. New: the trochophore larval stage in their life cycle ties them to annelids, and mollusks further evolved a veliger larva with the beginnings of a foot and shell. Terrestrial mollusks (e.g. land snails) innovated by laying eggs on land with protective gelatinous coatings (an adaptation for terrestrial life).
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Reproductive System (Replication): Present: Innate immune system. Mollusks possess immune cells called hemocytes circulating in hemolymph that phagocytose invaders and secrete antimicrobial substances. For example, snail hemocytes will encapsulate parasites, and bivalves have immune responses to pathogens in their open circulatory fluid. No adaptive immunity, but they do have molecular mechanisms for pathogen recognition (e.g. pattern recognition receptors). Some mollusks also have wound-healing processes aided by immune cells.
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Integumentary System (Protection): Present: Mantle and epidermis constitute the integument. The mantle is a specialized fold of skin that not only secretes the shell but also forms the mantle cavity protecting gills and organs. Mollusk skin is usually glandular – many produce mucus (e.g. snail slime) to prevent drying and ease movement. The integument can also have chemical defenses (some marine snails incorporate toxins in their skin or shell). In cephalopods, the skin contains pigment cells (chromatophores) for camouflage – an integumentary innovation in that class. Overall, a protective outer epithelium plus the shell (when present) form the defense against the environment.
Mollusks (early protostome branch).Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Present: Highly developed sensory organs in many mollusks. New innovations: Image-forming eyes evolved independently in this group – especially in cephalopods, which have camera-type eyes comparable to vertebrates. Even some snails have eyes (though simpler) on tentacles. All mollusks have statocysts (balance organs) to orient themselves. They also have chemosensory organs like the osphradium in aquatic mollusks – a water sampling organ in the mantle cavity to test for silt or prey in water. Tactile receptors cover their body (e.g. tentacles of snails feel the environment). In summary, mollusks introduced a variety of senses: vision (from simple ocelli to complex eyes), chemical sense, balance, and touch – making them far more sensorily adept than earlier worm-like ancestors.

Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Nervous System (Signal Response): Present: Complete digestive tract, straight and tubular, often with differentiated regions. Annelids (e.g. earthworms, polychaete worms) have a mouth, pharynx (sometimes with jaws in predatory polychaetes), esophagus, crop and gizzard (in earthworms for grinding soil), intestine, and anus. This allows continual feeding and processing. The novelty here is not the presence of the gut (that existed already) but the specialization: New: development of a muscular gizzard for mechanical breakdown (in some annelids) and long intestine with a typhlosole (internal fold) in earthworms to increase absorption surface.
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Present: Closed circulatory system in most annelids. Blood is confined to vessels – typically a dorsal vessel (pumps blood forward) and a ventral vessel (carries blood rearward), connected by segmental pairs of vessels. Many annelids have multiple “hearts” (contractile aortic arches) that pump blood between dorsal and ventral vessels (earthworms have ~5 pairs of pseudo-hearts). (New: a fully closed blood vascular system evolved here, independently of chordates, enabling efficient oxygen transport in these active worms). Some small annelids or those in low-oxygen environments lack closed systems, but the common annelid ancestor likely had it.
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Partial: Respiratory system varies – many annelids have no specialized respiratory organs, respiring through their skin (which must stay moist for gas exchange). This works for earthworms. However, in large or aquatic annelids (polychaetes), gills or branchiae often develop on segments (e.g. fan worms have feathery gills, polychaetes have parapodia with branched gills). The ancestral annelid was marine and likely had some form of external gill on its segments. So we mark as Partial: present in some. New in annelids: Segmental external gills (in polychaetes) to enhance gas exchange – an innovation for active burrowing or swimming worms that needed more oxygen than diffusion alone could supply.
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Present: Central nervous system with a brain (cerebral ganglia) and a ventral segmented nerve cord. Annelids show clear segmentation in their nervous system: a pair of fused ganglia (nerve cell cluster) in each body segment connected by the double ventral nerve cord, and an anterior brain in the head region. This design allows each segment to have some autonomous control (for locomotion) under the coordination of the brain. (New: segmentation of the nervous system – each segment’s ganglion helps coordinate localized muscle movement, a novel architecture for efficient control of a segmented body).
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Present: Well-developed muscles divided by segment. Each annelid segment contains circular muscles (encircling the segment) and longitudinal muscles (running lengthwise). By alternating contraction of these muscles and using the coelomic fluid as a hydraulic skeleton, annelids achieve peristaltic crawling. They can also anchor some segments via setae (bristles) and move others – giving them excellent burrowing ability. The segmentation allows localized muscle contractions without disturbing the whole body, which is a functional innovation.
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Partial: Hydrostatic skeleton via segmented coelomic compartments. Annelids have fluid-filled coelom in each segment, separated by septa (internal walls). Each segment’s fluid acts as a hydrostatic skeleton that the muscles work against. There is no hard skeleton, but the segmentation of the hydrostatic skeleton is new, allowing finer control of body shape (one segment can stiffen while adjacent ones contract). No bone or shell exists, but some annelids have minor hard parts: e.g. some marine annelids have chitinous jaws or support rods for gills, and tubeworms secrete tubes, but these are specific cases.
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Present: Excretory organs in each segment. Annelids typically have a pair of metanephridia in most body segments. These tubular excretory units collect coelomic fluid from one segment, filter out wastes, and expel urine through pores in the next segment. This segmentation of excretory function is an innovation – essentially a repeating kidney in each segment for efficient waste removal and osmoregulation. (Larval annelids start with protonephridia, but adults use metanephridia.) Earthworms, for example, have one pair of nephridia per segment that effectively remove metabolic waste.
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Muscular System (Movement): Present: Endocrine system (mostly neuroendocrine). Annelids produce hormones that regulate processes like reproduction and regeneration. For instance, in polychaete worms, seasonal breeding and the transformation into a reproductive form (epitoke) are controlled by neurohormones. Earthworms have hormones that regulate their cocoon production and metabolism. While annelids don’t have discrete endocrine glands (no thyroid, etc.), they do have groups of neurosecretory cells in the brain and segmental ganglia that release hormones into the body fluid. So an endocrine system exists, but it’s distributed. (An example: the hormone erythrophoredin in earthworms stimulates red blood cell production.)
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Sexual reproduction, often with interesting variations. Many marine annelids (polychaetes) have separate sexes and spawn gametes into the water; some even undergo epitoky – transforming into a swimming reproductive form – new behavior linked to endocrine control. Fertilization is external and larvae are trochophores (shared with mollusks). Earthworms and leeches (clitellates) are hermaphroditic – they have both ovaries and testes. They perform mutual cross-fertilization and produce cocoons via a special structure called the clitellum which secretes a cocoon for eggs and sperm. New innovations: the clitellum in oligochaetes/leeches for protecting fertilized eggs on land, and the aforementioned epitoky in polychaetes for synchronized breeding. Both are unique reproductive strategies in annelids.
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Reproductive System (Replication): Present: Innate immune system. Annelids have coelomocytes (immune cells) in their coelomic fluid that ingest bacteria and produce antimicrobial agents. Earthworms, for example, secrete lysenin (a protein) to defend against parasites, and have an immune memory-like phenomenon in their coelomocyte responses. They lack an adaptive immune system with antibodies, but can recognize repeated infections with a heightened response. Also, the mucus of earthworms and leeches has antibacterial properties. Thus, annelids possess a competent innate immune defense, on par with other invertebrates.
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Integumentary System (Protection): Present: Moist cuticle over epidermis as integument. Annelids have a thin flexible cuticle (made of collagen) secreted by the epidermis, which protects them and prevents dehydration (on land, earthworms must stay in moist soil to keep cuticle wet for respiration). The skin has glands – e.g. earthworms secrete mucus to keep skin moist and ease movement. Many annelids also have chitin bristles called setae projecting from their integument (four pairs of setae per segment in earthworms) – these aid in traction and defense (they make the worm harder to pull from its burrow). Some polychaete annelids have additional integumentary structures: e.g. parchment tube worms secrete papery tubes (protective housing), others have iridescent cuticles with bristles for defense. Overall, the annelid integument is a versatile protective layer for a soft-bodied organism.
Annelids (segmented worms, second protos.Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Present: Annelids often have well-developed sensory structures, especially in the head (for predatory or mobile species). Polychaete worms typically have a distinct head with eyes (from simple eyespots to fairly complex lensed eyes in some), antennae, palps, and nuchal organs (chemosensory pits). These allow them to detect light, movement, and chemicals – crucial for hunting or avoiding predators. Earthworms, which burrow in soil, have no eyes but do have light-sensitive cells in their skin (they detect light to avoid coming out in daylight) and are very sensitive to vibrations (ground vibrations signal danger). They also have chemo-receptors in their anterior to sense food in soil. Leeches have multiple pairs of eyes along their body to sense hosts. In summary, annelids made advances in sensory organization: New: the development of nuchal organs (a unique chemosensory structure in polychaetes) and segmental sensors that together give these worms a good perception of their environment.

Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Nervous System (Signal Response): Present: Complete digestive system with highly specialized feeding appendages. Early arthropods (e.g. trilobites) had a mouth on the ventral side and paired appendages that likely helped direct food to the mouth. They had a foregut, midgut with digestive glands (hepatopancreas in modern terms), and hindgut. Fossil trilobites show evidence of a crop and branching digestive caeca. Arthropods as a group innovated diverse mouthparts: New: jointed jaws – e.g. mandibles in later arthropods, and specialized diets. Trilobites themselves had mouthparts formed by hard edges of appendages (and a calcified lip called a hypostome). The through-gut with regional specialization (storage, grinding, enzyme secretion, absorption) was fully present.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Circulatory System (Internal Transport): Present: Open circulatory system with a dorsal tubular heart. Arthropods pump hemolymph through an open cavity (hemocoel). The heart is a longitudinal vessel with ostia (valved openings) that suck blood in and pump it forward. In a trilobite or primitive arthropod, the heart lay along the back and pushed blood toward the head; blood then percolated through sinuses and returned dorsally. This system is less efficient than closed circulation but sufficient given arthropods’ other adaptations for oxygen transport (like tracheae or gills). Most arthropods retain this open system. (Cephalopods are the only invertebrates that went closed – arthropods did not, aside from some small diffusion-based exceptions.) So, no new circulatory innovation compared to mollusks/annelids’ closed system, but New: the combination of a heart and extensive sinuses supporting a high metabolism with the help of respiratory innovations (like tracheal tubes in insects) is an arthropod hallmark.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Respiratory System (Gas Exchange & Energ: Present: Specialized respiratory systems. Aquatic arthropods (including trilobites) had gills – trilobites possessed filamentous gill structures on their appendages for gas exchange. These were likely the first clearly evident gills in the fossil record. Terrestrial arthropods later evolved tracheae – an extensive network of air-filled tubes delivering oxygen directly to tissues (insects, centipedes) – or book lungs (in arachnids). Thus, arthropods introduced new respiratory adaptations: New: book gills in horseshoe crabs (similar to what trilobites had), book lungs in spiders, and especially tracheal systems in insects which allowed arthropods to conquer land by delivering air internally. These are unique innovations not seen in earlier groups.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Digestive System (Nutrient Acquisition): Present: Highly centralized nervous system with a brain and ventral nerve cord. Arthropods inherited the annelid-like nervous system but took it further. They have a fused brain (typically 3-part: protocerebrum, deutocerebrum, tritocerebrum) in the head and a double ventral nerve cord with ganglia in each segment. In trilobites, for example, there would have been a cerebral ganglion in the head and a chain of ganglia along the body. Arthropods show great cephalization – in insects and crustaceans, the brain controls complex behaviors, and in some (like bees) even learning. New: arthropods also developed complex compound eyes and other advanced sensory inputs that required more sophisticated neural processing. So their nervous system is an upgrade in complexity and processing power relative to earlier worms. They can perform fast, coordinated movements and behaviors (e.g. escape reflexes, hunting tactics) thanks to this advanced CNS.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Excretory System (Waste Removal & Osmore: Present: Powerful, segmented muscles attached to exoskeleton for movement. Arthropods replaced the hydrostatic skeleton with a jointed exoskeleton and thus evolved striated muscles that attach internally to the exoskeleton (via infoldings called apodemes). Trilobites, for instance, had muscles to move each leg segment and to enroll (roll up the body). Arthropod muscles contract much faster than those of annelids, enabling quick motions. New: Flight muscles in winged insects (much later) are an arthropod innovation, giving insects the first powered flight on Earth. Even early on, arthropods achieved movements like rapid running and precise manipulation with jointed limbs, far surpassing the locomotor abilities of soft-bodied ancestors.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Immune System (Defense Mechanisms): Present: Exoskeletal system (hard external skeleton) made of chitin and proteins, often mineralized with calcium carbonate. Arthropods like trilobites encased their body in a jointed shell – providing protection and points for muscle attachment. This was a revolutionary innovation: New: a jointed exoskeleton that can be molted (ecdysis). The exoskeleton in trilobites had articulated segments allowing flexibility while maintaining armor. In later arthropods, this evolved into various forms (e.g. insect cuticle with wax layer against desiccation, crustacean carapaces). The exoskeleton also created specialized body regions (head, thorax, abdomen in many) by segment fusion. The cost of this system is the need to molt to grow, but its benefit is tremendous defense and support. Trilobite fossils show even the eyes had hard lenses of calcite. No earlier animal had such a complex exoskeleton – truly a defining arthropod feature.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Skeletal System (Support & Structure): Present: Excretory systems adapted to life in various environments. Arthropods evolved different excretory organs: aquatic ones (like crustaceans, including trilobites) have gland-based organs (antennal or maxillary glands, analogous to kidneys) that filter hemolymph and excrete urine. Terrestrial arthropods (insects, arachnids) use Malpighian tubules – thin tubes that empty waste into the gut for excretion with feces, an adaptation to conserve water. Trilobites likely had primitive glands at the base of legs (similar to green glands in modern crustaceans) to eliminate waste. So an excretory system was present and New adaptations: Malpighian tubules in insects allowed efficient nitrogen waste removal with minimal water loss – a key innovation for terrestrial life.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Muscular System (Movement): Present: Endocrine system well-developed. Arthropods have an array of hormones controlling molting, metamorphosis, reproduction, and metabolism. For instance, ecdysone hormone triggers molting of the exoskeleton – a unique need because of their growth by molting. Juvenile hormone in insects dictates whether a molt produces another juvenile stage or an adult – enabling complete metamorphosis. These are new endocrine innovations in arthropods. Also, neurohormones from the brain control these processes. So arthropods possess complex endocrine glands like the prothoracic gland (in insects) for ecdysone, corpora allata for juvenile hormone, etc. Such hormonal regulation of development and metamorphosis is a significant arthropod trait.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Endocrine System (Regulation): Present: Sexual reproduction (with rare exceptions like parthenogenesis in some insects). Arthropods typically have separate sexes and internal fertilization is common, especially in terrestrial groups. Early aquatic arthropods (trilobites) probably released eggs and sperm into the water (there’s evidence some trilobites may have carried eggs in specialized brood structures). Arthropods show immense variety: many insects perform elaborate mating behaviors and lay shelled eggs on land (a necessity for terrestrial life), while crustaceans often carry eggs until hatching. New innovations: Arthropods were the first to evolve internal fertilization in many lineages (e.g. insects, arachnids) to protect gametes from drying out, and the first to lay cleidoic (waterproof) eggs on land (insects). Additionally, metamorphosis – seen in many insects (holometabolism) – is an innovation where larval and adult stages are distinct, allowing exploitation of different niches. This extreme change is under hormonal control and is unique to arthropods among invertebrates.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Reproductive System (Replication): Present: Innate immune system advanced. Arthropods have both cellular and humoral innate immunity. They have hemocytes that do phagocytosis and encapsulation of parasites (similar to other invertebrates). Remarkably, arthropods also produce antimicrobial peptides (e.g. defensins) upon infection – for instance, insects upon detecting bacteria can synthesize potent antibiotics to clear infection. Horseshoe crabs (an ancient chelicerate arthropod) have amoebocytes in their blood that coagulate in presence of bacterial endotoxins – so efficiently that modern medicine uses their blood for endotoxin tests. While still no adaptive immune cells, the genetic toolkit for innate immunity in arthropods is quite sophisticated (Toll pathways, etc., which even informed vertebrate innate immunity). Thus, arthropods can survive infections in varied environments with a robust innate immune response.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Integumentary System (Protection): Present: Exoskeleton as integument – the arthropod cuticle is the integument, providing both support and protection from the environment (physical and chemical). It’s multilayered (waxy outer layer to prevent water loss in land arthropods, rigid layers for defense). Insects and spiders minimized dehydration with their cuticle – crucial for terrestrial success. New: The arthropod cuticle is not just armor; it forms specialized structures: e.g. waterproofing wax, coloration for camouflage or warning, sensory bristles that pierce through it, and in some, silk-spinning structures (spiders) or wing membranes (insects) – all integumentary derivatives. Arthropods also perform ecdysis – periodically shedding the old integument to grow – which is a vulnerability but necessary for a hard integument user. So the integumentary system in arthropods is dynamic and versatile, enabling life from deep oceans to dry deserts.
Arthropods (early ones like Trilobites).Lymphatic System (Fluid Balance & Immuni: Present: Highly acute sensory organs – one of arthropods’ greatest strengths. New innovations: Compound eyes with multiple ommatidia (facets) giving a broad field of vision – present even in the earliest trilobites (which had large compound eyes with calcite lenses). Compound eyes provided motion detection and mosaic vision with high frame rates, a huge leap in predator/prey awareness. Arthropods also developed antennae – segmented sensory appendages rich in chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors – essentially “smelling” and “feeling” the environment. Trilobites had antennae; modern insects’ antennae can detect pheromones miles away. They also have mechanosensory hairs and tympanal organs for detecting sound vibrations (e.g. cricket ears on legs). The arthropod head typically bundles major senses: eyes, antennae, sometimes palps for taste. Many arthropods (like bees or ants) can communicate via pheromones and detect them with exquisite sensitivity. Some insects evolved complex ocelli (simple eyes) in addition to compound eyes for light-level detection, and certain spiders (though not compound-eyed) evolved multiple lens eyes with high resolution. In summary, arthropods came to dominate environments in part due to their sensory/perceptive prowess – spotting predators or prey, finding mates by scent, hearing sounds – an array of senses unmatched in earlier animal groups.

Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Nervous System: Inherited: No nervous cells at all – like their unicellular ancestors, they rely on cell-level chemical signaling (no neurons). Innovated: Multicellular coordination without nerves; cells communicate chemically to respond to light and stress, but no true nervous system is present.
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Respiratory System: Inherited: Gas exchange by simple diffusion across cell surfaces (no respiratory organs needed in water). Innovated: Thalli (algal bodies) are thin/leafy to maximize surface area for O₂/CO₂ diffusion in aquatic environments; no specialized respiratory structures since water delivers gases directly.
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Digestive System: Inherited: Autotrophic nutrition via photosynthesis (chloroplasts from ancestral endosymbiosis) – no digestive organs; nutrients absorbed from water or produced internally. Innovated: Complex pigments (e.g. phycobilins) to capture low-light wavelengths and storage of sugars/starch internally; some can absorb dissolved organic matter, but there is no true digestive system (all feeding is at the cellular level).
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Circulatory System: Inherited: No circulatory system; internal transport occurs by cell-to-cell diffusion as in ancestral algae. Innovated: Simple cytoplasmic streaming and cell connections (e.g. pit plugs between cells) to distribute nutrients within the thallus; still no blood or vessels due to small size and aquatic habitat.
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Reproductive System: Inherited: Sexual reproduction with gametes (alternation of generations as in ancestral algae); still relies on water for fertilization. Innovated: Unique non-motile sperm (spermatia) and complex triphasic life cycle in some red algae – after fertilization, an enclosed carposporophyte develops on the mother plant, an innovation to increase zygote survival; spores (carpospores) are released, forming a separate generation. Also produce tough-walled spores that resist degradation, but still require aquatic dispersal.
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Muscular System: Inherited: No muscle or motile organs; cells change shape or grow toward stimuli (very limited movement). Innovated: Flexible, cartilaginous cell walls and slippery mucilage allow bending with currents (helps prevent breakage); some can contract gelatinous holdfasts slightly to cling to rocks, but movement is entirely passive (via water flow).
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Skeletal System: Inherited: Rigid cellulose cell walls for structural support (as in ancestral plants). Innovated: In coralline red algae, deposition of calcium carbonate in cell walls (a rudimentary exoskeleton) for added support and herbivore deterrence – a new trait among algae. Most red algae have a gel-like matrix (agar/carrageenan) in their walls, giving them flexibility and shock absorption against waves.
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Immune System: Inherited: Basic chemical defenses against microbes/grazers (e.g. inherited ability to produce antimicrobial compounds as many algae do). Innovated: Thick cell walls and mucilage act as a barrier to pathogens and small herbivores; many red algae synthesize unique secondary metabolites (e.g. brominated compounds) that deter herbivores or fungal infections – a chemical immune strategy in lieu of cellular immunity.
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Endocrine System: Inherited: Cell-to-cell signaling molecules for growth and development (e.g. ancestral algae used simple hormones for reproduction). Innovated: Release of pheromone-like chemicals to coordinate gamete release in water; otherwise no specialized endocrine organs (each cell can respond to environmental cues like daylength or nutrients individually).
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Excretory System: Inherited: No excretory organs; metabolic wastes (e.g. ammonia, oxygen from photosynthesis) diffuse out to the water directly. Innovated: Ability to deposit excess calcium or heavy metals in cell walls (effectively sequestering wastes); excess by-products can also be stored in inert form in cells. Red algae simply rely on water currents to carry away wastes, an unchanged strategy from single-celled ancestors.
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Integumentary System: Inherited: A simple epidermal cell layer with a polysaccharide cell wall (like ancestral algae). Innovated: Waxy and gelatinous coatings on the thallus that reduce desiccation during low tide exposure and protect against UV radiation; some (e.g. coralline algae) have a hard calcareous surface for protection. Overall, the “skin” is a mucilage-covered cell wall that deters pathogens and prevents drying, since true integument (multiple cell layers) is absent.
Red Algae (multicellular marine algae).Sensory System: Inherited: Light-sensitive molecules (e.g. phycoerythrin pigment) allow orientation to light; some reproductive cells can sense chemicals. Innovated: Though lacking eyes or nerves, red algae can detect light intensity changes and adjust photosynthesis. A few have primitive photoreceptor patches on spores, but generally rely on inherited phototaxis mechanisms of their microscopic ancestors; no dedicated sensory organs evolved in this group.

Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Nervous System: Inherited: No neurons or nervous system – like protist ancestors, communication is via chemical gradients and electric impulses along cells. Innovated: Mycelial network coordination – fungal hyphae can transmit signals (electrical and chemical) throughout the colony, functioning as a diffuse “network” that responds to nutrients or damage (e.g. a localized resource triggers whole-network growth toward it). There is still no true nervous system, but the fungus behaves as a coordinated organism despite lack of neurons.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Respiratory System: Inherited: Gas exchange by diffusion across cell surfaces (ancestral fungi absorbed O₂ directly). Innovated: Thread-like hyphae permeate substrate and provide a large surface area for O₂ uptake and CO₂ release; in terrestrial forms, fungi often grow in humid microenvironments or within tissues to ensure gases stay dissolved. No dedicated respiratory organs evolved – even large fruiting bodies exchange gases via pores or surfaces.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Digestive System: Inherited: External digestion – like ancestral decomposer microbes, fungi secrete enzymes and absorb the breakdown products. Innovated: Powerful hydrolytic enzymes secreted into the environment to decompose complex polymers (cellulose, lignin) that earlier organisms couldn’t digest; this extracellular digestion allows fungi to “digest” food outside their bodies and then absorb nutrients. Hyphae then transport these nutrients inward. Fungi can decompose wood and other tough substrates, a novel ability in the ecosystem.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Circulatory System: Inherited: No circulatory system; nutrient movement via diffusion from cell to cell. Innovated: Hyphal transport – cytoplasmic streaming within hyphae distributes nutrients throughout the mycelium (analogous to a simple circulatory function). Some fungi have septal pores between cells allowing nutrients and organelles to move freely. Thus, a fungus can translocate resources (e.g. send sugars from a sugar-rich area to growing tips elsewhere), an ability absent in single-celled ancestors.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Reproductive System: Inherited: Spore reproduction (both sexual and asexual) as in ancestral fungi – producing numerous spores that disperse in water or air. Innovated: Complex life cycles with distinct mating types; sexual spores formed after hyphal fusion (plasmogamy/karyogamy) allowing genetic recombination. On land, fungi evolved stress-resistant spores with tough walls that survive desiccation. Some early fungi retained motile zoospores (with flagella) in water (an ancestral trait), but terrestrial fungi innovated non-motile spores dispersed by wind and fruiting bodies to launch them.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Muscular System: Inherited: No muscle tissue; movement occurs by growth (hyphae extending toward food). Innovated: Turgor-driven growth and movement – fungi penetrate substrates by generating internal pressure in hyphae, and some can rapidly eject spores (e.g. Pilobolus shoots spores by building up pressure). A few have trap structures (like constricting rings to snare nematodes) that snap shut via sudden turgor changes. These are “movements” achieved chemically, not by muscle, but represent new mechanisms to achieve tasks like prey capture or spore dispersal.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Skeletal System: Inherited: Rigid cell walls (with chitin) providing shape (a trait shared with ancestral fungi). Innovated: Chitinous cell walls (a tough polysaccharide also found in arthropod exoskeletons) for strong structural support of hyphae; some fungi form large multicellular fruiting bodies (mushrooms) that stand erect – their cell walls and internal turgor form a rudimentary skeletal support. Fungi also produce hardened survival structures (sclerotia) that can be thought of as a protective “skeleton” to weather harsh conditions.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Immune System: Inherited: Basic innate defenses – fungi produce antimicrobial metabolites (ancestral trait to outcompete bacteria). Innovated: Potent antibiotic production (e.g. Penicillium produces penicillin) to kill competitors – essentially chemical warfare as an immune strategy. Fungi can recognize self vs. non-self hyphae: if genetically different mycelia meet, they often reject fusion (an innate allorecognition system preventing parasitic takeovers). These innovations protect the fungus from microbes and other fungi, fulfilling immune-like roles without immune cells.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Endocrine System: Inherited: Simple chemical regulation of growth and reproduction (e.g. ancestral fungi used pheromones for mating). Innovated: Mating pheromones that coordinate sexual reproduction (ensuring hyphae of different mating types grow toward each other); other hormones regulate processes like spore release and hyphal branching. While fungi have no discrete endocrine glands, specialized cells in the mycelium secrete signals (for example, to initiate fruiting body formation when conditions are right), acting as a primitive endocrine system.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Excretory System: Inherited: No excretory organs; waste metabolites diffuse out of cells. Innovated: External digestion blurs the line between digestion and excretion – fungi release enzymes and thereby “excrete” digestion byproducts into their environment, then reabsorb what they need. Toxic waste products can be retained in vacuoles or incorporated into inactive forms (e.g. oxalate crystals). Essentially, fungi innovate by dumping excess compounds into the environment (or into aging parts like fruiting body tissue that will be shed), relying on environmental dilution of wastes.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Integumentary System: Inherited: A single-cell-thick outer layer (no skin or cuticle); ancestral fungi had cell walls for protection. Innovated: Chitin-rich cell wall that guards against environmental stress and predators; in terrestrial fungi, many hyphae aggregate and may form a protective outer layer on fruiting bodies (a pseudo-skin) to reduce water loss. Some fungi produce melanin in cell walls, shielding against UV radiation – an integumentary adaptation for life on land.
Fungi (aquatic/early fungi).Sensory System: Inherited: Environmental sensing via receptors – ancestral fungi could sense chemicals and light (e.g. many spores germinate in response to nutrient cues). Innovated: Enhanced environmental sensitivity: fungi can detect subtle gradients of nutrients and grow towards them (chemotropism). Many fungi are light-sensitive; for instance, certain mushrooms only form when exposed to light, indicating evolved photoreceptors. They also sense gravity (negative gravitropism in mushroom stems to grow upward). Although fungi have no specialized sense organs, their mycelium acts as a diffuse sensory web, responding to touch, chemicals, light, and gravity to optimize growth.

Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Nervous System: Inherited: No nerve cells; each cell responds individually to stimuli (like light or chemicals) as did unicellular ancestors. Innovated: In motile forms (e.g. Volvox colonies), cells coordinate via chemical signals, allowing the whole colony to swim in a directed manner – an early step toward a nervous system. Some green algae show colony-wide coordination (e.g. flagellar beating in unison), but this is achieved chemically/electrically rather than by specialized neurons.
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Respiratory System: Inherited: Diffusion of gases across the entire cell or thallus surface (no respiratory organs, similar to ancestors). Innovated: Many developed flat, thin bodies or hollow tubes to maximize surface area for O₂/CO₂ exchange in water. No stomata in aquatic algae, but some charophyte algae living at land-water margins developed simple air‐exposed structures that could take up CO₂ from air when exposed. Overall, gas exchange remains via diffusion, but body shapes adjusted to facilitate it in new environments (e.g. surface-floating forms uptake CO₂ from air-water interface).
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Digestive System: Inherited: Photosynthesis provides food; no ingestive digestion (as with ancestral algae). Innovated: Some green algae can also absorb dissolved organic nutrients or even exhibit mixotrophy (ingesting particles) in low light, an ability beyond strictly autotrophic red algae. Advanced forms (charophytes) protect their reproductive cells with sterile tissue, akin to primitive gametangia, providing nutrients to the developing zygote – a precursor to feeding an embryo, though true nutrient provisioning (endosperm) comes later in land plants.
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Circulatory System: Inherited: No circulatory system; each cell or filament obtains nutrients by diffusion from surroundings. Innovated: In larger multicellular green algae, rudimentary internal transport appears – for example, siphonous algae (like Caulerpa) have streaming cytoplasm that moves nutrients within giant cells. Some filamentous forms have specialized “transfer cells” to shuttle nutrients between adjacent cells. This is not a true circulatory system, but it’s an innovation toward internal distribution in big algae.
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Reproductive System: Inherited: Aquatic reproduction with flagellated gametes that swim (like ancestral protists). Innovated: Oogamy in some groups – i.e. evolution of a large non-motile egg and a small motile sperm (e.g. in charophytes), which is a step toward land-plant reproduction. Some green algae (e.g. Chara) developed protective jackets around gametes (primitive antheridia and oogonia), an inherited trait that green algae share with land plants. Also, many green algae can reproduce asexually by fragmenting or via motile spores, giving them flexible reproductive modes.
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Muscular System: Inherited: No muscle tissue; motility comes from flagella on reproductive cells or motile unicells (a trait from unicellular ancestors). Innovated: Many green algae are motile in some stage – e.g. flagellar motility is refined: unicellular Chlamydomonas and colonial Volvox use eukaryotic flagella to swim. Colonial forms coordinate flagella for propulsion. A few large algae show minor contractile movements: for example, some filamentous algae can bend slowly toward light by differential growth. Nonetheless, contractile muscle did not evolve; movement remains limited to flagellar swimming or growth responses.
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Skeletal System: Inherited: Cellulose cell walls (like early plant ancestors) for structure. Innovated: Some calcify their tissues (e.g. Halimeda, a green alga, lays down calcium carbonate), giving a sturdier structure in wave-swept habitats. Charophyte algae (closest to land plants) developed plasmodesmata (tiny channels between cells) – an inherited trait passed to land plants – which structurally integrates multicellular algae and allows mechanical support via shared turgor pressure. While they have no true skeleton, turgid cell walls and sometimes calcium encrustation provide a simple support framework.
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Immune System: Inherited: Basic defense chemicals (e.g. antioxidants to handle UV or free radicals, like ancestral algae). Innovated: Green algae often form symbiotic relationships (e.g. with fungi in lichens), indicating biochemical compatibility and defense sharing. They produce deterrent molecules (some emit foul-tasting or toxic metabolites to avoid herbivory by fish/snails). Some filamentous green algae can differentiate a tough, dormant zygote with a resistant coat (sporopollenin in charophytes) – this protects the “embryo” from pathogens and harsh conditions, akin to an immune protective adaptation for that life stage.
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Endocrine System: Inherited: Simple chemical signaling for cell growth and reproduction (e.g. cues for gamete release tied to light cycles). Innovated: Introduction of plant hormones in rudimentary form: for instance, auxin-like substances are found in green algae and can influence cell elongation and division. Green algae also respond to pheromones during mating (e.g. Volvox releases sexual inducer proteins). These represent early endocrine-like communication, although dedicated organs are absent – every cell both senses and responds to such signals.
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Excretory System: Inherited: No excretory organs; waste (like excess oxygen from photosynthesis, or ammonia from protein metabolism) diffuses into the water. Innovated: Some freshwater green algae can actively expel excess water (via contractile vacuoles in unicellular forms) to cope with osmotic stress, an ability carried from unicellular ancestors. Multicellular forms simply rely on diffusion and shedding parts (e.g. a dying portion of a thallus may sequester heavy metals or waste, then break off). Essentially, waste management remains minimal – an algae doesn’t concentrate toxins internally but releases or isolates them in inert cell wall material.
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Integumentary System: Inherited: A single-cell-layer “body surface” (no epidermis per se, just cell walls in contact with environment). Innovated: Some algae secrete a gelatinous sheath around colonies (e.g. Hydrodictyon nets or Nostoc balls in symbiosis) to prevent desiccation and shield from UV or predators – a primitive integument. In charophytes at water’s edge, a rudimentary cuticle-like polymer (sporopollenin) covers zygotes to prevent drying. Though true cuticle on vegetative parts is absent until land plants, these algae began evolving surface protections, foreshadowing the land plant integument.
Green Algae (multicellular chlorophytes.Sensory System: Inherited: Light detection via eye-spots in motile cells – e.g. Chlorophyte algae like Chlamydomonas have a photoreceptive eyespot that guides swimming toward light, an ancestral sensory organelle. Innovated: Refinement of the eyespot and flagellar response for accurate phototaxis (green algae swim toward optimal light intensities for photosynthesis). Some green algae can sense gravity (negative geotaxis in certain planktonic forms) and many sense chemicals (moving toward nutrients). These sensory capabilities are still cell-autonomous (each cell reacts on its own), but in colonial forms, signals are coordinated so the entire colony moves as one toward light or nutrients.

Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Nervous System: Inherited: No neurons – sponges’ unicellular ancestors simply reacted to stimuli individually. Innovated: Intercellular communication that coordinates the whole sponge without nerves: sponge cells use chemical signals and calcium wave propagation to respond collectively (e.g. closing pores). They lack a true nervous system entirelycourses.lumenlearning.com, but can perform simple reflexes like contracting the body when irritated. This represents an early attempt at integrating responses among cells (myocytes around osculum contract together), even though no specialized neural tissue exists.
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Respiratory System: Inherited: Direct gas diffusion – every cell exchanges O₂/CO₂ with water, as did single-celled ancestors. Innovated: A constant water flow system: sponges pump water through their bodies (via choanocyte beating) which continuously brings in oxygen-rich water and expels CO₂ and wastes. This flow-through respiration means every cell is bathed in fresh water for gas exchange. There are no gills or respiratory organs; instead, the aquiferous canal system performs respiratory function by diffusion.
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Digestive System: Inherited: Intracellular digestion – as in protozoan ancestors, sponge cells (choanocytes) engulf food particles and digest them inside vacuoles. Innovated: Filter feeding architecture: choanocytes create currents and trap bacteria/particles on their collars, ingesting them (phagocytosis)courses.lumenlearning.com. Amoebocytes then distribute the nutrients. Sponges have no true digestive tract; the central spongocoel is not a stomach but a conduit for water. The innovation is a multicellular feeding strategy: filtering vast volumes of water to gather food, an ability unique to sponges at this stage.
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Circulatory System: Inherited: No circulatory system; ancestral condition of diffusion from cell to cell. Innovated: Internal water circulation doubles as nutrient transport: choanocytes capture food and amoebocytes wander, carrying nutrients to other cells. The constant flow of water acts like a primitive circulatory system, distributing oxygen and food throughout the sponge bodycourses.lumenlearning.com. Sponges also have a gelatinous matrix (mesohyl) where amoebocytes move nutrients around – a proto-circulatory role without distinct vessels or blood.
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Reproductive System: Inherited: Asexual reproduction by fragmentation or budding (a trait common in simple organisms). Innovated: Both sexual and asexual reproduction: sponges produce sperm and eggs (often hermaphroditically) – sperm are released into water and captured by other sponges’ choanocytes which transport them to eggs (an internal fertilization strategy unique for such a simple organism). They also form gemmules (in freshwater sponges) – resilient cyst-like bundles of cells that can survive harsh conditions and regrowcourses.lumenlearning.com, an innovation allowing colonization of new areas after dormancy.
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Muscular System: Inherited: No muscle fibers; ancestral cells could contract slightly with actin/myosin but no organized musculature. Innovated: Specialized contractile cells (myocytes) around openings and canals that can constrict the osculum or ostia, enabling the sponge to regulate water flow and “sneeze” out debris. The whole sponge body can also slowly contract by coordinating these cells. Though extremely slow and limited, this is the first appearance of multicellular body contractions without true muscle tissue.
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Skeletal System: Inherited: Structural support from spicules/minerals (some single-celled ancestors had biomineral structures). Innovated: A skeleton of spicules (silica or calcium carbonate spikes) and spongin fibers (collagen) that give the sponge its shape and rigidity. This internal meshwork is an innovation providing defense and support – spicules deter predators and support the canal system. Each sponge class has its own skeletal adaptation (glass sponges with elaborate silica networks, demosponges with spongin fibers), showing new evolutionary experiments in support structures.
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Immune System: Inherited: Basic self vs. non-self recognition at cellular level (even single cells can distinguish own vs. foreign). Innovated: Sponges exhibit primitive immune responses: if cells from a different sponge enter, they recognize and reject them (sponges will not fuse with non-kin – they “recognize” self tissue). This is an early immune system trait. Additionally, many sponges host symbiotic algae but can produce toxic chemicals to prevent over-colonization by microbes. These antimicrobial and antifouling compounds in their tissues are an adaptive defense, substituting for cellular immunity by chemically deterring pathogens.
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Endocrine System: Inherited: No distinct endocrine organs; ancestral sponges (and protozoans) used local chemical cues. Innovated: Sponge cells release chemical signals to coordinate activities – for example, pheromone-like substances can induce spawning (synchronized release of gametes) across many individuals. While lacking organs like glands, sponges rely on diffuse production of such signals. They also have growth factors within the mesohyl that regulate cell differentiation. This is a very rudimentary hormonal system operating within the sponge’s simple body plan.
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Excretory System: Inherited: No excretory organs; metabolic wastes diffuse from cells into the water (the ancestral mode). Innovated: Using the water-current system to expel waste – ammonia and other wastes simply diffuse into the internal water stream and get flushed out the osculumcourses.lumenlearning.com. Essentially, the sponge’s constant filtering serves as a primitive excretory mechanism as well. Sponges have also specialized amoebocytes that can sequester and remove unwanted products (sometimes migrating to the sponge surface to discard wastes).
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Integumentary System: Inherited: A simple outer cell layer (pinacoderm) functions as a protective surface, similar to a proto-epithelium in single-celled ancestors that just had a membrane. Innovated: The pinacoderm acts like an integument: pinacocyte cells form a skin-like layer that protects inner cells and can regulate pore size. Sponges also embed gritty spicules in their surface and often secrete mucus, deterring predators and fouling organisms. Some even have symbiotic bacteria on their surface that produce protective chemicals. So, while only one cell thick, the sponge “skin” plus its biochemical defenses form an early integumentary system.
Sponges (Phylum Porifera).Sensory System: Inherited: Each cell is individually sensitive (ancestral protists responded to touch/chemicals). Innovated: A coordinated reaction to stimuli: e.g. if one part of a sponge is touched or encounters toxic water, the whole sponge can gradually close its openings. Sponges have mechano- and chemo-receptor cells scattered in the pinacoderm that detect changes (like increased sediment) and trigger a whole-body response (stop pumping water). There are no sense organs (no eyes, ears, etc.), but ciliated oscula can sense flow rates, and cells detect light vs. dark (many sponges contract in bright light). This represents the very start of integrated sensory response in multicellular animals without dedicated organs.

Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Nervous System: Inherited: Primitive neural elements from a common ancestor with nerve nets (if we assume they diverged after nerves evolved, though it’s debated). Innovated: A diffuse nerve net throughout the body with an aboral (top) sensory organ integrating signals – ctenophores have no centralized brain, but a “subepidermal nerve net” that rings the mouth and concentrates near comb rows, pharynx, and tentacles. This nervous system, while still a net, is more structured than sponges’ absence of nerves. They independently evolved some neural circuitry (using unique neurotransmitters absent in other animals), possibly representing a parallel evolution of nervous systems.
Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Respiratory System: Inherited: Gas diffusion through body surface (like cnidarian ancestors; no specialized system). Innovated: Ctenophores are gelatinous with a large surface area to volume ratio, so every cell can obtain oxygen directly from water. They lack gills; instead, their highly vascularized gastrovascular canals and thin body walls allow efficient diffusion. The beating of comb plate cilia also creates water currents that refresh the surface for gas exchange. No specific respiratory organ was needed due to their aquatic, mostly small or thin-bodied nature.
Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Digestive System: Inherited: A single opening gastrovascular cavity (from cnidarian-like ancestors) where digestion begins. Innovated: Through-gut (partial) – most comb jellies have a mouth and anal pores, meaning they can expel some wastes from the opposite end. Food is captured by sticky colloblast cells on tentacles, brought to the mouth, digested in a pharynx and stomach, and nutrients spread via a branched canal system. The presence of anal pores (two small openings) allows elimination of small waste, though larger egesta are still regurgitated. This is a step toward a one-way digestive tract, increasing feeding efficiency by not mixing waste with incoming food.
Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Circulatory System: Inherited: No circulatory system; ancestral condition of gut cavity doubling as circulatory space. Innovated: A canal system branching through the jelly (from the central stomach to the comb rows and tentacles) that distributes digested nutrients and oxygenated fluid. The ctenophore mesoglea has muscle fibers that help stir the internal fluid. There is no heart or blood, but the gastrovascular canals functionally move nutrients around the body. The evolution of these canals is an innovation that supports their larger size compared to simpler nerve-net animals.
Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Reproductive System: Inherited: Sexual reproduction with gametes spawned into water (like early metazoans). Innovated: Most ctenophores are simultaneous hermaphrodites, producing both eggs and sperm, often daily. They practice external fertilization: gametes are released through the mouth or specialized pores into the water column. Some can self-fertilize if mates are not nearby, ensuring reproduction even at low population density. The fertilized egg develops directly into a small ctenophore (cydippid larva) without a drastic metamorphosis, a relatively direct development compared to the metagenetic life cycles of jellyfish – an innovation that allows rapid population increase in good conditions.
Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Muscular System: Inherited: Epitheliomuscular cells for limited contraction (from cnidarian-like ancestors). Innovated: Ctenophores have muscle cells within their jelly (mesoglea) that operate the tentacles and mouthparts, but their main locomotion comes from ciliary comb rows, not muscle. The comb rows – bands of giant fused cilia – are unique: they beat in a coordinated fashion to propel the animal. This is the largest use of cilia for locomotion in the animal kingdom (they are the biggest animals to swim via cilia). So while they did evolve smooth and striated muscle for feeding (like swallowing prey) and maneuvering tentacles, the major innovation is this non-muscular locomotion system.
Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Skeletal System: Inherited: Soft-bodied with hydrostatic support (like jelly ancestors). Innovated: A hydrostatic skeleton is formed by the fluid-filled gastrovascular canals and the mesoglea – by controlling the stiffness of their mesoglea and the volume of water in canals, comb jellies maintain body shape. They did not evolve hard parts; however, the statolith (a tiny grain of calcium carbonate in the aboral organ) rests on four tufts of cilia and acts as a weight for balance – this is a minuscule “hard” structure that helps orientation. Otherwise, the ctenophore’s form is maintained by elastic mesoglea fibers and muscle tension, an effective skeletal strategy for a pelagic gelatinous organism.
Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Immune System: Inherited: Basic innate immunity at cellular level (as in all early metazoans). Innovated: Not well-studied, but ctenophores seem to resist infections in the open ocean by producing mucus that can trap invading microorganisms. Their exterior is constantly washed by water, and any foreign particles that stick can be shuttled to the mouth and expelled. Also, comb jellies have remarkable regenerative ability – they can regrow damaged tissues quickly, indicating robust wound-healing mechanisms. This rapid regeneration is a kind of defense, ensuring that injuries (from predators or environmental damage) do not easily become lethal or infected.
Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Endocrine System: Inherited: No distinct endocrine organs; diffuse cellular regulation (like neurons releasing neuropeptides) as in jellyfish. Innovated: Ctenophores possibly use unique neurochemical messengers (since they lack some common neurotransmitters of other animals). They likely release hormones or hormone-like molecules to coordinate spawning (many ctenophores spawn daily at dawn or dusk, implying chemical timing signals). The aboral organ may also secrete factors that regulate ciliary beating rates. Though specifics are unclear, their life processes (growth, bioluminescence, reproduction) are controlled by chemical signals, which can be seen as a simple endocrine-like system spread through the nerve net and body cells.
Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Excretory System: Inherited: No specialized excretory organs; ammonia diffuses out of cells into the surrounding water. Innovated: The presence of anal pores allows them to eject some waste directly, reducing the need to expel everything via the mouth. Most metabolic waste (nitrogenous waste) still diffuses out through body surfaces. The anal pores in comb jellies are not true kidneys, but they represent a novel outlet for undigested particles and possibly excess water, which is a step beyond cnidarians. Essentially, ctenophores handle excretion by diffusion and occasional one-way expulsion through these small pores, an incremental improvement in “excretory” function.
Comb Jellies (Phylum Ctenophora).Integumentary System: Inherited: Diffuse sensitivity (ancestral nerve net detection of touch/chemicals). Innovated: A specialized apical sensory organ at the aboral end containing a statolith (gravity sensor) and ciliated balancers. This organ detects orientation – if the ctenophore tilts, the statolith presses on different cilia, which then signal to the comb rows to correct course, acting like an inner ear for balance. Comb jellies also have rudimentary light receptors in their epidermis (some species are attracted or deterred by light), though not image-forming eyes. Their tentacles are loaded with sensory cells that feel prey contact. Bioluminescence in many ctenophores may serve as a defensive sensory cue (flashing when touched to startle predators). In summary, while they lack eyes or ears, comb jellies innovated a gravity-sensing organ and distributed touch/chemo-receptors, giving them surprising awareness for an animal with no brain.

Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Nervous System: Inherited: A simple nerve net or paired nerve cords from a diploblastic ancestor. Innovated: Cephalization – nerves concentrated at the front end forming a primitive brain (cerebral ganglion) to process sensory input from the anterior (where sense organs cluster). Bilaterians evolved longitudinal nerve cords (often ventral) connecting to this brain, coordinating the body. The nervous system became centralized and directional: signals travel along nerve cords to coordinate movement on both sides of the body. This is a major step up from a diffuse net, enabling faster and more complex responses.
Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Respiratory System: Inherited: Gas exchange by diffusion through body surface (sufficient for small, flat animals). Innovated: A triploblastic body plan allowing larger size, which in turn drove evolution of specialized respiratory surfaces in some groups. Early bilateria were small worms that likely still breathed through skin. But the body flattening (as seen in flatworms) or development of a pseudocoelom (in roundworms) improved surface-area-to-volume ratio for diffusion. The innovation was flexibility: bilaterians in water could stay small and diffuse or grow larger and start evolving gills (seen later in bigger protostomes/deuterostomes). In sum, the bilaterian innovation was the potential for specialized respiratory organs (gills, etc.), though the very earliest remained diffusion-dependent.
Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Digestive System: Inherited: An incomplete gut cavity from ancestors (like a sac gut). Innovated: A through-complete digestive tract with mouth and anus, allowing one-way flow of food – many early bilaterians developed a tubular gut so they could continuously feed. This meant specialization of regions: e.g. a mouth for ingestion, enzymes secreted in a foregut, absorption in a hindgut. (Note: flatworms are an exception with no anus, possibly a secondary loss.) Overall, bilaterians established the complete digestive system as the norm, vastly improving digestive efficiency and enabling animals to process more food and energy.
Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Circulatory System: Inherited: No discrete circulatory system; ancestral diffusion through a gastrovascular space. Innovated: Internal fluid transport – the evolution of a mesodermal layer allowed formation of a coelom or pseudocoel that could distribute nutrients and fluids. Many early bilaterians (like roundworms) use their fluid-filled body cavity as a simple circulatory medium (fluid moves as the animal moves). In others, a network of vessels and a contractile heart evolved (e.g. ancestral molluscs and annelids) to actively pump fluid. So the bilaterian lineage innovated the first circulatory systems (open or closed) to supply internal organs, with blood confined in vessels in some lineages for more efficient transport.
Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Reproductive System: Inherited: External fertilization in water – releasing eggs and sperm to the environment (ancestral mode). Innovated: More complex reproductive systems with specialized gonads and often internal fertilization in some groups. Early bilaterians likely had paired gonads and could store gametes.
