Some (like flatworms) became hermaphroditic and evolved internal copulation (e.g. penis fencing in flatworms) – an innovation to ensure reproductive success without relying solely on chance meetings of gametes in water. Larval stages also diversified: bilaterians developed specific larvae (like trochophore in marine annelid/mollusk lineages, or direct development in some) to exploit new niches. These changes mark a shift to more controlled, efficient reproduction than the scatter-shot spawning of earlier animals.
Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Muscular System: Inherited: Longitudinal contractile fibers for body movement (from worm-like ancestors). Innovated: Mesodermal muscle layers – bilaterians developed well-organized muscle blocks, often with circular and longitudinal muscles working in coordination, enabling peristaltic locomotion (e.g. crawling or burrowing). Segmentation of muscles in many bilaterians (e.g. in early annelid-like forms) allowed different parts of the body to move independently. This gave bilaterians far more mobility – they could swim, crawl, burrow with precision. For example, a primitive bilaterian worm could undulate its body due to segmented muscle bands, achieving directed movement to chase food or escape predators, a big improvement over radially symmetric drifting or crawling.
Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Skeletal System: Inherited: Hydrostatic support – maintaining shape by fluid pressure (ancestral cnidarians and flatworms use this). Innovated: Coelomic hydrostatic skeleton – the evolution of a fluid-filled cavity (coelom or pseudocoel) enclosed by muscles allowed efficient shape change and force transmission. By contracting longitudinal muscles against a fluid-filled chamber, an early worm could shorten and widen; contracting circular muscles lengthens the body. This dual muscle system and coelom enabled burrowing and wriggling with power. Additionally, some bilaterians began depositing hard materials: the first mineralized spicules or shells appear in bilaterian lineages (e.g. tiny calcareous scales in certain Precambrian bilaterians), foreshadowing exoskeletons. But the hallmark skeletal innovation was the modular body plan – repeated segments that could specialize or support appendages, giving structural modularity.
Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Immune System: Inherited: Innate immune responses (phagocytic cells ingesting bacteria) from single-celled ancestors. Innovated: A dedicated immune cell population in the coelomic fluid or hemolymph – bilaterians evolved wandering amoebocytes/hemocytes that travel the body, engulf pathogens, and seal wounds (e.g. clotting in insects, coelomocytes in worms). They also evolved molecular immunity: producing lysozymes, antimicrobial peptides, and beginning the complement system (seen later in deuterostomes). In segmented bilaterians, if one segment is infected, others can respond by immune cells migrating there. So while still “innate immunity,” it became more systematized and effective in bilateria.
Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Endocrine System: Inherited: Neurosecretory cells releasing simple hormones (like ancestors had for basic functions). Innovated: Endocrine organ precursors – bilaterians show the first distinct clusters of hormone-secreting cells. For instance, flatworms have cells in the brain that secrete hormones regulating growth and regeneration. As bilateral animals got more complex, they needed internal coordination: hormones like ecdysone (molting hormone) in protostomes or thyroid-like hormones in early deuterostomes evolved. Thus, bilaterians set the stage for true endocrine systems: they introduced signaling molecules that travel through the internal fluids to target distant organs, controlling metamorphosis, reproduction cycles, and metabolism in a more integrated way than before.
Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Excretory System: Inherited: Diffusion of waste out of cells into the environment. Innovated: Specialized excretory organs for osmoregulation and waste removal: protonephridia (flame cell systems) in the earliest bilaterians. Flatworms, for example, developed flame cells – ciliated cells that drive extracellular fluid through tubules, filtering out waste and excess water, excreting it through pores. This was a significant innovation to maintain internal chemical balance. In coelomate bilaterians, metanephridia (tubules with nephrostomes) evolved next. The appearance of these excretory structures meant bilaterians could regulate their internal environment and invade freshwater or variable salinity habitats that prior animals couldn’t tolerate as easily.
Bilateria (First bilaterally symmetric a.Integumentary System: Inherited: Basic sensory cells (light-sensitive ocelli, touch-sensitive cilia) from earlier metazoans. Innovated: Concentration of sense organs in the head (due to cephalization): the first bilaterians evolved paired eyespots (pigment-cup eyes that can detect light direction), paired chemosensory organs (e.g. auricles in flatworms to “smell” dissolved chemicals), and mechanoreceptors. With bilateral symmetry, animals could compare inputs from left vs. right – enabling true orientation (e.g. sensing which side the light or smell is stronger on and turning accordingly). Many bilaterians also evolved statocysts (balance organs with grains inside) to sense up vs. down. These innovations – clustering multiple sensor types in a head – made bilaterians far more responsive to their environment, actively seeking food and mates and avoiding danger in a directed manner.

Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Nervous System: Inherited: No nerves, just cell-to-cell signaling as in aquatic algae. Innovated: Plasmodesmata between cells – charophyte green algae (ancestors of land plants) evolved microscopic channels connecting cells, allowing communication and coordination across the multicellular plant body. This meant one part of a filament could send chemical or electrical signals to another (e.g. to coordinate growth or reproduction). It’s not a nervous system, but it set the stage for whole-plant integration (all cells can respond to a localized stimulus via shared signals).
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Respiratory System: Inherited: Gas exchange by diffusion across plant surfaces (as in algae). Innovated: Waxy cuticle on exposed surfaces to prevent desiccation – but this barrier makes gas exchange harder, so early land plants developed stomata or fixed pores to allow CO₂ inbio.libretexts.org. For example, some simple land “algae” (bryophyte-like) have pores on their surface, and slightly later, stomata with guard cells evolved (in moss sporophytes, etc.). Thus, these pioneers balanced water retention with the need for air, an innovation absent in their aquatic forebears. Internally, they had air spaces in tissues to facilitate gas diffusion from the pore on inward cells.
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Digestive System: Inherited: Photosynthesis for food (no need for digestive system). Innovated: Rhizoids – filamentous root-like structures to anchor and absorb water/minerals from soil, an analog to roots in true plants. Early land algae likely formed symbiosis with fungi (mycorrhizae) to enhance nutrient uptake from barren rock/soil. They also retained the ancestral alternation-of-generations but innovated by keeping the zygote/embryo attached to the parent for nourishment (a key embryophytic trait). Essentially, nutrient acquisition extended beyond photosynthesis: these algae scraped minerals from substrata and began internally transporting them to nourish the growing embryo.
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Circulatory System: Inherited: No vascular transport; relied on diffusion and capillary action (as in algal mats). Innovated: Primitive conducting cells: early land plants (e.g. mosses) evolved hydroid cells for water transport and leptoid cells for sugar transport in their tiny “stems” – a precursor to xylem and phloem. Even without true wood, these channels moved fluids a few centimeters, supporting taller growth than a flat algal film. This is an evolutionary foothold for full vascular systems. The early land green algae were generally small, so diffusion still played a large role, but the trend toward internal conduction had begun.
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Reproductive System: Inherited: Water-dependent reproduction – flagellated sperm swimming to eggs (as in algae). Innovated: Retention of the egg and developing zygote on the parent plant (the defining feature of embryophytes). In these early land plants, the fertilization happened in a protected chamber (archegonium), and the multicellular embryo grew there, gaining nourishment from parent tissues. Also, they produced spores with tough sporopollenin walls that could survive air travel without drying outbio.libretexts.org. This combination allowed reproduction on land: though sperm still needed a film of water (rain/dew) to swim to the egg, the resulting offspring had a much better start, and spores could disperse through the air to new moist spots.
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Muscular System: Inherited: No muscle; movement via growth (still true). Innovated: Tropisms became pronounced – these plants could orient growth toward light (phototropism) or against gravity (gravitropism) thanks to hormones and differential growth. For instance, charophyte algae and early mosses would bend towards light, an early “motion” to optimize photosynthesis. They also developed rapid turgor movements in some cases: e.g. liverworts explosively disperse spores by sudden shrinkage of elaters (cells that twist when dry). This isn’t muscular movement, but it’s an active, controlled motion new to land colonizers, aiding spore dispersal.
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Skeletal System: Inherited: Cellulose cell walls for support (like algae). Innovated: Lignin-like compounds start appearing in some tissuesbio.libretexts.org – the earliest vascular plant fossils show lignified tracheids, but even early non-vasculars had some phenolic fortification of cell walls. These algae/plant hybrids stayed very small (cm-scale at most) because they lacked extensive support. They hugged moist ground, often forming low mats. But as an innovation, they produced a waxy cuticle and sometimes a rudimentary cortex that kept their shape on land. Cushiony mosses, for example, have supporting dead cell networks and turgid cells – an analog to a skeletal support that works only when wet. It was the subsequent evolution of true vascular tissue that fully solved the support issue.
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Immune System: Inherited: Baseline chemical defense (e.g. antimicrobial and anti-herbivory chemicals as algae had). Innovated: UV-protective pigments (flavonoids) to cope with intense sunlight on land – an “immune” response to UV stress that algae underwater didn’t face. These early land plants also had to contend with terrestrial pathogens and herbivores (initially few, but some arthropods started grazing). They evolved the first gene-for-gene pathogen interactions: secreting chemicals when attacked and having cellular responses to wall off infections. Also, the cuticle served as a first physical barrier to microbes. In short, embryophyte precursors ramped up their passive immunity: tougher spore/seed coats, antibiotic metabolites, and the ability to deactivate parts of tissue to contain an infection (localized cell death as a defense).
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Endocrine System: Inherited: Simple hormonal signals from algae (e.g. auxin-like molecules affecting growth). Innovated: A suite of plant hormones regulating growth and stress: early land plants used auxin to guide shoots upward and roots (or rhizoids) downward, and abscisic acid (ABA) likely evolved to deal with drought by inducing spore/seed dormancy and closing stomata in later groupsbio.libretexts.org. They also use pheromones to attract symbiotic fungi. While they have no endocrine “glands,” each plant part can produce hormones that travel through the plant’s thin tissues to target cells – establishing an internal communication network essential for coordinating development (like telling a bud to become a reproductive structure at the right time).
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Excretory System: Inherited: No special organs; waste O₂, CO₂, etc., diffuse out as in algae. Innovated: Controlled water loss which is closely tied to excretion in plants: by developing stomata, they could regulate transpiration – effectively controlling the loss of excess water and oxygen. Nitrogenous wastes were mostly reused or stored in vacuoles as innocuous compounds (since plants are adept at recycling). Early land plants probably began storing heavy metals or toxins in cells (since dropping leaves wasn’t applicable yet for the very first land plants). Additionally, as a quasi-excretory function, they released secondary metabolites into the soil that could inhibit competing plants or microbes – effectively using excretion as a competitive tool.
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Integumentary System: Inherited: Thin “skin” of cells directly exposed to environment (like algal thallus). Innovated: Cuticle – a waxy layer over epidermal cells to seal moisture in and block UVbio.libretexts.org. This was vital to prevent drying on land. However, cuticles could be patchy on early plants (perhaps on upper surfaces). Early land plants also kept a simple epidermis but some developed sporopollenin coating on spores (an integument for reproductive propagules). Over time, multicellular protective structures evolved: e.g. in mosses, a few layers of cells protect the sporophyte. These developments mark the beginning of a true integumentary system – a protective outer coating (waxy skin, multi-layered embryo sac) shielding the organism from terrestrial threats.
Land Green Algae (Early land plant-like.Sensory System: Inherited: Light sensors (phytochromes, etc.) to orient to light, as in algae. Innovated: Multiple sensory responses: early land plants could detect gravity via specialized starch-filled cells (statocytes) in root analogs, ensuring roots grew downward and shoots upward. They refined photoreceptors to distinguish day length (photoperiod) – crucial for timing reproduction in seasonal climates. They also evolved touch responses: for example, tendrils of some primitive vascular plants (later) coil when touching a support (thigmotropism), and even these earliest land plants likely had mechanosensitive cells to detect when they were in a damp crevice versus exposed. Additionally, they respond to drought by sensing internal water status (through hormone ABA). Though they lack a nervous system, land plants developed an intricate sensory network at the cellular level, allowing them to react appropriately to light, gravity, moisture, and physical contact.

Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Nervous System: Inherited: Diffuse nerve cells from a common eumetazoan ancestor (none in sponges, but by cnidarians nerves existed). Innovated: A proper nerve net – cnidarians evolved true neurons that form a network across the body, coordinating muscle-like cells. There is no brain, but local nerve rings (e.g. around a jellyfish’s bell margin) act as pacemakers. This nerve net allows behaviors like tentacle contraction and swimming. It’s an innovation over ancestral animals with no nerves: cnidarians can sense and react rapidly (for instance, a touch causes a reflex tentacle retraction).
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Respiratory System: Inherited: Direct diffusion of gases in water (no respiratory organ). Innovated: Use of the gastrovascular cavity for gas exchange: because their body walls are thin and the gut cavity circulates water, oxygen can reach internal cells. Many cnidarians (jellyfish) are mostly water and have a large surface area relative to volume, so diffusion suffices. Some large anemones have internal septa that increase surface area inside the gut for both digestion and gas exchange. Still, no gills – reliance on body surface and gut cavity water flow remains the strategy.
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Digestive System: Inherited: Sac-like digestion from a single opening (as in ancestral gastrula-like organisms). Innovated: Extracellular digestion in the gastrovascular cavity – cnidarians secrete enzymes into their central cavity to break down prey, allowing them to consume items larger than a single cell could digest. Nutrient broth is then absorbed by gastrodermal cells. The gastrovascular cavity also distributes food to all parts of the body. However, it has one opening (mouth = anus). In corals and anemones, the gut may have partitions and filaments loaded with digestive cells to increase efficiency. This is a step beyond purely intracellular digestion, letting cnidarians subdue and digest multicellular prey.
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Circulatory System: Inherited: No separate circulatory system; the gut cavity and water serve for transport. Innovated: Gastrovascular circulation – after digestion, the same cavity moves nutrients around the body; ciliary currents in the canals of jellyfish or the septa of anemones circulate fluid. In medusae (jellyfish), radial and ring canals branch through the bell, moving nutrients and oxygen to distant tissues. This functions as a primitive circulatory system (though it’s also the digestive cavity). Additionally, diffusion between the two cell layers (epidermis and gastrodermis) is quick because mesoglea is non-cellular. In sum, cnidarians achieved internal distribution of sustenance without dedicated blood vessels by using their gut as a transport network.
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Reproductive System: Inherited: External fertilization (gametes shed into water) like simple ancestors. Innovated: Alternation of sexual and asexual generations – many cnidarians alternate between a sessile polyp stage that reproduces asexually (budding off new polyps or medusae) and a motile medusa stage that reproduces sexually (spawning eggs and sperm). This metagenesis maximizes reproductive output. Polyps like corals and Hydra can also bud off exact clones, forming colonies. Some cnidarians (e.g. hydra) lost the medusa and do sexual reproduction as polyps with temporary gonads. The innovation is having both inherited methods (broadcast spawning) and new asexual proliferation, plus the protection of embryos in some cases (fertilized eggs often develop into free-swimming larvae inside the parent briefly, or in jellyfish they form a planula that settles).
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Muscular System: Inherited: Contractile fibers (epitheliomuscular cells) in body wall, from ancestral muscle precursors. Innovated: True muscle-like cells derived from ectoderm and endoderm: cnidarians have circular and longitudinal fiber layers in polyps that allow them to shorten and elongate. Jellyfish evolved sheet-like muscle around the bell margin – a ring muscle that on contraction ejects water, propelling the medusa (jet propulsion). This gave cnidarians mobility: medusae can actively swim, and anemones can bend or even crawl slowly. Though not mesodermal muscle (cnidarians are diploblastic), functionally these are muscle cells enabling predation (entangling prey with tentacles) and reactive movement (retracting into a ball when threatened for anemones).
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Skeletal System: Inherited: Hydrostatic skeleton – like ancestral worms, they maintain shape by fluid in the gut cavity and contractile cells. Innovated: Some cnidarians developed exoskeletons: corals and many hydrozoans secrete calcium carbonate or chitinous skeletons outside their polyps. This provides structure and protection (reef-building corals create massive limestone frameworks that support colonies). Non-skeletonizing cnidarians rely on mesoglea (a jellylike substance) which acts as an elastic endoskeleton – for example, jellyfish mesoglea springs the bell back to shape after a contraction. So either through stony exoskeletons (corals) or gelatinous endoskeleton (mesoglea), cnidarians found ways to support their bodies beyond simple hydrostatic pressure.
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Immune System: Inherited: Innate defense – generalized cells that can engulf particles (some amoebocytes in mesoglea). Innovated: Cnidocytes (stinging cells) – a unique offensive/defensive cell containing a nematocyst harpoon that can inject toxin into prey or predators. This is a major innovation: these cells (especially abundant on tentacles) protect cnidarians from predators and help capture food by stunning prey. In terms of immunity, cnidarians can distinguish self from not-self to some extent (coral colonies of different genotypes will fight or reject each other on contact). They also have symbiotic algae (in corals) and have to manage immune tolerance to these symbionts – an immune modulation trait.
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Endocrine System: Inherited: Diffuse neural control of physiology (neurons that release peptides affecting cells). Innovated: Cnidarians produce neuropeptides and hormones that regulate digestion, growth, and metamorphosis. For example, spawning in many jellyfish is coordinated by light-sensitive nerve cells that trigger gamete release – a neuroendocrine response. Also, in Hydra, neurons secrete a head activator peptide that influences bud formation and a foot activator for basal disk formation (effectively hormonal patterning signals). No distinct glands exist, but the nerve net doubles as an endocrine system, with certain neurons acting like gland cells. This integration of neural and hormonal control in cnidarians is an evolutionary stepping stone to the separate endocrine organs of higher animals.
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Excretory System: Inherited: Diffusion of wastes/ammonia from each cell to water. Innovated: Use of the gastrovascular cavity for expulsion of indigestibles and metabolic waste – essentially, anything not needed is flushed out the mouth when the animal contracts its body. While there are still no separate excretory organs (ammonia simply diffuses out through tentacles and surfaces), some specialization occurs: for instance, sea anemones can eject their internal water to remove waste or respond to stress (a form of “vomiting” waste and restarting with fresh seawater internally). Thus, excretion remains primitive: no nephridia or kidney-like structure evolved, but the combination of diffusion and active purging via the single opening suffices.
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Integumentary System: Inherited: One-cell-layer epidermis from earlier metazoans. Innovated: A two-layer body with an outer epidermis and inner gastrodermis, separated by mesoglea. The epidermis functions as a true integument: cnidarians have contractile epitheliomuscular cells for movement, sensory cells, and mucus-secreting cells in this layer. Many secrete mucus or slimy coatings over their surface to protect from abrasion and parasites. Some (jellyfish) have epidermal light-sensing organs (ocelli) embedded. Corals and anemones incorporate protective substances (like fluorescent proteins that act as sunblock for symbiotic algae). In essence, cnidarians established a dedicated body covering that not only protects (often with stinging cells embedded) but also aids in interaction with the environment (through gland cells and sensory cells).
Cnidarians (Jellyfish, Corals, Anemones).Sensory System: Inherited: Primitive light- and touch-sensitivity from nerve net ancestors (e.g. scattered sensory cells). Innovated: Dedicated sensory structures: many medusae have rhopalia – specialized structures containing ocelli (simple eyes that detect light intensity) and statocysts (balance organs with a mineral concretion to sense orientation). For example, box jellies even have image-forming eyes with lenses – an astounding development for an invertebrate with no brain, allowing them to navigate around mangrove roots. Polyps like Hydra have rudimentary photoreceptors and will contract in response to sudden shadows. Chemoreceptors on tentacles allow cnidarians to “smell” prey in water. These advancements mean cnidarians can actively respond to their environment: swim toward light or prey, keep balance in water columns, and recoil from harmful stimuli. Their sensory evolution, while not centralized, laid the groundwork for more complex sense organs in bilaterians.

Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Nervous System: Inherited: Bilaterian nervous system with an anterior ganglion and nerve cords. Innovated: Ventral nerve cord with segmental ganglia – protostomes established a nerve cord running along the belly (ventral side) as the main highway of signals, in contrast to the later dorsal cords of chordates. This often consisted of two fused cords with ganglia in each body segment controlling local muscles. The brain (anterior ganglia) became more complex, especially with the development of sensory mouthparts. This configuration (brain + paired ventral cords) is an innovation that would persist in arthropods, annelids, mollusks, etc., enabling refined motor control and integration of sensory input for forward-moving organisms.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Respiratory System: Inherited: Diffusion and integumentary respiration (small ancestors absorbed O₂ through skin). Innovated: Gills in aquatic protostomes (the groundwork): as protostomes increased in size and metabolic activity, many evolved branchial structures. The earliest protostome might have been worm-like without true gills, but protostome lineages soon produced gill-like organs – from feathery external gills in marine worms to book gills in arthropods. Additionally, a dorsal heart pumping blood in an open system (in arthropod ancestors) helped carry oxygen in some groupsquora.com. In smaller or flat early protostomes, no special respiratory organ was needed, but the innovative potential for developing ones (like tracheae in terrestrial forms or internal gills in mollusks) was a protostome hallmark as they diversified.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Digestive System: Inherited: Complete gut with mouth and anus (from the bilaterian ancestor). Innovated: Mouthparts and specialization – protostomes evolved diverse feeding appendages and structures. The earliest protostome likely had a simple mouth opening with rings of cilia or primitive jaws to ingest food. Over time, this lineage innovated toothed tongues (radula in mollusks), muscular pharynges (in flatworms and nematodes), and jaws (as seen in early arthropods). The digestive tract also gained regions: a protostome foregut (ectodermal) often lined with cuticle for grinding, a midgut for digestion/absorption, and a hindgut for egestion. These regional specializations and feeding tools allowed protostomes to exploit a range of diets from detritus to active predation.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Circulatory System: Inherited: No closed blood vessels; nutrients moved in a coelomic cavity or mesenteries. Innovated: Dorsal tubular heart and hemocoel in many – the protostome design (especially in arthropods) features a dorsal heart that pumps hemolymph forward, then it percolates back through the body cavityquora.com. Ancestral protostomes likely had an open circulatory system if any – a pulsatile vessel or peristaltic waves moving fluid in the body cavity. In wormy protostomes (annelids), a closed circulatory system with vessels and multiple “hearts” evolved, showing the plasticity of this trait. The key innovation is active circulation of internal fluid: whether open or closed, protostomes did not rely solely on diffusion – they developed pumping organs (hearts) to distribute nutrients and gases, a big jump in physiological capability.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Reproductive System: Inherited: Sexual reproduction with external fertilization (and some hermaphroditism) from bilaterian ancestor. Innovated: Internal fertilization and complex life cycles in many protostomes. For example, early protostomes in marine settings developed a trochophore larva (in mollusks/annelids) – a free-swimming larval stage with ciliary bands for feeding, which is a new addition to the life cycle aiding dispersal. Furthermore, as protostomes invaded land (e.g. insects, snails), they evolved internal fertilization to protect gametes from drying. The earliest protostome may have been a simple marine worm releasing gametes into water, but the lineage soon displayed remarkable flexibility: egg cases in some, live birth in others (e.g. some cockroaches), colony-level brooding in others. This is the clade where reproductive strategies exploded in variety.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Muscular System: Inherited: Well-developed longitudinal and circular muscles (from bilaterian ancestor). Innovated: Jointed appendage muscles and segmentation – protostomes, particularly arthropod ancestors, evolved limb muscles that attach to an exoskeleton, enabling complex leg movements. The ancestral protostome might have been segmental (like a primitive annelid) with repeated muscle blocks; this allowed the evolution of localized control (each segment’s ganglion controlling its muscles). In later protostomes, segments fused or specialized with their muscles (like the strong flight muscles in insects or the foot muscle in mollusks). Thus, protostomes innovated not in having muscles (they already did) but in how they used them: e.g. rapid body movements – squid jet propulsion via mantle muscles or insect flight – all trace back to the protostome propensity for evolving new muscle systems on their basic body plan.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Skeletal System: Inherited: Hydrostatic skeleton (coelom or pseudocoel) from bilaterian ancestor. Innovated: Exoskeletons in Ecdysozoa (the molting protostomes) – the protostome line gave rise to chitinous exoskeletons (in early arthropods) that provided support and attachment for muscles. The earliest protostome might not have had an exoskeleton, but the capacity was there and realized early in Cambrian arthropods (e.g. Trilobites with jointed exoskeleton). Another innovation in others was rigid internal elements: some worms developed tiny bristles or spicules. Additionally, many protostomes evolved segmentation of the body cavity by septa (in annelids), which compartmentalized the hydrostatic skeleton for finer control. So, whether via an external cuticle or internal septa, protostomes greatly expanded skeletal adaptations, enabling larger size and terrestrial life (with support against gravity).
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Immune System: Inherited: Innate immune cells and enzymes in body fluids. Innovated: Chitinous exoskeleton or cuticle as a first-line defense in arthropods (preventing pathogen entry and physical injury). Protostomes also developed more specialized immune responses: for example, in insects, wounding triggers melanin deposition to encapsulate pathogens (phenoloxidase system), and production of antimicrobial peptides that specifically target bacteria or fungi. These are more advanced innate immune mechanisms than seen in earlier animals. The circulatory fluid of protostomes (hemolymph) contains hemocytes that can coagulate and form clots at wound sites, an innovation protecting against blood loss and infection. Overall, while still lacking adaptive immunity, protostomes honed their innate immunity and physical barriers significantly.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Endocrine System: Inherited: Neurosecretory control of basic functions (e.g. reproductive timing by neurons) from bilaterians. Innovated: True endocrine glands in some – e.g. in insects, distinct organs like the prothoracic gland secrete ecdysone to drive molting, and corpora allata secrete juvenile hormone for metamorphosis control. These endocrine organs are a protostome hallmark, especially in insects: they coordinate complex life stages (larva -> pupa -> adult) via hormones. Also, mollusks have hormone-secreting cells that regulate growth and gamete development. The advent of such hormonal coordination allowed protostomes to achieve metamorphosis, diapause (dormancy in adverse conditions), and other life-history strategies, tightly integrating their physiology in ways simpler animals could not.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Excretory System: Inherited: Protonephridia (flame cells) in basal forms for osmoregulation and waste removal. Innovated: Diverse excretory systems: metanephridia in segmented protostomes (annelids) where each segment filters coelomic fluid and excretes waste, and Malpighian tubules in terrestrial insects for efficient nitrogenous waste removal with minimal water loss. The protostome lineage explored multiple solutions to excretion. The earliest protostome likely had simple tubules expelling to the outside. As habitats expanded, protostomes innovated: e.g. insects convert waste to uric acid crystals (solid urine) to save water, an advanced excretory adaptation. Overall, protostomes established regulated excretion, enabling them to thrive in freshwater (preventing salt loss) and on land (preventing water loss).
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Integumentary System: Inherited: One-cell-layer epidermis (possibly ciliated in larvae or flatworms) as a body covering. Innovated: Protective cuticle or shell – most protostomes developed an integument optimized for their environment. Roundworms (nematodes) have a flexible but tough collagen cuticle they molt; arthropods have a hardened, jointed chitinous cuticle (exoskeleton) that is also part of their integument, often with a waxy layer to prevent desiccation in terrestrial species. Mollusks grew a calcium carbonate shell over a mantle tissue – an external integumentary structure for defense. Additionally, many protostomes have specialized epidermal structures: setae (bristles) in annelids that help in movement and sensing, or trichomes (hairs) in caterpillars for defense. All these represent a big leap in integumentary complexity: from a simple skin to a multi-functional protective coat.
Earliest Protostome (ancestral protostom.Sensory System: Inherited: Basic photo- and chemo-receptors from bilaterian ancestor. Innovated: Advanced eyes and sensor organs – protostomes were the first to evolve image-forming eyes (the compound eyes of early arthropods like trilobites). Compound eyes gave a mosaic vision useful for detecting motion, crucial for survival. In mollusks, the protostome line eventually produced camera-type eyes (as in cephalopods), independently rivaling vertebrate eyes. Protostomes also excelled in chemosensation: early aquatic forms had paired antennae or palps with dense chemoreceptors to “smell” water for food or mates. Mechanoreceptors like sensory bristles and equilibrium sensors (statocysts) became common. The earliest protostome likely had simple ocelli and statocysts, but the pathway to highly specialized sensors (antennae, eyes, ears in some insects that detect sound via tympanic membranes) was set. Protostomes turned the anterior end into a sophisticated sensor array, driving active foraging and complex behavior.

Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Nervous System: Inherited: Bilaterian nervous system with anterior ganglia. Innovated: Likely a dorsal nerve cord (in the lineage toward chordates) and a generally more diffuse nervous system in others. The common deuterostome ancestor (perhaps a worm-like creature) had a nerve net and strands; one hypothesis is a dorsal neural tube beginning to formsunyorange.edu (as seen in hemichordates’ collar cord and chordates’ hollow nerve cord). While hemichordates still have a nerve net and some dorsal, some ventral cords, the trend in deuterostomes was to concentrate the nervous tissue dorsally. This inversion relative to protostomes is notable. Additionally, deuterostomes (hemichordates, etc.) showed less cephalization – the earliest deuterostome might not have had a clear head brain, focusing instead on a network that controlled filter-feeding and crawling. The innovation here is subtle: reorganization of nerve placement and laying the groundwork for the chordate central nervous system.
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Respiratory System: Inherited: Diffusion and skin respiration (ancestral tiny worms breathed through surface). Innovated: Pharyngeal gill slits – a hallmark of deuterostomes was the evolution of openings in the pharynx that could serve dual roles in feeding and respirationsunyorange.edu. The earliest deuterostome likely was a filter-feeder that passed water out through gill slits, extracting oxygen in the process. Hemichordates (acorn worms) have many pharyngeal slits and use them to breathe (much like primitive gills). This innovation meant water flowing through the mouth could deliver O₂ to blood vessels in the slits before exiting – essentially the first gill system. In chordates, these slits would become true gills (in fish) or other structures. Thus, deuterostomes were primed for effective respiration even at larger sizes thanks to this pharyngeal slit design.
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Digestive System: Inherited: Complete gut from mouth to anus (the bilaterian inheritance). Innovated: Suspension-feeding pharynx – the ancestral deuterostome likely had a pharynx with gill slits and possibly a mucus-generating endostyle to trap food (as seen in modern acorn worms and lancelets). This allowed continuous one-way feeding: water in mouth, out gill slits, filtering food in the process. The stomach and intestine would process this caught food. Notably, the mouth in deuterostomes is a secondary opening (the blastopore becomes the anus), but functionally the innovation is the separation of feeding and respiratory flow by those slits. So while digestive enzymes and absorption remained similar to other bilateria, the front end was specialized into a filter-feeding apparatus that increased feeding efficiency and could be co-opted into new feeding modes (e.g. the evolution of jaws in chordates later on that repurposed gill arch supports).
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Circulatory System: Inherited: No dedicated circulatory system or an open system with contractile vessels (ancestral state). Innovated: Hemal system with a directional flow – early deuterostomes like hemichordates developed a rudimentary circulatory system: a dorsal heart-kidney (glomerulus) and a network of vessels. Typically, blood in deuterostomes flows forward along a ventral vessel and back along a dorsal vessel (opposite of protostomes)sunyorange.edu. The earliest deuterostome likely had a simple pulsatile sinus or heart-like vesicle pumping blood through pharyngeal slits (for gas exchange) and distributing nutrients from the gut. In chordate lineage, this would become a muscular heart ventrally and a closed circuit. In echinoderms, it became an open hemal system plus the water vascular system. So deuterostomes innovated by organizing circulatory flow pattern (dorsal and ventral vessels) and linking it to their respiratory structures, setting the stage for efficient closed circulation in later chordates.
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Reproductive System: Inherited: External spawning in water. Innovated: Eggs with substantial yolk and possibly protective coats – deuterostome ancestors might have had larger, yolk-rich eggs compared to protostomes, as suggested by patterns in extant deuterostomes (e.g. tunicate eggs, some echinoderm eggs). The earliest deuterostome likely released eggs and sperm into the ocean (like hemichordates and echinoderms do), but an innovation was the development of bilaterally symmetric larvae (the dipleurula concept) that characterize deuterostomes. For instance, hemichordates have a tornaria larva (which resembles echinoderm larvae), with ciliary bands for swimming and feeding – a different larval strategy than the trochophore of protostomes. This larva suggests the ancestor had a distinct larval stage adapted to planktonic life. Additionally, in-line with deuterostome traits, separate sexes were common, and some brood protection evolved in certain lines (e.g. some acorn worms protect eggs in tubes). But internal fertilization was not a general deuterostome feature until much later (in amniotes).
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Muscular System: Inherited: Longitudinal muscles and ciliary movement for locomotion (from tiny worm ancestor). Innovated: Many early deuterostomes were sessile or semi-sessile (e.g. hypothesized ancestors of echinoderms and hemichordates might have been attached filter feeders), but the lineage that led to chordates emphasized muscular locomotion. The notochord’s advent in chordates provided an anchor for segmental muscles to produce powerful lateral swimming strokes. However, in the common ancestor, innovation might have been limited to modified musculature for burrowing (as in acorn worms with a muscular proboscis) or swimming larvae. One key development could be the partitioning of the body coelom into sections (proto-somites) allowing localized muscle control – hemichordates show tripartite body (proboscis, collar, trunk) each with its coelomic cavities and musculature. This is a hint of segmentation and regionalization that the chordate line amplified (into myomeres along a notochord).
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Skeletal System: Inherited: Hydrostatic skeleton (fluid-filled coelom chambers for support). Innovated: Stiffened supportive structures: the early deuterostome likely evolved the stomochord in hemichordates (a rod-like structure in the proboscis) or a dorsal notochord precursor in chordatescourses.lumenlearning.com. The stomochord was once thought homologous to the notochord, though now disputed, but it does serve to stiffen the proboscis for burrowing. The true notochord, appearing in chordate lineage, was an innovation: a flexible rod that allows axial support for swimming. Echinoderms took a different route: they evolved internal calcite plates (endoskeleton) and eventually pentaradial symmetry with a water vascular system to act as a hydrostatic skeleton for tube feet. So the deuterostome heritage is dual: chordates inherited a dorsal supporting rod (notochord)courses.lumenlearning.com, while others developed unique endoskeletons. The key early innovation was the idea of an internal supportive element that muscles could work against, breaking away from total reliance on coelomic pressure.
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Immune System: Inherited: Innate immunity with coelomic cells ingesting invaders. Innovated: Deuterostomes eventually produced the first hints of adaptive immunity (though not in the earliest forms) – for example, elements of the recombinase system are present in chordates. The immediate ancestor likely had a slightly more complex innate system than protostomes: complement proteins (primitive forms) and cytokine-like molecules for cell signaling in immune responses. Modern hemichordates possess phagocytic cells and can produce iodine-rich antimicrobial substances (their blood has an iodoform smell, possibly for defense). Also, being larger, deuterostomes evolved lymphatic-like channels in echinoderms (axial organ) and specialized immune organs in chordates (thymus, spleen, etc. later). So while the very first deuterostome didn’t have those latter features, the groundwork for a more sophisticated immune response was laid, with certain deuterostome-specific immune genes evolving (e.g. those for allograft rejection seen in colonial tunicates).
Earliest Deuterostome (ancestral deutero.Endocrine System: Inherited: Diffuse neuroendocrine system (neurons releasing hormones) from bilaterian ancestor. Innovated: Endostyle in the floor of the pharynx – present in early chordates (and possibly an analog in hemichordates with their stomochord region). The endostyle concentrated iodine and produced thyroxine-like compounds, making it the forerunner of the thyroid gland【28†L230

Earliest Cephalopods.Nervous System: (H) Basic molluscan nerve ring and paired ganglia controlling body functions. (I) Enlarged brain and giant nerve fibers for fast signal conduction, coordinating agile swimming and tentacle movement; image-forming eyes for predation (advanced among molluscs).
Earliest Cephalopods.Digestive System: (H) Complete gut with mouth, esophagus, and radula from molluscan ancestors for scraping food. (I) Powerful chitinous beak and jaws to tear prey (predatory adaptation); a crop and stomach with digestive caecum for extra cellular digestion. Possibly an ink sac evolved for predator evasion (unique to cephalopods).
Earliest Cephalopods.Respiratory System: (H) Pair of gills in mantle cavity like other aquatic molluscs for gas exchange. (I) Muscular mantle pumping water over gills, enabling active respiration and jet propulsion. Developed siphuncle in shell for buoyancy control, freeing mantle for strong jet-driven breathing/outflow.
Earliest Cephalopods.Circulatory System: (H) Dorsal heart and blood vessels from common molluscan design. (I) Only mollusk lineage with a closed circulatory system (blood fully contained in vessels) and multiple hearts (two gill hearts plus one systemic) to support high activity. High-pressure blood flow improved oxygen delivery for predation.
Earliest Cephalopods.Reproductive System: (H) Separate sexes with external fertilization ancestral to molluscs (spawning eggs and sperm into water). (I) Evolution of internal fertilization via spermatophores (packages of sperm) to ensure fertilization in open water; larger yolky eggs laid in protective gelatinous clutches, reducing drift and predation.
Earliest Cephalopods.Excretory System: (H) Nephridia (“kidneys”) filtering blood and releasing ammonia into mantle cavity water (typical aquatic waste removal). (I) Enhanced excretion to handle high-protein diet: efficient ammonia diffusion at gills. No major new organs, but likely higher renal output to eliminate metabolic wastes from active lifestyle.

Euthycarcinoids.Nervous System: (H) Arthropod ventral nerve cord with segmented ganglia and simple brain (control of appendages and senses). (I) Well-developed compound eyes and antennae for both aquatic and terrestrial sensing (facilitating amphibious foraging); improved coordination for walking on land in short bouts (integrating leg movements and balance).
Euthycarcinoids.Digestive System: (H) Straight alimentary canal with foregut (lined in chitin) and hindgut as in primitive arthropods. (I) Mandibulate mouthparts (jaws derived from appendages) for biting/chewing microbial mats or detritus; digestive ceca to aid in breaking down tough plant detritus, supporting early land herbivory/omnivory.
Euthycarcinoids.Respiratory System: (H) Aquatic gills on appendages or along body (like crustacean gills) for underwater breathing. (I) Ability to breathe air briefly: possibly retained water around gills under a closeable cover or kept gills moist, enabling gas exchange in air (analogous to modern isopods). First arthropods to make short terrestrial forays.
Euthycarcinoids.Circulatory System: (H) Dorsal tubular heart and open hemolymph circulation (like ancestral arthropods) with hemocyanin to carry oxygen. (I) Perhaps slightly higher hemocyanin levels or heart rate to supply oxygen during excursions on land (supporting muscle activity out of water), but overall no closed vessels (still an open system).
Euthycarcinoids.Reproductive System: (H) External fertilization in water (eggs and sperm released in moist environments, as ancestral aquatic arthropods). (I) Transition toward land reproduction: eggs laid in damp mud or water’s edge to stay moist; tougher egg coatings to resist desiccation compared to fully aquatic eggs, foreshadowing terrestrial life cycle needs.
Euthycarcinoids.Excretory System: (H) Coxal glands (primitive excretory organs at leg bases) filtering hemolymph and excreting ammonia, like ancestral arthropods. (I) Partial shift to uric acid or less toxic waste when on land to avoid ammonia buildup (akin to later terrestrial arthropods). Still largely ammonia when in water, but some capacity for water retention during land travel.

Jawless Fish.Nervous System: (H) Dorsal hollow nerve cord and three-part brain from chordate ancestors (forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain). (I) Enclosed brain within a cartilaginous skull for protection; developed sense organs feeding into brain (image-forming paired eyes, inner ear balancing with 2 semicircular canals, olfactory bulbs) for active navigation and survival.
Jawless Fish.Digestive System: (H) Filter-feeding pharynx with gill slits from proto-chordates. (I) Muscular pharynx pump to draw in water/food, using gills now exclusively for respiration and mouth for feeding. Appearance of a true liver and pancreatic tissue (digestive glands) for improved nutrient processing in the vertebrate lineage.
Jawless Fish.Respiratory System: (H) Multiple gill slits along the throat for gas exchange (as in ancestral chordates). (I) Gills repurposed solely for respiration (no longer for feeding) with gill filaments and rich blood supply; a muscular gill pouch system (in lampreys) or gill pouches pumping water, greatly improving oxygen uptake for a more active lifestyle than filter feeders.
Jawless Fish.Circulatory System: (H) Basic circulation with ventral heart tube pumping blood forward (proto-heart). (I) True two-chambered heart (atrium and ventricle) evolving to push blood to gills then body; blood cells with hemoglobin appear, vastly increasing oxygen transport. This closed-loop cardiovascular innovation supports higher activity than in non-vertebrate chordates.
Jawless Fish.Reproductive System: (H) External spawning in water – eggs and sperm released into the environment, as with amphibian-like reproduction inherited from ancestors. (I) More yolk in eggs to nourish developing larvae (e.g., lamprey eggs develop into filter-feeding larvae), and a clear metamorphosis from larval stage to adult (an extended developmental strategy unique to vertebrates).
Jawless Fish.Excretory System: (H) Diffusion of ammonia across gills and skin (sufficient for small ancestors). (I) Primitive kidneys (pronephros/mesonephros) with segmented nephrons that filter blood and remove waste into the cloaca. These vertebrate kidneys allow regulation of salt and water, an advance over the simple diffusion and flame cells of invertebrate precursors.

Bony Fish.Nervous System: (H) Vertebrate CNS with brain regions (cerebrum, cerebellum, etc.) similar to earlier fish. (I) Enlarged optic tectum for acute vision, and cerebellum for precise motor control of fins. Enhanced integration of sensory input (sight, lateral line, smell) supports complex behaviors like schooling and predator evasion in diverse aquatic niches.
Bony Fish.Digestive System: (H) Complete digestive tract with stomach, intestine, liver, pancreas as in basal jawed fish. (I) Moveable jaws with calcified teeth for grabbing and chewing prey (first time jaws used for true biting). Many bony fish evolved a protrusible jaw for suction feeding (allowing them to slurp prey). Also, pyloric caeca (blind sacs) off the intestine increase nutrient absorption.
Bony Fish.Respiratory System: (H) Gill-based respiration with gill arches and filaments. (I) Bony operculum covering the gills, which pumps water over gill surfaces, allowing breathing even when stationary (major efficiency gain over sharks). Some developed a swim bladder that doubles as a lung in low-oxygen water, an air-filled organ homologous to lungs, allowing gulping air to survive oxygen-poor environments.
Bony Fish.Circulatory System: (H) Single-loop circulation (heart → gills → body) from ancestral fish. (I) Stronger two-chambered heart with an S-shaped ventricle for more force; addition of elastic bulbus arteriosus to smooth blood flow. Erythrocytes with hemoglobin are standard. Some bony fish later evolved accessory hearts in tail for venous return (e.g., in eels – a minor circulatory innovation).
Bony Fish.Reproductive System: (H) External fertilization by ancestral pattern (spawning): females release eggs and males shed sperm over them in water. (I) Complex reproductive strategies: many bony fish produce thousands of eggs with minimal yolk (broadcast spawning), while others evolved demersal sticky eggs or even mouth-brooding and nest guarding (parental care as a new behavior). Some lineages even developed internal fertilization and live birth (e.g., guppies), showing early viviparity.
Bony Fish.Excretory System: (H) Kidneys and gills jointly manage waste (ammonia diffuses out at gills). (I) Advanced osmoregulation: marine bony fish drink seawater and excrete excess salt through gills; freshwater bony fish produce very dilute urine to expel water. Nitrogen waste is mostly ammonia (highly toxic but easily flushed in water) – an efficient strategy for aquatic life, with urea production in a few cases when needed (e.g., lungfish during drought).

Scorpions.Nervous System: (H) Arthropod nervous system (brain plus ventral nerve cord with segmental ganglia) inherited from chelicerate ancestors. (I) Fused ganglia forming a larger nerve mass in the cephalothorax for better integration of sensory input from multiple eyes and touch receptors. Specialized circuits control the pedipalps (pincers) and tail stinger with precise aim and timing during hunting/defense.
Scorpions.Digestive System: (H) Arthropod gut with foregut (esophagus, sucking stomach) and hindgut. (I) External digestion: scorpions secrete digestive enzymes onto prey, liquefying tissues to slurp up (pre-oral digestion adaptation). The muscular pharynx acts as a pump to suck in prey fluid. A large hepatopancreas (digestive gland) produces enzymes to break down the meal and also stores nutrients, an innovation supporting their feast-and-fast lifestyle.
Scorpions.Respiratory System: (H) Book gills in aquatic ancestors (like horseshoe crabs). (I) Book lungs – internal stacked lamellae in abdominal sacs for air breathing, evolved from book gills to function in air. Four pairs of book lungs connect to outside via slit-like spiracles on the underside, enabling scorpions to live in oxygen-poor burrows. This was a key terrestrial adaptation, allowing gas exchange while conserving water.
Scorpions.Circulatory System: (H) Open circulatory system with tubular heart and hemolymph, as in all arthropods. (I) Long dorsal heart with multiple ostia running through the abdomen, pushing hemolymph into sinuses including fine vessels in book lungs for gas exchange. Hemocyanin pigment carries oxygen. The system is efficient enough for a predatory but low-metabolic lifestyle, and scorpions can survive low oxygen by slowing circulation – an ancestral trait leveraged for terrestrial life.
Scorpions.Reproductive System: (H) Internal fertilization via spermatophore (male deposits sperm packet on ground, then positions female to take it up) – present in early arachnids. (I) Viviparity (live birth): embryos develop inside the female, nourished by a “uterine milk” secretion. Young are born alive and crawl onto the mother’s back. This innovation (rare among invertebrates) gives the young a higher survival rate. Extended maternal care (carrying young until first molt) is also a new behavioral strategy improving offspring success.
Scorpions.Excretory System: (H) Malpighian tubules (excretory organs emptying into hindgut) from arachnid ancestors, removing wastes from hemolymph. (I) Very efficient water conservation: scorpions convert nitrogenous waste to insoluble compounds like guanine and uric acid, excreting a dry powdery feces with minimal water loss. This adaptation, along with a waxy cuticle, allows survival in deserts. They also have a rectal gland to reabsorb water, maximizing retention.

“Plants Take Root”.Nervous System: (H) No nerves; cellular signaling via hormones and electrical potentials inherited from algal ancestors. (I) Expanded cell-to-cell communication: e.g., action potentials in plant cells (especially root hairs) to coordinate responses (similar to a primitive nerve signal). Early land plants evolved gene networks for environmental sensing (light, gravity) without neurons – effectively an innovation to perform “nervous” functions through slow chemical and electrical signaling in tissues.
“Plants Take Root”.Digestive System: (H) Photosynthetic “digestive” strategy – chloroplasts (from algal endosymbiosis) in cells produce sugars; nutrients absorbed across surfaces. (I) True roots developing at the plant base, an organ specifically for water and mineral uptake. Roots featured root hairs (single-cell extensions) to greatly increase absorptive surface area in soil. Also, symbiosis with mycorrhizal fungi was established, an innovation allowing nutrient exchange: fungi provided minerals (phosphate, etc.) to the plant, and the plant gave sugars – enhancing “digestion” of soil resources beyond the plant’s own enzymatic capabilities.
“Plants Take Root”.Respiratory System: (H) Gas exchange by diffusion through surfaces (ancestral aquatic algae absorbed CO₂ from water). (I) Stomata – adjustable pores on stems and leaves to regulate gas exchange and water loss, present even in early Devonian plants. A cuticle (waxy layer) on epidermis prevented uncontrolled evaporation, so plants could take in CO₂ without desiccating. Internal air spaces evolved in tissues, facilitating gas diffusion to all cells. These innovations allowed efficient respiration (oxygen release and CO₂ uptake) in a terrestrial atmosphere while conserving water – a balance aquatic ancestors didn’t need to achieve.
“Plants Take Root”.Circulatory System: (H) Simple diffusion and cytoplasmic streaming in ancestor plants to move substances. (I) Vascular tissue: xylem for water/mineral transport upward from roots, and phloem for distributing sugars from photosynthetic parts. Early vascular plants evolved lignified tracheids in xylem (rigid, tube-like cells) that could carry water under tension from soil to aerial organs. Phloem sieve cells carried organic nutrients. This circulatory analogue in plants was a breakthrough enabling height and complexity – resources could be moved efficiently throughout the organism, unlike in non-vascular mosses.
“Plants Take Root”.Reproductive System: (H) Reproduction by spores and swimming sperm (a trait of bryophyte ancestors requiring water). (I) Retention of embryo on parent plant (hence “Embryophyte”) – the fertilized egg (zygote) grew into a multicellular embryo while attached to and nourished by the mother plant, a crucial land plant innovation. True roots allowed plants to anchor and support larger sporophytes that produce many spores. These early rooted plants were still tied to water for fertilization (sperm swam to egg), but spores could disperse through the air to new locations. Some later Devonian plants evolved heterospory (different spore sizes for sexes), presaging seeds.
“Plants Take Root”.Excretory System: (H) No specialized excretory organs; plants typically sequester or recycle metabolic waste. (I) Cuticle and stomata indirectly manage “excretion” of water vapor and oxygen (byproducts of photosynthesis). Toxic byproducts (e.g., oxygen free radicals) were mitigated by antioxidants – an innovation given high light exposure on land. Additionally, plants began to store waste in vacuoles or dead tissues (e.g. depositing heavy metals or calcium oxalate crystals in leaves) which would later be shed. The loss of leaves or shedding of bark in more derived plants is an excretory strategy to remove wastes – these mechanisms had their origins in the first rooted plants as simple waste compartmentalization in certain cells.

“Woody Stems” (Early Trees).Nervous System: (H) No nervous system; hormonal signaling continued as primary coordination method. (I) Height-related signaling: larger size prompted evolution of new chemical signals to coordinate growth between roots and an expanding shoot system. For example, auxin produced at the shoot tip travels down and influences the vascular cambium (secondary growth) – a hormonal integration to ensure balanced wood production and root support. Also, detection of gravity (gravitropism) became more critical: woody plants use statolith cells in roots to guide downward growth, an enhanced sensory-hormonal response due to increased size.
“Woody Stems” (Early Trees).Digestive System: (H) Same autotrophic “digestion” via roots and photosynthesis. (I) Secondary growth (wood formation) allowed the development of thick trunks, necessitating deeper roots to uptake sufficient nutrients and water. Early trees like Archaeopteris (a Late Devonian woody plant) had extensive root networks to mine minerals and a vascular cambium to continually supply the growing crown. Leaves (or needles) in woody plants increased in number and area, requiring an efficient transport of nutrients from roots – the coordination between a broad root base and broad leaf area is an innovation of woody architecture, effectively maximizing “feeding” from soil and sun.
“Woody Stems” (Early Trees).Respiratory System: (H) Stomata and cuticle from earlier land plants. (I) Woody bark with lenticels – as stems thickened into trunks, gas exchange for inner tissues was enabled by lenticels (small porous breaks in bark) which allow oxygen in for living cells and CO₂ out. Additionally, many early trees evolved leaf stomatal control attuned to height: leaves in the canopy might have smaller, sunken stomata to limit water loss in drying winds. Wood itself contains hollow xylem which also stores some air; in some cases this helps with buoyancy of water transport. These adaptations together ensured that even at larger size, respiration at the cellular level in all tissues was maintained.
“Woody Stems” (Early Trees).Circulatory System: (H) Vascular system with xylem/phloem. (I) Wood (secondary xylem) – concentric rings of lignified xylem added each year from a vascular cambium. Wood gave strong support and contained vessels/tracheids for water conduction to great heights. The vascular cambium and cork cambium were new meristems: one producing wood and inner bark, the other producing outer bark, respectively. This allowed the plant to grow thicker indefinitely. The woody stem also served as storage for water and nutrients, helping trees survive seasons. Essentially, the evolution of wood and bark created an internal circulation and support system unparalleled in earlier herbaceous plants, enabling the first forest ecosystems.
“Woody Stems” (Early Trees).Reproductive System: (H) Spores and free-swimming sperm (in early tree-like plants like ferns or progymnosperms). (I) Seeds (in seed ferns and early gymnosperms) – by the late Devonian/Carboniferous, woody plants evolved seeds, though the category “woody stems” may precede true seeds. If considering just wood: some woody plants like Archaeopteris were still spore-bearing. But shortly after, seeds evolved, providing embryos with a nutrition package and protective coat, liberating reproduction from water. This meant fertilization via pollen (air-borne or carried) instead of swimming sperm, a revolutionary reproductive strategy for land. Woody seed plants could colonize drier habitats because the embryo was safe inside a seed until germination conditions were right.
“Woody Stems” (Early Trees).Excretory System: (H) No dedicated excretory organ; wastes often stored in plant tissues. (I) Heartwood formation – older xylem in the center of a woody trunk becomes clogged with wastes (tannins, resins) and turns into heartwood, a durable core that also sequesters metabolites the plant doesn’t need. Leaves of deciduous woody plants became an excretory route: trees withdraw nutrients and then drop the leaves, effectively excreting accumulated waste products (and getting rid of excess minerals). Also, thick bark often stores waste compounds (resins, gums) which can be periodically shed or are inert, thus preventing toxin buildup in living cells.

Cartilaginous Fish.Nervous System: (H) Gnathostome brain with developed cerebellum and optic tectum, similar to bony fish. (I) Emphasis on sensory brain regions: extremely large olfactory bulbs in sharks for smell (a key innovation for tracking prey over long distances). Their lateral line and electroreception systems are wired into the central nervous system, giving them a “sixth sense” integration. The cerebellum in fast-swimming sharks is enlarged for balance and coordination in three dimensions. Overall, their nervous system became tuned for predatory efficiency in open water.
Cartilaginous Fish.Digestive System: (H) Jaws and complete gut as in other jawed fish. (I) Spiral valve intestine in sharks – a corkscrew-shaped fold inside a short intestine that increases surface area for nutrient absorption (compensating for a shorter gut). Also, continuous tooth replacement (teeth arranged in conveyor-belt rows) is a feeding innovation ensuring they always have sharp teeth for prey capture. Their stomach is very stretchy and acidic, allowing them to consume large meals infrequently. Some large sharks (and rays) evolved plankton-filtering mechanisms (gill rakers), showing digestive flexibility despite the typical image of them as macropredators.
Cartilaginous Fish.Respiratory System: (H) Gills with multiple gill slits for water exit, inherited from early fish. (I) Refined gill ventilation: most have muscular pumping of water via mouth and spiracle, but many must swim to ram ventilate. Sharks have no operculum, but a spiracle behind each eye (reduced first gill opening) that draws water in, especially useful when mouth is occupied or when resting on seafloor (e.g., rays breathe through spiracles). The blood-gill interface is efficient, and some active sharks have extremely high gill surface area to support their metabolism. No swim bladder; instead, many sharks can ventilate both while moving and by gulping water, and some can even buccal pump (nurse sharks), showing a range of respiratory strategies.
Cartilaginous Fish.Circulatory System: (H) Single-loop circulatory plan (heart → gills → body). (I) Modifications for osmoregulation: sharks retain urea in their blood in high concentrations, making their blood iso-osmotic with seawater (an innovation in blood chemistry). The heart remains two-chambered, but blood from the gut can bypass the liver in a special shunt (the arterial cone with valves) to maintain blood pressure. Their capillary networks in certain muscles (rete mirabile) allow countercurrent heat exchange in some sharks (e.g., makos), an innovation enabling regional endothermy (warm muscles). Overall, while the basic circulation is inherited, chemical adjustments (urea, trimethylamine oxide in blood) are innovative to their niche.
Cartilaginous Fish.Reproductive System: (H) Internal fertilization traces back to some early placoderms, adopted by cartilaginous fish (males have claspers to introduce sperm into females). (I) Live birth (viviparity) in many species – e.g., some sharks and rays have uterine adaptations to support embryos (yolk-sac placenta in requiem sharks, uterine milk in stingrays). Even oviparous sharks lay tough leathery egg cases (“mermaid’s purses”) that protect the embryo from desiccation and predation – an innovation over simple fish eggs. Extended gestation and fewer, well-developed offspring (K-selection strategy) is a major reproductive shift from spawning huge numbers of eggs as most bony fish do.
Cartilaginous Fish.Excretory System: (H) Kidneys that filter blood and gills that excrete ammonia, as in other fish. (I) Urea retention – rather than excreting all nitrogenous waste, sharks convert ammonia to urea and keep high levels in blood for osmotic balance. Excess salts from seawater are excreted via a specialized rectal gland (salt gland) – a unique organ of cartilaginous fish. Thus, the excretory system innovated to serve osmoregulation: kidneys also reabsorb urea actively. When necessary, they still excrete some ammonia through gills (especially if in low-salinity water). This dual approach (retain urea, expel salt) lets them live in marine environments without dehydrating.

Lobe-Finned Fish.Nervous System: (H) Brain and nerves similar to other bony fish (forebrain controlling smell, etc.). (I) Neural circuits preadapted for weight-bearing: these fish occasionally use their lobed fins to “walk” under water, and in lungfish, to push through mud. The nervous system controlling fins had to coordinate a front-back limb-like gait (a rudimentary walking rhythm), an innovation from the usual fin-stroke pattern. Additionally, lungfish have an increased olfactory region to detect airborne scents when they gulp air at the surface – showing their nervous system’s adaptability to both water and air cues.
Lobe-Finned Fish.Digestive System: (H) Carnivorous digestive system with jaws, teeth, stomach, intestines akin to other fish. (I) Some lobe-fins developed unique dentition: labyrinthodont teeth (infolded enamel surfaces) providing strength for crushing prey – a trait seen in early sarcopterygians and later early tetrapods. Lungfish have grinding tooth plates to eat hard foods like snails and plants. A spiral valve is present in the intestines of coelacanths (like in sharks), an ancient feature retained to improve nutrient absorption. These modifications hint at a more diverse diet and tougher plant material processing, anticipating partial herbivory or omnivory in land environments.
Lobe-Finned Fish.Respiratory System: (H) Gills for aquatic respiration, as with any fish. (I) Lungs in lungfish (and a primitive lung/swim-bladder in coelacanths). Lungfish have a paired lung connected to the gut, allowing them to breathe air in oxygen-poor waters. They can aestivate in mud by breathing air when water dries up – a significant respiratory innovation. Coelacanths have a vestigial lung (fat-filled) but rely on gills; still, the presence of a lung structure shows the lineage’s propensity for air-breathing. The dual respiratory modes in lungfish (gills in water, lungs in air) represent a pivotal evolutionary step toward terrestrial respiration.
Lobe-Finned Fish.Circulatory System: (H) Fish circulatory layout with a two-chamber heart and single circuit. (I) Partial double circulation: Lungfish hearts have a partially divided atrium and ventricle, plus a spiral valve in the outflow tract to separate oxygenated blood going to body from deoxygenated blood going to gills/lungs. This is an innovation approaching the 3-chambered heart of amphibians. Blood can bypass the lungs or gills as needed (e.g., when breathing air, more blood is shunted to systemic circulation). This flexibility in circulation and the beginnings of a pulmonary circuit were crucial adaptations for surviving in variable aquatic environments (and foreshadow the tetrapod circulatory plan).
Lobe-Finned Fish.Reproductive System: (H) External fertilization in water (spawning), as in most fish. (I) Internal fertilization and viviparity appeared in coelacanths – modern coelacanths give live birth, indicating that some ancient lobe-fins may have evolved this (fossil evidence of this is scant, but the capacity is there). Lungfish still lay eggs in nests, but exhibit parental care: male African lungfish guard the nest and even have vascularized structures on their pelvic fins to oxygenate the water for the young – a novel reproductive behavior. These innovations show a trend towards fewer, better-provisioned offspring, aligning with more challenging freshwater environments.
Lobe-Finned Fish.Excretory System: (H) Kidneys that excrete ammonia when in water. (I) Estivation metabolism (in lungfish): when lungfish burrow in mud during drought, they switch to producing mostly urea (less toxic than ammonia) and store it in tissues to avoid poisoning themselves – a temporary shift in excretory strategy to survive without water. Coelacanths, interestingly, retain urea like sharks, making themselves osmotic with seawater. So among lobe-fins, we see an innovation of ureotelism in two different contexts: one as a permanent marine strategy (coelacanth) and one as a seasonal survival strategy (lungfish). Both indicate advanced kidney regulation of nitrogen waste depending on environment.

Trees.Nervous System: (H) No neurons; uses hormones for internal communication. (I) Canopy-level signaling: large trees evolved complex hormonal and perhaps electrical signaling over long distances (from root to crown). For instance, when under attack (herbivory), some trees send electrical signals and jasmonate hormones from the leaves under attack to other parts, “alerting” them to ramp up defenses – a quasi-nervous communication across a big organism. They also coordinate leaf shedding and growth in response to daylength via phytochrome signals interpreted across the whole plant. This scale of integrated response is an innovation in tall, long-lived plants.
Trees.Digestive System: (H) Root absorption and leaf photosynthesis from earlier vascular plants. (I) Deep, extensive root systems with perhaps root grafting between trees of the same species (roots fusing, sharing resources) – an innovation in forest trees to stabilize and mutually support. Also, the development of a central trunk and branching architecture ensures efficient transport of nutrients: this is supported by “source-sink” hormonal signals that direct nutrients from high-production areas (leaves) to growth areas (buds, fruits, roots). Many trees also form mycorrhizal networks linking multiple trees (sometimes called the “wood-wide web”), enabling communal nutrient sharing – effectively an innovation turning a forest into a cooperative digesting network that can redistribute resources.
Trees.Respiratory System: (H) Stomata, cuticle, lenticels as in woody plants. (I) Massive transpiration engine: tall trees pull enormous volumes of water from soil to leaves (transpiration stream), which also brings CO₂ in and oxygen out. The cohesion-tension mechanism in xylem is pushed to its limits in tall trees, and they evolved bordered pits in xylem cells to prevent air bubbles (emboli) from breaking the water column – a micro-structural innovation ensuring steady gas exchange. Additionally, many trees regulate stomatal opening in different microclimates (sun vs shade leaves) to optimize gas exchange. Some tree species (conifers) evolved needle-like leaves with recessed stomata to continue gas exchange in extremely dry or cold environments without losing too much water – allowing them to inhabit climates that broadleaf ancestors could not.
Trees.Circulatory System: (H) Vascular system with wood and bark from earlier woody plants. (I) Large-diameter xylem vessels (in angiosperm trees) for very efficient water transport, and phloem companion cells for active transport of sugars – these appeared as plants diversified into true trees. The ability to grow a hundred feet tall and a broad canopy is supported by a refined vascular cambium that can produce reaction wood (compression or tension wood) to physically support branches at different angles. In addition, structural adaptations like buttress roots in tropical trees or taproots in deep soil are skeletal innovations to support massive size. Essentially, trees evolved the most elaborate vascular “circulatory” and support systems in the plant kingdom, including wood anatomy that resists bending and torsion from wind.
Trees.Reproductive System: (H) Seed-based reproduction (in gymnosperm and angiosperm trees) from earlier seed plant innovations. (I) Pollen and seed dispersal strategies at large scale: tall trees use height to their advantage by spreading pollen and seeds over long distances (wind dispersal in conifers, or via animals in fruit-bearing angiosperm trees). Many evolved seasonal reproduction cycles (flowering/seed set annually or mast years) timed with environmental cues – a higher order integration of reproduction with climate and ecosystem. Additionally, trees often have long juvenile periods and very long lifespans, requiring innovations in meristem maintenance (some can produce seeds even after centuries, showing incredible somatic longevity). All this ensures that reproduction in trees, though slower, has wide reach and high success in variable environments.
Trees.Excretory System: (H) Same plant strategy of sequestering wastes in tissues. (I) Deciduous habit in many trees: by shedding leaves annually, trees discard loads of metabolic wastes that have accumulated, effectively a dump-and-regenerate strategy for excretion. Some evergreens sequester resins and complex waste in heartwood or bark, then periodically shed bark (e.g., eucalyptus peeling bark releases wastes). The production of secondary metabolites (tannins, alkaloids) in wood and leaves – often considered defenses – also serves to tie up nitrogenous or other wastes in inert forms. So, trees innovated in using their large size and tissue turnover to manage wastes over decades, something short-lived plants face less.

Tiktaalik.Nervous System: (H) Fish-like brain structure (optic lobe, olfactory bulb, cerebellum) and lateral line nerves. (I) Neural control for a movable neck – first fish to lift its head independently of body, requiring new muscle control and brainstem integration. Also, expanded motor neurons to limbs: its pectoral fins (proto-limbs) had to bear weight and push, so Tiktaalik’s nervous system was adapting to coordinate limb-like movements on substrate. This foreshadows the neural requirements for walking in tetrapods, an innovation beyond purely aquatic locomotor patterns.
Tiktaalik.Digestive System: (H) Predatory diet with jaws and sharp teeth, swallowing prey whole like a fish. (I) Flat, crocodile-like skull with a strong jaw allowed snapping up prey at water’s edge. Tiktaalik likely could gulp air and food: it had a robust ribcage suggesting muscles to gulp down air or food against gravity (unlike fish which rely on water buoyancy). It may have had a stronger tongue or throat musculature beginning to form, to help manipulate food in shallows (where suction feeding is less effective) – a minor but vital digestive adaptation as it started feeding in very shallow water/land interface.
Tiktaalik.Respiratory System: (H) Gills for aquatic breathing, like any fish (likely covered by gill flaps). (I) Lungs present: evidence suggests Tiktaalik had lungs (as indicated by rib structure and its place among lunged fish) and spiracles on top of its head that could function as breathing holes. This means it could raise its head to gulp air, an adaptation to oxygen-poor swamp water. The ribs were stout, forming a partial ribcage to prevent the lungs from collapsing out of water – an innovation towards terrestrial breathing. Thus Tiktaalik could breathe both in water (with gills) and air (with lungs), a dual capability critical in the transition to land.
Tiktaalik.Circulatory System: (H) Fish-type circulation (two-chambered heart, blood flows from heart to gills to body). (I) With functional lungs, a rudimentary pulmonary circulation was evolving. Likely a partial partitioning of the atrium (as seen in lungfish) to direct some blood to lungs and some to gills.
