Its blood oxygenation could occur in either gills or lungs, requiring flexibility in circulation. The robust physiology to handle both oxygen sources is innovative. Additionally, a stronger vascularization of limbs would be needed (to supply muscle now occasionally working against gravity), so Tiktaalik’s circulatory system was beginning to accommodate weight-bearing limb muscles by delivering more blood there when on land.
Tiktaalik.Reproductive System: (H) External fertilization in water – eggs and sperm released in aquatic environment, like amphibian eggs. (I) Tiktaalik likely still reproduced in water, but as a transitional form it may have sought shallow, plant-choked water to lay eggs, reducing predation (a behavioral shift). The eggs might have larger yolk than typical fish to support development in potentially warmer, variable shallows. While not a full amniote, Tiktaalik’s life history was trending toward the amphibian strategy of seasonal breeding in specific shallows. It did not yet have any amniotic features (no hard egg or internal fertilization), so reproduction was largely inherited, with slight ecological adjustments.
Tiktaalik.Excretory System: (H) Kidneys and gills excreting ammonia (the standard fish mechanism). (I) In shallow water or mud, Tiktaalik might sometimes experience higher ammonia levels; it possibly could excrete some waste through skin when in air (ammonia can diffuse out through moist skin surfaces). If stranded in low water, it may have reduced ammonia production temporarily. Some speculate semi-terrestrial fish can switch to more urea production to avoid ammonia toxicity out of water – Tiktaalik may have had a nascent ability to detoxify ammonia to urea when air-breathing for extended periods. This would be an analog to lungfish estivation physiology, a forward-thinking excretory tweak in an evolving tetrapod.

Earliest Tetrapods.Nervous System: (H) Tetrapod brain derived from fish (with regions for vision, smell, etc.). (I) Improved motor control for limbs – spinal cord and brain circuitry evolved to generate walking gaits on land. Enlarged cerebellum to coordinate four-limbed locomotion and balance on uneven surfaces. The lateral line system is still present in aquatic juveniles but is lost in adults that live on land, indicating neural plasticity (the nervous system retools as the animal metamorphoses). Additionally, cranial nerves adapted: the hyomandibular nerve now serving hearing (via stapes) rather than gill support, a repurposing of neural function tied to the new auditory sense.
Earliest Tetrapods.Digestive System: (H) Carnivorous diet, gulping prey as inherited from fish (many early tetrapods ate fish or invertebrates in water). (I) Muscular tongue development – to feed on land, a sticky tongue or at least a mobile tongue was necessary to manipulate food (since suction feeding doesn’t work in air). Early tetrapods developed a fleshy tongue attached to the floor of mouth (from ancestral gill arch musculature) to help swallow prey on land. Their teeth were labyrinthine (folded enamel) like their lobe-finned ancestors, good for gripping slippery prey. Also, salivary glands likely began to appear to lubricate food (keeping mouth and food moist for swallowing in air, an innovation absent in fish).
Earliest Tetrapods.Respiratory System: (H) Lungs in adults (inherited from lungfish-like ancestors) and gills in larvae – amphibian ancestors had both respiratory modes. (I) Cutaneous respiration – the skin became a respiratory organ, exchanging O₂/CO₂ when moist. This is a novel strategy that supplements relatively inefficient lungs. Also, earliest tetrapods retained internal gills (Acanthostega had fish-like internal gills), but as tetrapods diversified, adults lost gills entirely and relied on lungs & skin. A buccal pump mechanism (throat pumping) evolved to inflate lungs since ribs were still not fully developed to ventilate. These innovations allowed survival both in water and on land, albeit clumsily – needing moist habitats due to cutaneous breathing.
Earliest Tetrapods.Circulatory System: (H) Heart with partial separation (from lungfish/tetrapod ancestor) sending blood to lungs and body. (I) Three-chambered heart fully established – two atria and one ventricle with a partial septum, so oxygen-rich and poor blood are better separated. This supported higher activity on land by improving oxygen delivery. Double circulation (pulmonary vs systemic) was now obligatory: blood goes heart → lungs → heart → body. Additionally, blood pressure increased to overcome gravity and push blood up into the head and through limbs. Early tetrapods likely developed valves and lymphatic systems to maintain circulation in a terrestrial posture.
Earliest Tetrapods.Reproductive System: (H) Eggs without shells laid in water, as per amphibian reproductive mode (inherited from fish). (I) Gelatinous egg clutches in moist environments – earliest tetrapods (early amphibians) began laying eggs in very shallow water or wet land, sometimes wrapping eggs in vegetation to keep them moist. Some evidence suggests they experimented with laying eggs on land in very humid areas. They also had an aquatic larval stage with metamorphosis into a land adult, a distinct innovation of amphibians. Parental investment increased slightly: guarding of egg masses or choosing nursery pools (a behavior not seen in fish) started to appear, protecting offspring until metamorphosis.
Earliest Tetrapods.Excretory System: (H) Kidneys excreting ammonia in water (larval stage) as fish do. (I) Urea excretion – adult tetrapods (amphibians) shifted to primarily excreting urea through the kidneys, which requires less water than ammonia. They evolved urinary bladders to store urine (a new organ to accumulate dilute urine and reabsorb water from it, especially in terrestrial life). Skin and lungs also became routes of excretion for CO₂ and some ions. Overall, earliest tetrapods had a flexible excretory strategy: ammonia release in water, urea on land – bridging the gap until the more water-conserving amniote system took over.

Insects (wings & size).Nervous System: (H) Segmented ventral nerve cord and fused brain (proto-cerebrum, etc.) as in arthropod ancestors. (I) Flight circuitry – insects evolved specialized motor neuron clusters and central pattern generators to control wing flapping at high frequencies, a neural innovation for powered flight. Giant Carboniferous insects had to coordinate much larger bodies, so their nervous system likely had larger diameter nerves for faster conduction to far extremities. Compound eyes became more complex, feeding massive visual data to the brain for flight navigation. Some insects also evolved sophisticated social behaviors (later on), hinting at neural plasticity, but the initial big leap was the neural integration required for flight and aerial acrobatics.
Insects (wings & size).Digestive System: (H) Typical arthropod digestive tract (foregut with crop, midgut for digestion, hindgut for water absorption). (I) Extracellular enzyme digestion and symbiosis for herbivory: as insects grew in size and diversified, many (like giant Paleozoic cockroaches) harbored gut microbes to help digest cellulose – an adaptation to consuming high-fiber plant matter. The evolution of a compartmentalized gut (crop for storage, gizzard-like proventriculus for grinding, midgut caeca for enzyme secretion) allowed efficient processing of food to fuel high metabolism (especially in flyers). Some flying insects developed sugar-rich diets (nectar feeding in early forms) requiring long proboscises and the ability to digest liquid diets quickly – new feeding strategies tied to specialized mouthparts.
Insects (wings & size).Respiratory System: (H) Tracheal system: network of internal air tubes delivering O₂ directly to tissues, present in primitive hexapods. (I) Spiracles with valves – insects evolved muscles to open/close spiracles, preventing water loss while ensuring gas exchange as needed, crucial for living in dry air. The tracheal system scaled up in giant insects: high atmospheric O₂ (≈30%) in the Carboniferous allowed tracheae to supply even huge bodies, enabling dragonflies with 70 cm wingspans. Additionally, flying insects evolved air sacs and synchronized abdominal movements to pump air, enhancing oxygen flow during flight. The ability to ventilate tracheae (instead of relying purely on diffusion) was an innovation supporting sustained powered flight.
Insects (wings & size).Circulatory System: (H) Open circulatory system with heart (dorsal vessel) pumping hemolymph, as in arthropods. (I) Although blood does not carry O₂ in insects, circulation was refined for other roles: rapid distribution of nutrients and heat. In large insects, the dorsal heart gained multiple chambers and auxillary pumps (e.g., in wing base) to ensure even hemolymph flow to far extremities like wings. Some insects evolved antifreeze proteins and thermal regulation behaviors (e.g., shivering flight muscles to warm up) – not circulatory organs per se, but physiological innovations to support an active lifestyle. The open system remained, but high metabolic insects showed increased hemolymph circulation rates and better pressure control during flight (an adaptation to avoid pooling of blood in the abdomen when upside down, for example).
Insects (wings & size).Reproductive System: (H) Internal fertilization (spermatophores or copulation) producing eggs, inherited from early land arthropods. (I) Amniotic-like egg: insect eggs have a hard or leathery chorion shell that resists desiccation, often with specialized micropyles for sperm entry and that protect the developing embryo on land. The evolution of metamorphosis is also key: many winged insects (especially later, in Permian) evolved complete metamorphosis – eggs hatch into larvae specialized for feeding, then a pupal stage, then adult – a strategy to exploit different niches and reduce competition between life stages. Even primitive winged forms (hemimetabolous) had distinct nymph stages often aquatic (e.g., dragonfly nymphs), showcasing an innovation of life cycle complexity that allowed exploitation of both water (young) and air (adult). Wings themselves are an enormous reproductive boon – facilitating dispersal to new habitats to lay eggs.
Insects (wings & size).Excretory System: (H) Malpighian tubules emptying into hindgut, excreting nitrogenous waste – an arthropod trait. (I) Uric acid production: insects predominantly excrete nitrogen as solid uric acid or related compounds, a crucial water-saving innovation for terrestrial life. They can absorb water from feces in the rectum, producing nearly dry pellets – key for survival in air. In huge insects of the Carboniferous, water was plentiful (swampy environments), but the uricotelic system still allowed them to maintain ion balance efficiently. Additionally, some insects evolved the ability to “reflex bleed” defensive fluids (not true excretion, but a use of excretory pathways for defense by ejecting noxious blood when threatened). Overall, the insect excretory system became superbly frugal with water, which along with the waxy cuticle, set the stage for their conquest of land.

Early Crabs & Shrimps.Nervous System: (H) Arthropod CNS with brain and ventral nerve cord controlling segmented body and many appendages. (I) Fusion of ganglia in thorax to coordinate complex limb movements (e.g., the rapid beating of swimmerets in shrimp or the sideways walk of crabs). In crabs, the antennae and eyestalks feed sensory data to a relatively advanced brain for an arthropod. Some crabs show primitive learning (maze navigation) indicating a neural upgrade. The crustacean nervous system also evolved stomatogastric ganglia (for rhythmic gut movements) that are finely tuned – not new, but well-developed. Unique behavior like polarization vision in mantis shrimp is beyond early forms, but early decapods did refine their equilibrium sensing via statocysts to aid complex locomotion – a neural-sensory integration improvement.
Early Crabs & Shrimps.Digestive System: (H) Typical crustacean digestive tract with two-chambered stomach and digestive gland. (I) Gastric mill – many decapods have a set of chitinous “teeth” in the cardiac stomach that grind food, an innovation for processing hard food (e.g., mollusk shells). The hepatopancreas (digestive gland) is large and multi-lobed, efficiently secreting enzymes and absorbing nutrients; its role is so extensive that it’s akin to a liver-pancreas combo, refined in these crustaceans. Filter-feeding shrimps evolved setae (bristles) on limbs to sieve food, requiring modifications in the gut to handle fine particles. Also, storage excretion (accumulating calcium in gut ceca between molts) is notable – prior to molting, they reabsorb calcium from old shell via the digestive system, an innovative recycling mechanism linked to digestion.
Early Crabs & Shrimps.Respiratory System: (H) Aquatic gills on appendages or inside branchial chambers, as in ancestral crustaceans. (I) Branchial chamber and scaphognathite: decapods like crabs have gills enclosed in a chamber under the carapace, with a specialized leaf-like appendage (the scaphognathite) that pumps water actively over the gills. This efficient ventilator allows crabs to breathe even when stationary or partly out of water. Terrestrial crabs later modified gills or developed pseudolungs, but early forms perhaps had rudiments of this (e.g., isopod-like pleopodal lungs in some). The key innovation here is active ventilation and protecting gills from drying – the sealed branchial cavity of crabs retains moisture, enabling some to venture onto land briefly. Hemocyanin in blood binds O₂ in these crustaceans, and some evolved very high affinity hemocyanins for low-oxygen environments, reflecting respiratory protein innovation.
Early Crabs & Shrimps.Circulatory System: (H) Dorsal heart and open hemolymph circulation, like all arthropods. (I) Decapods often have a well-developed network of arteries from the heart to vital organs (brain, muscles), an improvement over a simple open wash. This quasi-closed network in larger crustaceans ensures adequate blood flow to brain and limbs during rapid movement. Blue copper-based blood (hemocyanin) is present; in some crabs, hemocyanin is so effective that it supports surprisingly high activity levels (some crabs can sustain chasing prey, hinting at an optimized circulatory delivery). Additionally, crustaceans have an ostial heart that can adjust rate based on oxygen demand (neural control of heart rate akin to vertebrate regulation), a refinement for their often active or variable lifestyle (e.g., burrowed vs. swimming).
Early Crabs & Shrimps.Reproductive System: (H) Typically separate sexes with internal fertilization or close coupling (sperm transfer) and egg brooding, inherited from some earlier crustaceans. (I) Brood care: female decapods carry fertilized eggs on their swimmerets (pleopods) until hatching, fanning water over them – this is a significant behavioral and morphological innovation (the pleopods have setae to hold eggs). The eggs have more yolk and often hard protective coverings compared to those of simpler crustaceans, improving embryonic survival. Larval stages (nauplius, zoea, megalopa, etc.) are specialized for planktonic life, indicating that reproduction was tuned to disperse young widely. The innovation of a protected, multi-stage life cycle (with metamorphoses between larval stages) allowed these crustaceans to exploit various niches from deep water to shoreline during development.
Early Crabs & Shrimps.Excretory System: (H) Antennal or green glands (renal glands) at head filter blood and excrete ammonia, like ancestral crustaceans. (I) Ion regulation: many decapods live in estuaries – they evolved efficient osmoregulatory function in their excretory organs and gills, tolerating varying salinity. Some early crabs could even store water in their gill chambers and venture on land, excreting wastes intermittently when back in water (proto-terrestrial adaptation). While still primarily ammonotelic (ammonia-excreting through gills), the ability to produce some urea or uric acid in land-crabs evolved later. However, a key innovation in these crustaceans is the reabsorption of salts in the excretory gland, allowing them to conserve salts when in freshwater and to excrete excess when in the sea – a flexibility crucial for their diverse habitats.

Ferns.Nervous System: (H) No nervous system, only chemical signaling as in plants. (I) Response to light and touch: many ferns (like sensitive fern) can move their fronds slightly in response to stimuli, via changes in cell turgor – a very primitive “irritability” function. They also coordinate spore release with humidity changes (synchronized via physical-hormonal cues). While they lack nerves, the ability of the annulus mechanism on sporangia to catapult spores when dry is a controlled response to environment, an almost mechanical “decision” encoded in their tissues – an innovative adaptation for spore dispersal timing.
Ferns.Digestive System: (H) Photosynthetic autotroph with uptake of water/minerals via roots and rhizomes (inherited vascular plant nutrition mode). (I) Large fronds (megaphylls) – ferns were among the first plants with true large leaves, increasing photosynthetic area dramatically. These fronds also enabled ferns to tap into new nutrient sources: as they die and decay, they form rich humus benefiting the plant’s own roots (a self-fertilization loop in forest floors). Some ferns evolved mutualisms (e.g., nests for ant colonies that provide nutrients via wastes), showing versatility in nutrient acquisition strategies. Additionally, ferns often grow in low-light understorey; they innovated extremely efficient low-light photosynthesis and sunfleck usage – an adaptation of their “digestive” energy-gathering strategy to the dappled forest environment.
Ferns.Respiratory System: (H) Stomata on leaves for gas exchange, as in other vascular plants. (I) Ferns often inhabit moist, shaded habitats and can also absorb water and exchange gases through their fronds and even gametophyte bodies directly. Some ferns (epiphytes) get moisture from air – their respiratory exchange partly occurs over exposed root structures or scales that trap water. A unique feature: the independence of the tiny gametophyte (prothallus) – it performs gas exchange directly with the environment as a thin film-like structure. The fern life cycle innovated by separating a free-living photosynthetic gametophyte that can handle its own respiration apart from the sporophyte, a strategy that gives ferns two shots at occupying suitable microhabitats (one as a spore that grows into a tiny plant, then as the fern itself).
Ferns.Circulatory System: (H) Xylem/phloem vascular system for internal transport, inherited from earlier tracheophytes. (I) Many ferns have a siphonostele (a tube-like arrangement of vascular tissue with a pith) which allows them to have multiple leaf gaps – letting many fronds connect to the vascular cylinder without weakening transport. This is a step up from simpler protosteles of earlier plants, enabling robust circulation to numerous large fronds. Tree ferns evolved trunk-like stems with a mantle of roots that also conduct water, an innovative augmentation of the circulatory system to reach heights of several meters without true wood. In essence, ferns diversified stele types and added hydraulic redundancy (roots and rhizomes complementing the main stem), ensuring effective nutrient/water flow in their often large, feathery bodies.
Ferns.Reproductive System: (H) Spore reproduction with water-dependent fertilization (sperm swim to egg), same as their primitive plant ancestors. (I) Dominant sporophyte stage: unlike bryophytes, ferns innovated by making the spore-producing plant the large, dominant generation, with the gametophyte small and transient. This allowed spores to be elevated and dispersed by wind more effectively from the large fronds. Some ferns became heterosporous (producing microspores and megaspores, e.g., aquatic ferns like Salvinia), an innovation foreshadowing seed plants by specializing spores for male and female – ensuring cross-fertilization and provisioning the female gametophyte with more resources. These reproductive tweaks increased genetic diversity and survival of offspring, pushing the boundaries of the primitive spore system.
Ferns.Excretory System: (H) No dedicated excretory organ; plants sequester or repurpose wastes. (I) Silica deposition: many ferns deposit silica in their tissues (which deters herbivores but also sequesters a mineral waste). Some ferns concentrate arsenic or metals in their fronds, effectively removing it from their metabolism and shedding it when fronds die. Additionally, ferns in nutrient-poor environments evolve to be very efficient in nutrient cycling (their shed fronds rapidly decompose, returning nutrients near their roots). The shedding of older fronds can be seen as an excretory process, as it rids the fern of accumulated metabolic byproducts. Also, many ferns produce allelopathic chemicals (affecting neighboring plants) – these could be considered waste products put to use as defense; once excreted into the soil, they inhibit competitors, thus turning excretion into an advantage.

Amphibians.Nervous System: (H) Tetrapod brain (forebrain for smell, midbrain for vision, hindbrain for balance) from fish ancestors. (I) Auditory sense: developed a tympanic membrane (eardrum) and a single ear ossicle (stapes) to hear airborne sounds, with brain circuits to process them – a new neural pathway for hearing on land. The spinal cord had to coordinate limbs for walking/jumping, an upgrade from the simple undulatory swimming patterns of fish. Additionally, amphibians exhibit neuroendocrine control of metamorphosis (brain-pituitary-thyroid axis) which orchestrates their drastic transition from water to land form, a complex integration not seen in earlier vertebrates.
Amphibians.Digestive System: (H) Carnivorous diet in adults with simple gut; larval stages often herbivorous with longer gut. (I) Projectile tongue in many (frogs) – a front-attached, sticky tongue flips out to catch insects, a novel feeding mechanism requiring specialized muscles and adhesive saliva. Salivary glands emerged to help swallow on land. Amphibian larvae (tadpoles) have unique keratin beaks and long guts for algae grazing, then during metamorphosis the digestive system remodels to a short carnivorous form – an unparalleled dietary transition that maximizes resource use in two environments.
Amphibians.Respiratory System: (H) Functional lungs and skin used for gas exchange (gills in larval stage) inherited from lobe-finned fish. (I) Cutaneous respiration: skin richly vascularized to absorb O₂ and release CO】, allowing breathing through skin especially during diving or hibernation. Adults retained a buccal pump method to ventilate lungs (swallowing air) since they lack a diaphragm. Many larvae have external gills, and some adults (salamanders like Necturus) keep gills – an innovation of developmental plasticity. These multiple respiratory options let amphibians exploit water and air, though binding them to moist habitats.
Amphibians.Circulatory System: (H) Partially divided circulation from fish (two atria, one ventricle heart) sending blood to both lungs and body. (I) Refined double circulation: oxygenated and deoxygenated blood streams stay somewhat separate within the single ventricle via a spiral valve, improving efficiency. Amphibians can shunt blood away from lungs when underwater. They also evolved lymphatic hearts (tiny auxiliary pumps) to move lymph fluid, critical because their leaky capillaries (for skin breathing) require extra help returning fluid to the bloodstream. While not as efficient as amniote circulation, these tweaks support their dual life – providing sufficient oxygen whether submerged or on land.
Amphibians.Reproductive System: (H) External fertilization in most (e.g., frogs): ancestral condition of laying jelly-coated eggs in water. (I) Amplexus behavior – male amphibian clasps the female to synchronously release sperm as eggs are laid, ensuring higher fertilization success (a behavioral innovation). Eggs are usually laid in water or very moist environments and hatch into aquatic larvae (tadpoles), a continuation of the ancestral cycle. However, amphibians diversified strategies: some salamanders evolved internal fertilization via spermatophores, and a few frogs/caecilians lay eggs on land or retain them internally, reflecting the first steps towards freeing reproduction from water (e.g., foam nests, brood pouches). Metamorphosis (egg → gilled larva → lunged adult) is a signature amphibian innovation allowing exploitation of two niches in one lifetime.
Amphibians.Excretory System: (H) Kidneys similar to fish (mesonephric) that excrete ammonia in water. (I) Ureotelism: adult amphibians excrete primarily urea (less toxic) when on land, conserving water – a shift from ammonia excretion. They possess a urinary bladder that stores dilute urine and can reabsorb water from it, an adaptation for dry periods. Amphibian skin also allows ammonia diffusion when in water, and some tree frogs can reabsorb water through a specialized pelvic patch of skin, minimizing urine output. These flexible excretory tactics are key for living in alternating aquatic and terrestrial settings, bridging the gap until the more water-conserving amniote kidney evolved.

Amniotes (first).Nervous System: (H) Tetrapod brain with similar regions to amphibians. (I) Expanded cerebrum for more complex behavior and sensory processing on land (e.g., improved olfaction and vision integration). The loss of lateral line systems freed up neural resources for other senses. Enhanced motor control for more agile locomotion appears (as early amniotes were more active runners than amphibians). Overall, the nervous system became better at terrestrial life – faster reflexes, better balance (thanks to a longer neck providing more sensory input about head position), and more intricate social/mating behaviors driven by a bigger forebrain.
Amniotes (first).Digestive System: (H) Carnivorous or insectivorous diet (simple gut) like many amphibians. (I) Salivary glands well-developed – amniotes moisten food and begin digestion in the mouth, a new feature since swallowing dry food required lubrication. A muscular tongue and stronger jaws allowed amniotes to bite off pieces of food (some early amniotes had small peg-like teeth suited to insects). The longer neck enabled them to reach food and manipulate it better. Also, in some early amniotes, neck muscles helped swallow (since they couldn’t use water to wash food down), an innovation for fully terrestrial feeding.
Amniotes (first).Respiratory System: (H) Lungs as primary respiratory organ (no gills in adults), inherited from tetrapod ancestors. (I) Costal (rib) breathing: amniotes used muscles between the ribs (intercostals) to expand the chest and draw in air, rather than throat pumpin】. This innovation allowed a longer neck and larger lungs, since air could be pulled through a long trachea. The throat was freed from breathing duty and could be used for feeding/vocalizing. The lungs themselves became more compartmentalized (increasing surface area with inner folds) to support higher metabolism. Some amniotes (later synapsids) even added a diaphragm-like muscle for even more efficient ventilation – but the key first step was rib-powered inhalation, markedly improving respiratory capacity on land.
Amniotes (first).Circulatory System: (H) Partial separation of circuits as in amphibians. (I) High-pressure, dual-circuit circulation: amniote hearts evolved a septum that was more developed, especially in active species, to separate oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. Early amniotes likely had a 3-chambered heart with an improved septum in the ventricle (and some vascular shunts). This delivered higher blood pressure to the body, crucial for animals with higher activity and raised posture. Blood was thus more efficiently oxygenated from lungs and delivered to tissues. Over time, this would lead to the fully four-chambered heart (in later archosaurs and mammals), but even the earliest sauropsids and synapsids showed circulatory refinement beyond amphibians.
Amniotes (first).Reproductive System: (H) Still laid eggs in water or very damp areas (ancestral condition). (I) Amniotic egg: the defining innovation – eggs enclosed in a shell with internal membranes, allowing them to be laid on land without drying ou】. The amnion membrane forms a fluid-filled sac around the embryo (providing a “pond” for development】, the chorion facilitates gas exchange through the shel】, and the allantois stores nitrogenous waste and aids respiratio】. Early amniote eggs likely had leathery shells (as in modern reptiles) and required humid environments, but they freed the lineage from returning to water for reproduction. Internal fertilization became obligatory (sperm must fertilize the egg before the shell forms), leading to the evolution of intromittent organs (penis) or cloacal apposition for mating – another departure from amphibians.
Amniotes (first).Excretory System: (H) Kidneys similar to amphibian’s but improved concentration ability. (I) Water-conserving excretion: early amniotes shifted toward uric acid excretion (in sauropsids】 or concentrated urea (in synapsids), to package nitrogen waste in a less toxic, less water-dependent form within the eggshell (embryos cannot eliminate ammonia easily in a closed egg). The embryonic allantois stores waste safely away from the developing embry】. In adults, amniote kidneys evolved longer tubules and (in synapsids) beginnings of loops to concentrate urine. Many early reptiles also had salt glands to excrete excess ions from diet, an innovation for life in arid or marine environments. Overall, amniotes could retain water far better than amphibians – a critical factor in fully colonizing land.

Earliest Sauropsids.Nervous System: (H) Basal amniote brain plan. (I) Vision-centric brain: early sauropsids (reptile line) likely had very keen vision (large optic tecta), as modern reptiles and birds are visual hunters. Color vision was probably well-developed (many sauropsids have four cone types). The forebrain (pallium) in sauropsids started to develop a different layout than synapsids, with the first signs of the dorsal ventricular ridge – an area that in birds/reptiles handles visual and spatial processing. These neural tweaks suggest sauropsids were adapting to daytime, visually guided activity, in contrast to synapsid’s nocturnal tendency.
Earliest Sauropsids.Digestive System: (H) Carnivorous/insectivorous diet. (I) Some early sauropsids (like Captorhinus in the Permian) evolved multiple rows of teeth on the jaws, possibly to grind plant material – an early experiment in herbivory. In general, sauropsids maintained a simple gut for meat, but those dabbling in plants likely had longer intestines or fermentation chambers. Sauropsids also evolved keratinous horny beaks or pads in some lineages (turtles, later) – the beginnings seen in herbivorous captorhinids with thickened jaw bones and roughened bone that suggest a beak. Salivary glands in sauropsids sometimes included venom glands (by Late Permian some reptiles were venomous) – a novel digestive aid for subduing prey.
Earliest Sauropsids.Respiratory System: (H) Costal lung ventilation (rib movement) as in ancestral amniotes. (I) Faveolar lungs: sauropsids tend to have lungs with a spongy interior of faveoli (pocket-like chambers) rather than alveoli. Early sauropsids likely developed more subdivided lungs to increase surface area. They also had relatively narrow, elongated ribcages, indicating efficient airflow. Some may have evolved accessory air sacs or unidirectional airflow earlier than birds/crocs, but evidence is scant for the very first sauropsids. We do see in later sauropsids (archosaurs) the seeds of one-way airflow. But initially, the key respiratory edge was simply a dry, keratinized airway and the ability to take deeper breaths, enabling higher activity in arid environments than amphibians could manage.
Earliest Sauropsids.Circulatory System: (H) Improved three-chambered heart from base amniotes. (I) Selective shunting: many sauropsids can direct blood flow dynamically (e.g., away from lungs when diving). Early sauropsids had the beginnings of this ability, via partial septa and arterial bypasses. Their blood pressure was higher than amphibians, enabling a more active life and higher stance. While the earliest sauropsids didn’t yet have a full four-chamber heart, the groundwork was laid. Over the Permian, some lineages (ancestors of crocodilians) improved the septum. But even the “anapsid” grade sauropsids had coronary arteries feeding the heart muscle (a sign of higher metabolism) and a division of the ventricle during contraction, indicating a step toward endotherm-level circulation (realized much later in birds).
Earliest Sauropsids.Reproductive System: (H) Amniotic egg with internal fertilization, as per the clade. (I) Hard-shelled eggs: early sauropsids probably still had soft, leathery shells, but the move toward calcium carbonate stiff shells (like in dinosaurs and modern birds) is a sauropsid trend. A harder shell provides better protection and allows parents to bury or even brood eggs. Sauropsids also pioneered temperature-dependent sex determination (seen in modern turtles and many reptiles) – this may have been present in the earliest sauropsids, using incubation temperature to influence sex ratios (a unique reproductive twist not found in synapsids). Parental care in earliest sauropsids was minimal (likely just choosing good sites for eggs), but the stage was set for later reptiles to guard nests (as some Permian pareiasaurs might have).
Earliest Sauropsids.Excretory System: (H) Uric acid–based excretion (uricotelism) typical of reptiles, to conserve water. (I) Bladder for water reabsorption: most sauropsids evolved a urinary bladder that can reclaim water from urine, allowing them to live in dry conditions. Also, early sauropsids had relatively small glomeruli in kidneys – an adaptation to produce less initial filtrate and thus less water loss. The solid uric acid waste could be expelled as a semi-solid paste along with feces, an efficient strategy. Some early sauropsids in coastal areas likely evolved salt glands (e.g., in the nose or near eyes) to excrete excess salt from a carnivorous diet, an innovation that let them drink saline water or eat salty prey without dehydrating.

Earliest Synapsids.Nervous System: (H) Similar basic brain to other amniotes. (I) Olfactory emphasis: synapsids (mammal lineage) placed greater importance on smell; their olfactory bulbs enlarged, indicating these early synapsids (like Archaeothyris) were possibly nocturnal hunters using scent. The synapsid brain began developing a different cortex (pallium) structure, which would later become the mammalian neocortex – at this stage, just slight increases in brain folding and size, particularly in areas for smell and perhaps hearing. The single temporal fenestra in skull allowed a larger jaw muscle, but also potentially provided space for expanded jaw muscle proprioceptors and nerves – improving neural feedback for precise chewing, a prelude to later complex mastication.
Earliest Synapsids.Digestive System: (H) Insectivorous/carnivorous diet with modestly complex gut. (I) Differentiated teeth (heterodonty): even the earliest synapsids showed beginnings of distinct tooth types – notably large canines for piercing prey, and smaller rear teeth for cutting (not yet true molars, but headed that way). This is an innovation for more efficient food processing. Jaw mechanics also shifted: the synapsid jaw became more muscular and began to chew, not just snap. To support higher feeding rates (if endothermy was creeping in), some later synapsids evolved a secondary palate to eat and breathe simultaneously – though earliest ones likely had only a partial palate. Another digestive innovation down the line was milk (though earliest synapsids didn’t have that, the groundwork of glandular skin was being laid).
Earliest Synapsids.Respiratory System: (H) Costal ventilation of lungs, inherited from amniote ancestor. (I) Alveolar lung trend: synapsid lungs developed millions of tiny alveoli (in later forms) for high surface area; in early synapsids, we infer an expansion of the bronchial tree and perhaps a primitive diaphragm muscle beginning to form to enhance tidal volume. The sprawling gait of early synapsids still impeded breathing while running (carrier’s constraint), so as an innovation some evolved a more upright posture in later Permian to avoid that – early synapsids likely relied on short sprints and then deep breaths. Nasal turbinates (bony scrolls) for warming and humidifying air – essential for endothermic breathing – might have had their rudimentary start in late synapsids, but earliest evidence is later. Nonetheless, the synapsid line was on the path to high-performance lungs, possibly including better separation of food and air pathways with a partial palate allowing breathing during feeding.
Earliest Synapsids.Circulatory System: (H) Three-chambered heart (partial ventricular septum) from base amniotes. (I) Synapsids likely increased the degree of septation in the ventricle earlier than sauropsids, as a prelude to the four-chambered mammalian heart. Evidence: living mammals and their ancestors developed a complete septum; some late Permian synapsids (therapsids) show possible higher activity levels implying improved circulation. Early synapsids also had a higher systemic blood pressure to drive a possibly higher metabolism (some were active predators). They might have had a sinus node and AV node specialization for better heart control (inference from mammalian trait). The single systemic aortic arch (left arch in mammals) vs right in birds is a subtle circulatory divergence that began in these lineages – earliest synapsids would have two systemic arches like other amniotes, but the groundwork for streamlining to one was set in their anatomy.
Earliest Synapsids.Reproductive System: (H) Amniotic egg with internal fertilization. (I) While earliest synapsids laid eggs (like reptiles), the synapsid line would eventually lead to live birth and lactation. By analogy with later pelycosaurs/therapsids, some parental care might have been present – e.g., guarding eggs or nest. The big synapsid reproductive innovation came later with the origin of mammary glands (possibly from sweat or scent glands) to feed young; earliest synapsids didn’t have milk but may have had glandular skin that could keep eggs moist or offer some nourishment to hatchlings (hypothesized intermediate steps). Additionally, synapsids likely had genetically determined sex (like mammals today), a different mode from many sauropsids’ temperature-dependent sex determination – this genetic sex determination may itself be an innovation that stabilizes sex ratios across environments.
Earliest Synapsids.Excretory System: (H) Urea as main nitrogen waste (ancestral amniote condition leaning synapsid). (I) Synapsids trended towards highly efficient kidneys with Loop of Henle (appearing in mammals) to concentrate urine. Early synapsids likely produced more urea than uric acid and had modest concentrating ability. They didn’t yet have the advanced mammalian nephron, but they may have begun retaining more water and excreting more urea in solution – a strategy that fits a perhaps more nocturnal lifestyle (where they could afford to drink water when available and didn’t need to store solid urates in eggs because some synapsids may have given live birth eventually). Also, synapsid skin lacked a thick waterproof scale coat, so they may have had to conserve water via internal means more – possibly an ancestral innovation of more active renal regulation (hormonal control via ADH-like systems to concentrate urine when needed).

Turtles (basal).Nervous System: (H) Reptilian-grade brain (moderate size relative to body, emphasis on vision and smell). (I) Reorganized nerve pathways for neck retraction: turtles evolved a specialized cervical nerve plexus and musculature to retract the head into the shell, an action requiring precise coordination of neck vertebrae and muscles – a new neural control feature among amniotes. Their brain is still like other sauropsids, but the motor map for limbs must account for moving legs in and out of the shell (timing with breathing since shell expansion is limited). Turtles also show long-term memory and navigational ability (e.g., sea turtle migration) – indicating their neurons can support complex spatial maps, an evolutionary refinement perhaps in tandem with their longevity and slow life history.
Turtles (basal).Digestive System: (H) Standard reptilian digestion (stomach, intestines, etc.). (I) Beak instead of teeth: turtles lost teeth and developed a keratinous beak for cropping food. This required a strong bite force delivered by jaw muscles and a rigid skull. Herbivorous turtles have serrated beaks and elongated guts with fermentation chambers to break down plant matter – symbiotic gut bacteria help digest cellulose, an innovation allowing giant land tortoises to thrive on fibrous diets. Some aquatic turtles have specialized papillae in their throat to extract oxygen from water (buccopharyngeal respiration), technically a respiratory feature but tied to the digestive tract’s morphology.
Turtles (basal).Respiratory System: (H) Lung breathing with no gills, like other amniotes. (I) Muscular sling breathing: because a turtle’s ribs are fused into the shell (cannot expand), turtles evolved sheets of muscle (attached to organs and shell) to pump air in and ou】. They contract certain muscles to push viscera upward, expelling air, and others to pull viscera down, drawing air in. Some turtles can also perform cloacal respiration (drawing water in and out of their cloaca where specialized sacs absorb O₂) – an innovation for prolonged underwater stays. Their lungs are large and attached to the carapace, ventilated by this unique apparatus. This system is unlike any other reptile’s and showcases an inventive solution to the constraint of a rigid shell.
Turtles (basal).Circulatory System: (H) Typical reptile three-chambered heart (incomplete septum) with dual circuits. (I) Turtles can actively shunt blood between circuits – for example, diverting blood away from lungs when underwater for long periods. While not a full four-chamber heart, they have a functionally five-chambered heart (with a divided atria and three ventricular sub-compartments) that can shift blood flows. This is an innovation that maximizes efficiency under their variable conditions (a trait shared with many reptiles, but turtles perfected it for diving). Also, turtles have very low metabolic rates and can tolerate low oxygen (even some anaerobic metabolism during hibernation), so their circulatory system is adapted to supply tissues in low-O₂ scenarios – e.g., high buffering capacity in blood against lactic acid.
Turtles (basal).Reproductive System: (H) Oviparous with amniotic eggs (like other reptiles). (I) Hard-shelled eggs and TSD: most turtles lay eggs with rigid calcium-carbonate shells, burying them in nests. They exhibit Temperature-Dependent Sex Determination (hatchling sex based on incubation temperature), an ancient sauropsid reproductive mode retained. Turtles do not exhibit parental care beyond nesting, which is inherited, but their long maturation time and multiple nesting attempts per season are a life-history innovation for survival in uncertain environments. Internally, female turtles can store sperm for long periods (delayed fertilization), allowing one mating to fertilize several clutches – a reproductive strategy that maximizes use of scarce mates.
Turtles (basal).Excretory System: (H) Uric acid–oriented excretion via kidneys and cloaca, as in other reptiles. (I) Bladder water storage: turtles, especially desert tortoises, have an oversized urinary bladder that stores water and can reabsorb it in drought conditions – essentially a canteen. They accumulate solid urates in the bladder which can be expelled when water is available. Aquatic turtles excrete more ammonia and urea (taking advantage of water to dilute waste), whereas land turtles excrete mostly uric acid paste. Some freshwater turtles can also excrete urea through specialized cloacal or pharyngeal tissues while underwater, effectively using water to wash out wastes without using their kidneys – a quirk that shows the versatility of their excretory routes. And turtle kidneys are efficient at reabsorbing salts, which helps them live in saline or brackish environments without dehydration.

Crocodiles (Archosaur reptiles).Nervous System:
• Cerebrum and limbic system moderately developed – enables complex social behavior like parental care (innovation among reptiles).
• Strong instinctual patterns (e.g. guarding nests, vocal communication with young – innovation).
• Brain still small relative to body, but efficient; capable of learning simple routines (inherited).
Crocodiles (Archosaur reptiles).Digestive System:
• Very acidic stomach (pH ~1–2) – one of the strongest of any animal, dissolving bones (innovation for digesting whole preyfacebook.com】.
• Gizzard-like pylorus with gastroliths (stones) to grind food (innovation, similar to birds).
• Secondary palate in mouth allows breathing while eating (innovation shared with mammals) – can hold prey in jaws and still breathe.
Crocodiles (Archosaur reptiles).Respiratory System:
• Powerful lungs with unidirectional airflow (archosaur trait) – some flow-through respiration, though less efficient than birds (inherited archosaur innovation).
• Hepatic piston: a diaphragmaticus muscle pulls liver to act as a diaphragm, aiding breathing (unique innovationphys.org】.
• Can stay submerged ~1–2 hours by slowing metabolism.
Crocodiles (Archosaur reptiles).Circulatory System:
• Four-chambered heart (like birds/mammals) – fully separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood (innovation among reptilesfountainmagazine.com】.
• Foramen of Panizza – a special valve connecting aortas that shunts blood when diving, aiding oxygen conservation (unique innovationfountainmagazine.com】.
• High blood pressure to perfuse large bodies (inherited archosaur trait).
Crocodiles (Archosaur reptiles).Reproductive System:
• Oviparous: lay hard-shelled eggs on land (inherited archosaur trait).
• Temperature-dependent sex determination – nest temperature decides offspring sex (innovation).
• Parental care: mothers guard nests and assist hatching, even carrying young to water (innovation in reptiles).
Crocodiles (Archosaur reptiles).Excretory System:
• Uric acid excretion via kidneys and cloaca (inherited reptile trait).
• Salt glands on tongue excrete excess salt (innovation for semi-aquatic life).
• Cloaca also used for water reabsorption when on land (inherited).

Dinosaurs (non-avian, Mesozoic).Nervous System:
• Increasing brain size in some (e.g. small theropods like Troodon had large brains for their size – innovation), but many large dinos had small brains (inherited limitation).
• Complex behaviors: herding in hadrosaurs, nesting colonies, and brooding (fossil evidence) – indicates advanced brain functions for social behavior (innovation】.
• Balance and coordination refined in bipedal forms via expanded cerebellum (innovation).
Dinosaurs (non-avian, Mesozoic).Digestive System:
• Diverse diets: herbivores developed gastroliths in stomach to grind tough plant material (innovation), and some (hadrosaurs, ceratopsians) evolved dental batteries – tightly packed teeth that self-sharpen for grinding (innovation).
• Carnivores had serrated teeth to slice flesh (inherited from reptiles, optimized in theropods).
• No chewing in most – food swallowed in chunks (inherited), but some had cheek-like structures to retain food while chewing (possible innovation in some ornithischians).
Dinosaurs (non-avian, Mesozoic).Respiratory System:
• Avian-style air sac system in many saurischians (theropods and sauropods) – hollow bones evidence suggests they had flow-through lungs with air sacs for continuous one-way airflow (innovationjournals.plos.orgjournals.plos.org】.
• High oxygen demand: likely four-phase breathing like birds (innovation), enabling active lifestyles. Others (ornithischians) had less air sac development but still efficient lungs (inherited archosaur trait).
• Some gigantothermy: large dinos could sustain stable body temps due to size, reducing need for rapid breathing (inherited strategy of ectotherms supplemented by mass homeothermy).
Dinosaurs (non-avian, Mesozoic).Circulatory System:
• Four-chambered heart (inferred for all archosaurs, including dinos – likely innovation for high metabolismfountainmagazine.com】.
• High blood pressure in tall sauropods to pump blood to heads (innovation: very large hearts and perhaps accessory pumps).
• Haversian bone structure in fast-growing dinos suggests high metabolic rate supported by vigorous circulation (innovation toward endothermy).
Dinosaurs (non-avian, Mesozoic).Reproductive System:
• Egg-laying with hard-shelled eggs (inherited from archosaur ancestors).
• Elaborate nesting: fossils of brooding (e.g. oviraptorids sitting on nests) show incubation behavior (innovation) – adults regulated egg temperature like birds.
• Some young altricial (requiring care) – evidence of juveniles in nests fed by parents (innovation), vs others precocial (inherited reptilian style).
Dinosaurs (non-avian, Mesozoic).Excretory System:
• Uricotelic like other reptiles: excreted uric acid paste via kidneys and cloaca (inherited).
• Salt glands in some (e.g. marine or desert dinos) to excrete excess salt (possible innovation by convergence with birds).
• Large herbivores had immense gut systems – likely copious urine/feces processed, with water reabsorption in hindgut (inherited reptile trait).

Earliest Mammals (Triassic small mammals.Respiratory System:
• Lungs with diaphragm starting to form – early mammals evolved a muscular diaphragm to pump lungs efficiently (innovation).
• Turbinate bones in nose to retain moisture and heat during breathing (innovation aiding endothermy).

Earliest Mammals (Triassic small mammals.Circulatory System:

• High blood pressure and rapid circulation to sustain higher metabolic rate (innovation).

Earliest Mammals (Triassic small mammals.Reproductive System:
• Viviparity emerges: some early mammals may have birthed live young (proto-therians), but earliest ones (like Morganucodon) likely still laid eggs or had very tiny young (transitional).
• Milk production to nourish young – mammary glands with nutrient-rich milk (innovation enabling altricial young to survive).
