Earliest Mammals (Triassic small mammals.Excretory System:
• Urea excretion replaces uric acid – early mammals likely shifted to less toxic urea, needing more water but compatible with their nocturnal, moisture-rich environments (innovation vs reptileswww2.gwu.edu】.
• Loops of Henle in kidney evolving to concentrate urine moderately (early innovation toward efficient kidneys).
• Separate anal and urethral openings (ureters to bladder) apart from reproductive tract, though monotreme-like cloaca still possible in earliest forms (transition stage).

Lizards & more Reptiles (Squamates).Nervous System:
• Mid-sized brains – larger than amphibians but smaller than mammals; capable of learning simple tasks (inherited reptile brain).
• Vomeronasal organ well-developed – tongue flicking delivers scent particles, integrated in brain for acute chemosensing (innovation).
• Reflex-driven prey capture (rapid visual processing for hunting insects, inherited).
Lizards & more Reptiles (Squamates).Digestive System:
• Mostly carnivorous/insectivorous – simple tubular gut (inherited) with strong stomach acid for whole prey digestion (inherited).
• Some herbivorous lizards evolved longer guts and hindgut fermentation chambers (ceca) to break down plant cellulose (innovation).
• Kinetic skulls in many lizards (movable jaw joints) to swallow large prey (innovation).
Lizards & more Reptiles (Squamates).Respiratory System:
• Lung ventilation by ribs (like other reptiles, inherited). Small lizards may also use throat pumping to assist breathing when running (innovation).
• Some developed air sacs in lungs (e.g. monitors) for more efficient gas exchange (minor innovation).
• Cutaneous respiration negligible – dry skin (inherited constraint, rely fully on lungs).
Lizards & more Reptiles (Squamates).Circulatory System:
• Three-chambered heart with partial septum in some (e.g. monitors) – moderate separation of blood (inherited baseline).
• Lymphatic heart present: accessory pumps move lymph (innovation in some lizards).
• Relatively lower blood pressure than mammals (ectothermic metabolic needs, inherited).
Lizards & more Reptiles (Squamates).Reproductive System:
• Hemipenes in males – paired intromittent organs (innovation of squamates) for internal fertilization.
• Oviparity common: lay flexible or rigid-shelled eggs buried in soil (inherited reptile trait); some lizards and many snakes later evolved viviparity (live birth) as an innovation in harsh climates.
• Minimal parental care – most abandon eggs (inherited), though a few guard nests (minor innovation).
Lizards & more Reptiles (Squamates).Excretory System:
• Uric acid excretion via kidneys and cloaca (inherited reptile trait) – thick, whitish paste in droppings.
• Salt glands in marine iguanas and desert lizards excrete excess salt (innovation for osmoregulation).
• Cloaca expels feces and urine together (inherited).

Monotremes (Platypus, Echidna).Nervous System:
• Mix of reptilian and mammalian traits: brain relatively small, no corpus callosum connecting hemispheres (inherited primitive trait】, but highly developed sensory regions (e.g. tactile bill in platypus – innovation).
• Electroreception processing in platypus brain – unique sensory neurons map in cortex (innovation).
• Capable of REM and non-REM sleep, indicating mammalian neural organization (inherited).
Monotremes (Platypus, Echidna).Digestive System:
• Edentulous (toothless) as adults – platypus has grinding plates, echidna has none; food (invertebrates) ground between tongue and palate (inherited primitive trait】.
• Keratinous pads/spines in mouth to grind food (innovation replacing teeth).
• Cloaca present – single opening for digestive and urinary wastes (inherited reptile-like feature】.
Monotremes (Platypus, Echidna).Respiratory System:
• Lungs and diaphragm like other mammals (inherited mammal trait), so monotremes do use a diaphragm for breathing (though body temperature is lower).
• Lower metabolic rate means slower breathing rate; can also enter torpor (echidnas hibernate) – endocrine regulated slowing of respiration (innovation for energy saving).
• Nostrils at snout tip (platypus) or on face (echidna) – can close underwater (adaptation for diving in platypus).
Monotremes (Platypus, Echidna).Circulatory System:
• Four-chambered heart (like all mammals, inherited).
• Low body temperature (~32°C), so heart rate and blood pressure are lower than in placentals (innovation – secondarily lower metabolism】.
• Large azygous vein in platypus, aiding venous return from their sprawled posture (adaptation).
Monotremes (Platypus, Echidna).Reproductive System:
• Oviparous mammals – females lay small, leathery eggs (inherited reptilian trait). Eggs hatch after short incubation, and tiny young nurse on milk (innovation: mammalian lactation】.
• No nipples – milk “sweated” from mammary gland openings on belly fur patches, licked by youn】 (primitive mammal trait).
• Cloaca (“monotreme” means one opening) for reproductive tract (inherited】; males have penis but only used for semen transfer, retracted otherwise.
Monotremes (Platypus, Echidna).Excretory System:
• Urea excretion (like other mammals, inherited) – kidneys produce urea, excreted via cloaca with feces (urine and feces mix in cloaca).
• No urinary bladder in platypus (urine stored in cloaca/rectum area briefly), echidna has a rudimentary bladder; overall still cloacal (reptilian-like) system (inherited).
• Electrolyte regulation: kidneys less efficient than placentals, but sufficient given their lower metabolism (inherited).

Marsupials (Kangaroos, Koalas, etc.).Nervous System:
• Moderately sized brains – smaller than placental mammals of similar body size (especially reduced cerebral cortex folding, inherited constraint).
• No corpus callosum connecting brain halves (like monotremes】 – neural fibers cross via anterior commissure instead (primitive trait).
• Strong olfaction and hearing – nocturnal ancestry maintained keen smell and mobile ears (inherited trait).
Marsupials (Kangaroos, Koalas, etc.).Digestive System:
• Varied diets: some are herbivores (kangaroos, koalas) with large chambered stomachs or elongated cecum for fermentation (innovation similar to ruminants), others carnivorous (Tasmanian devil) with short gut (inherited mammal trait).
• Dentition often specialized: e.g. kangaroos have high-crowned molars for grinding tough grass (innovation), opossums have 50 teeth for omnivory (inherited generalized trait).
• Lactation highly tuned: milk composition changes as joey develops in pouch (innovation – early milk high in simple sugars, later milk richer in fats/protein).
Marsupials (Kangaroos, Koalas, etc.).Respiratory System:
• Lungs and diaphragm like other mammals (inherited); breathing rates linked to hopping in kangaroos (they synchronize breathing with hops to save energy – innovation).
• Lower metabolic rate on average than placentals, so slightly lower lung ventilation needs (inherited trait).
• Nasal turbinates present for water conservation (inherited).
Marsupials (Kangaroos, Koalas, etc.).Circulatory System:
• Four-chambered heart (inherited mammalian).
• Many marsupials have lower metabolic output, thus slightly larger red blood cells and lower blood pressure than placentals (adaptation to lower O₂ needs).
• Double circulation fully developed (inherited).
Marsupials (Kangaroos, Koalas, etc.).Reproductive System:
• Short gestation – young born extremely underdeveloped, essentially embryo-like (marsupial hallmark innovation).
• Pouch (marsupium) in most: newborns crawl to nipple in pouch, latch on and continue development (innovation – external womb).
• Bifurcated reproductive tract: females have two uteruses and two vaginas; males often have bifid (forked) penis – unique marsupial anatomy (innovation), linked to giving birth to very small young.
Marsupials (Kangaroos, Koalas, etc.).Excretory System:
• Urea excretion (inherited mammal trait) – kidneys concentrate urine moderately.
• Many marsupials conserve water well (desert species produce very concentrated urine – innovation).
• Cloaca in marsupials: not truly separate openings – single opening for excretion and reproduction (partial retention of primitive trait, though some have a slight separation internally).

Pollinating Insects (e.g. early Bees).Nervous System:
• Brain with mushroom bodies enlarged for learning and memory – bees can learn flower colors and navigate using sun compass (innovation among insects).
• Social behavior in some (honeybees) indicates complex neural communication (dance language interpretation – innovation).
• Ventral nerve cord with segmental ganglia controls flight and reflexes (inherited arthropod trait).
Pollinating Insects (e.g. early Bees).Digestive System:
• Modified mouthparts – long proboscis/tongue to sip nectar (innovation for pollination).
• Honey stomach (crop) in bees to carry nectar without digesting, and pollen baskets on legs to transport pollen (innovation).
• Digestive division: foregut (crop), midgut (enzyme digestion), hindgut (water reabsorption) – fairly standard insect design (inherited).
Pollinating Insects (e.g. early Bees).Respiratory System:
• Tracheal system – a network of internal air tubes (tracheae) delivering O₂ directly to tissues (inherited insect innovation】.
• Spiracles (valved openings) on body regulate air intake and water loss (inherited).
• Flight muscle pumping: active insects like bees ventilate tracheae by contracting flight muscles, moving air in and out (innovation to support high metabolism).
Pollinating Insects (e.g. early Bees).Circulatory System:
• Open circulatory system – hemolymph bathes organs, pumped by a tubular heart (inherited】.
• Dorsal heart with ostia drives hemolymph circulation; not used for oxygen transport (tracheae handle O₂】.
• Hemolymph transports nutrients, hormones, waste; contains immune cells (inherited】.
Pollinating Insects (e.g. early Bees).Reproductive System:
• Oviparity – lay eggs (inherited from insects). Many pollinators (bees, butterflies) lay eggs on or near host plants.
• Holometabolous metamorphosis – complete life cycle (egg, larva, pupa, adult) (innovation) allowing larvae and adults to occupy different niche】.
• Haplodiploidy in bees/wasps: fertilized eggs become females, unfertilized become males (innovation influencing social structure).
Pollinating Insects (e.g. early Bees).Excretory System:
• Malpighian tubules in hindgut filter wastes from hemolymph, excreting uric acid into the intestin】 (inherited insect excretory system).
• Uric acid – nitrogenous waste excreted as solid or semisolid, conserving water (inherited adaptation to land).
• Minimal water loss in frass (feces) – efficient for tiny bodies (inherited).

Birds (Aves, avian dinosaurs).Nervous System:
• Enlarged brains relative to body – especially cerebellum for flight coordination and optic tectum for vision (innovation for flight).
• High learning ability in crows, parrots etc., and complex social behavior (tool use, vocal learning) – advanced cognitive capacity (innovation beyond typical reptiles).
• Efficient thermoregulation control – hypothalamus well-developed to maintain high body temp (innovation).
Birds (Aves, avian dinosaurs).Digestive System:
• No teeth – keratinous beak instead (innovation to lighten head for flight). Birds swallow food whole or in chunks; gizzard (muscular stomach) with grit grinds food (innovation replacing chewing).
• Crop in many birds – a storage pouch in esophagus to soften food or feed young via regurgitation (innovation).
• Rapid digestion – high metabolic rate necessitates quick processing; short intestines in carnivores, longer with ceca in herbivores for fermenting plant matter (inherited but optimized).
Birds (Aves, avian dinosaurs).Respiratory System:
• Flow-through lungs with air sacs – unique unidirectional airflow through parabronchi for continuous gas exchange (major innovation】.
• Air sacs (9+ sacs) act as bellows: fresh air passes through lungs on both inhale and exhal】, giving very efficient O₂ uptake (innovation】.
• Cross-current blood flow in lung capillaries maximizes O₂ extraction (innovation).
Birds (Aves, avian dinosaurs).Circulatory System:
• Four-chambered heart, large relative to body, supporting high-pressure circulation (inherited from archosaurs, refined).
• Resting heart rates high, and can beat extremely fast in small birds (e.g. hummingbird ~1200 bpm) – powerful cardiac muscle (innovation for endothermy).
• Nucleated red blood cells (inherited reptilian trait, birds did not evolve mammalian anucleate RBCs) – slightly less efficient O₂ carry but compensated by rapid flow and high blood O₂ capacity.
Birds (Aves, avian dinosaurs).Reproductive System:
• Oviparous – all birds lay hard calcified eggs (inherited from dinosaurs). Internal fertilization via cloaca "kiss".
• Extensive parental care – most incubate eggs using body heat (feathers) and feed hatchlings (innovation at high level among vertebrates).
• Single ovary in females (most species) to reduce weight (innovation for flight); reproductive organs shrink in off-season to save weight (innovation).
Birds (Aves, avian dinosaurs).Excretory System:
• Uric acid excretion (inherited reptile trait) – white paste-like urine mixed with feces in cloaca, eliminated as semisolid droppings (efficient water conservation).
• No urinary bladder (most birds) – minimizes weight; uric acid is expelled frequently (innovation for flight).
• Salt glands in marine birds (e.g. gulls) excrete salt from nostrils (innovation for osmoregulation in oceanic life).

Earliest Placental Mammals (Eutherians).Nervous System:
• Expanded neocortex and corpus callosum present – placentals evolved a nerve fiber bridge between hemispheres (innovation absent in marsupials】, allowing faster interhemispheric communication.
• Generally small, shrew-like animals with agile behavior and improving learning (inherited from small mammal ancestors).
• Nocturnal sensory bias still – strong olfaction and hearing; vision likely dichromatic and less acute (inherited).
Earliest Placental Mammals (Eutherians).Digestive System:
• Generalized insectivore/omnivore diet – earliest placentals (e.g. Eomaia) likely ate insects and fruits; tribosphenic molars (three-cusped) allowed both slicing and crushin】 (innovation for dietary flexibility).
• Short digestive tract suited for nutrient-dense foods (inherited).
• Suckle young in utero via placenta (no lactation until birth, but placenta partly replaces prolonged milk-only phase – innovation freeing mother somewhat).
Earliest Placental Mammals (Eutherians).Respiratory System:
• High metabolic lungs – similar structure to other mammals, but with smaller body size, rapid breathing to sustain endothermy (inherited mammal trait).
• Diaphragm fully developed (inherited) enabling active ventilation even during running.
• Some may have had nasolabial glands to moisten air intake (speculative minor trait).
Earliest Placental Mammals (Eutherians).Circulatory System:
• Complete separation of circuits (inherited 4-chamber heart); likely high heart rates as small animals.
• Placenta’s blood supply: maternal-fetal blood in close proximity – placenta acted as an exchange interface for nutrients/gases (innovation: chorioallantoic placenta to nourish embryo internally).
• Umbilical cord present attaching fetus to uterine wall (innovation connecting to maternal circulation).
Earliest Placental Mammals (Eutherians).Reproductive System:
• Longer gestation than marsupials – fetus nourished by placenta for extended time (major innovation). Newborns therefore more developed at birth (hair, open eyes in some cases).
• Loss of epipubic bones in eutherians to allow abdominal expansion during pregnancpubmed.】 (innovation facilitating longer gestation).
• Small, helpless young still, but less embryonic than marsupial joeys – required maternal care and lactation post-birth (inherited mammal trait).
Earliest Placental Mammals (Eutherians).Excretory System:
• Advanced kidneys with longer Loops of Henle than monotremes/marsupials – better urine concentration (innovation improving water retention).
• Ureotelic (urea) excretion (inherited mammal trait), with separate urinary opening (no cloaca) in most – distinct urethra (innovation separating systems fully).
• Placenta also acted as excretory organ for fetus, removing wastes to mother’s blood (innovation of embryonic waste management).

Flowering Plants (Angiosperms).Nervous System:
• No nervous system – instead use chemical and electrical signaling between cells (e.g. action potentials in phloem) to coordinate responses (alternate strategy).
• Plant hormones (auxins, etc.) act analogous to nerves, guiding growth and response (inherited plant strategy, more complex in angiosperms).
• Rapid electrical signals in some (Mimosa, Venus flytrap) allow quick movement without nerves (innovation in plants).
Flowering Plants (Angiosperms).Digestive System:
• Autotrophic (photosynthetic) – chloroplasts convert sunlight to sugars, so no digestive organs (inherited from ancestors).
• Roots absorb water/minerals; symbiotic fungi (mycorrhizae) assist nutrient uptake (innovation enhancing “digestion” of soil nutrients).
• Carnivory in a few angiosperms (e.g. sundew, pitcher plants) – evolved specialized leaves to trap insects and digest them with enzymes (innovation beyond typical autotrophy).
Flowering Plants (Angiosperms).Respiratory System:
• Gas exchange via stomata on leaves – open to take in CO₂, release O₂, with guard cells regulating to reduce water loss (inherited from earlier vascular plants).
• No lungs: each cell respires individually; diffusion of gases through intercellular air spaces (inherited).
• Some aquatic angiosperms have snorkel-like structures or aerenchyma (air-filled tissues) to get O₂ to submerged parts (innovation for aquatic life).
Flowering Plants (Angiosperms).Circulatory System:
• Vascular system (xylem & phloem) acts as circulatory analog: xylem vessels (an angiosperm innovation) conduct water and minerals upwar】, phloem sieve tubes distribute sugars from leaves (inherited from earlier vascular plants).
• Heartless circulation: driven by transpiration pull (water evaporation from leaves) and osmotic pressure – an efficient passive system (inherited plant strategy).
• Vessel elements in xylem (wider, perforated cells) allow faster flow than tracheid】 (innovation unique to flowering plants).
Flowering Plants (Angiosperms).Reproductive System:
• Flowers – highly specialized reproductive organs (major innovation): contain stamens (produce pollen) and carpels (ovary containing ovules】. Enable directed pollination by attracting animals (innovation vs wind-only in gymnosperms).
• Double fertilization – two sperm from pollen: one fertilizes egg (forming embryo), another fuses with central cell to form triploid endosperm (nutritive tissue) (unique innovationwww-archiv.fdm.uni-hamburg.de】.
• Fruit – mature ovary enclosing seeds, aids dispersal by attracting animals or other mechanisms (innovation: protects seeds and enhances spread】.
Flowering Plants (Angiosperms).Excretory System:
• No discrete excretory organs – plants don't actively excrete nitrogen waste; they incorporate excess nitrogen into amino acids or other compounds (inherited strategy).
• Gas waste: O₂ from photosynthesis simply diffuses out via stomata (inherited).
• Leaf drop (abscission) to shed accumulated waste or heavy metals stored in leaves (innovation as seasonal “excretion”).

Tortoises (Land Turtles).Nervous System:
• Slow metabolism brain – small brain, adequate for routine behaviors (inherited reptile trait). Can learn simple spatial tasks over long lifespan.
• Longevity with minimal cognitive decline – suggests effective neuronal maintenance (perhaps an immune/neuroendocrine adaptation).
• Relies heavily on innate behaviors (e.g. homing to specific nesting sites, inherited).
Tortoises (Land Turtles).Digestive System:
• Herbivorous diet in giant tortoises – high-fiber diet processed in a large hindgut; they have an enlarged colon with symbiotic bacteria to ferment grass and leaves (innovation for herbivory). Smaller tortoises may be omnivorous.
• Slow digestion – can go long periods between meals, extracting maximum nutrients and water (inherited strategy with cold-blooded efficiency).
• Tongue and beak: no teeth, sharp horny beak to cut vegetation (inherited from turtle ancestors).
Tortoises (Land Turtles).Respiratory System:
• Rigid shell prevents rib expansion, so tortoises use a unique muscular sling to breathe (innovation): muscles attached to the shell contract to force air in and out of lungsciencedaily.comsciencedaily.com】.
• Peripheral respiration: some gas exchange through moist cloacal tissue when water is scarce (a form of accessory breathing, minor innovation).
• Large lung capacity – helps tortoise float when crossing water (inherited turtle trait, secondary use).
Tortoises (Land Turtles).Circulatory System:
• 3-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle) like other turtles – but with partial separation and ability to shunt blood during dives or when withdrawn in shell (inherited).
• Low resting heart rate and blood pressure, reflecting slow metabolism (inherited).
• Can tolerate anoxia for periods (e.g. when holding breath in shell), by heart shunting and high lactic acid tolerance (innovation).
Tortoises (Land Turtles).Reproductive System:
• Oviparous: female tortoises dig nests and lay eggs in soil (inherited reptile mode). No parental care after laying (inherited).
• Temperature-dependent sex: eggs incubated at higher temps often yield females (common in turtles, inherited trait).
• Slow maturation – tortoises take many years to reach sexual maturity, but can reproduce for decades (inherited trait linked to longevity).
Tortoises (Land Turtles).Excretory System:
• Uric acid excretion (inherited from reptiles) – pasty urate excreted via cloaca to conserve water.
• Bladder large – can store water and dilute wastes; tortoises often reabsorb water from urine in bladder during drought (innovation for arid habitat survival).
• Salt glands absent; rely on kidney and bladder; desert tortoises precipitate excess salts as solids in bladder (innovation).

Snakes (Serpentes).Nervous System:
• Streamlined nervous system – elongated body means spinal cord with many repeated segments, but brain relatively small (inherited from lizards).
• Specialized prey response circuits – fast strike and swallow reflexes coordinated by brainstem and spinal patterns (innovation for limbless predation).
• Some have heat-sensing trigeminal nerve integration (pit vipers) allowing infrared “vision” in the optic tectum (innovation】.
Snakes (Serpentes).Digestive System:
• Carnivorous diet – highly adapted. Skull kinesis allows swallowing huge prey whole; jaws separate at symphysis (innovation). Prey is digested slowly over days with powerful enzymes and acids (inherited from carnivorous reptiles, intensified).
• Some have venom glands (modified salivary glands) delivering toxins via fangs to immobilize and pre-digest prey (major innovation】.
• Simple linear gut – stretchable stomach, short intestine; can handle large prey pieces (inherited but extreme).
Snakes (Serpentes).Respiratory System:
• One functional lung – right lung developed, left lung vestigial or absent in most species (innovation: body elongation trade-off】.
• Posterior part of lung often a saccular air sac without much blood supply, used for buoyancy in water snakes or as a bellows reserve (innovation】.
• Glottis can protrude out of mouth to breathe while swallowing large prey (innovation).
Snakes (Serpentes).Circulatory System:
• 3-chambered reptile heart with ability to shunt blood when diving or during long prey swallowing (inherited from lizards).
• Elongated blood vessels to serve long body – organs staggered in placement to fit (innovation in circulatory layout).
• Generally low blood pressure and intermittent heart activity after big meals (snakes can lower heart rate while inactive, then raise after feeding – flexible cardio response, inherited ectotherm trait).
Snakes (Serpentes).Reproductive System:
• Internal fertilization with hemipenes (paired penises) in males – stored inverted in tail, used one at a time (inherited squamate trait).
• Mostly oviparous – lay leathery eggs hidden in secure spots (inherited), but many colubrids and vipers are ovoviviparous/viviparous – retaining eggs internally until live birth (innovation for cooler climates).
• No parental care in most (inherited); a few like pythons coil around eggs to incubate (innovation of maternal care by shivering thermogenesis).
Snakes (Serpentes).Excretory System:
• Uricotelic – excrete uric acid as semisolid white paste (inherited reptile trait), via cloaca.
• No bladder in most snakes – ureters empty directly into cloaca; uric acid is voided periodically (innovation consistent with lightweight, narrow body – no bulky bladder).
• Cloacal scent glands – at tail base excrete foul-smelling musk when threatened (chemical defense, modified excretory product).

Grass (e.g. early Grasses, Poaceae).Nervous System:
• No neurons – growth and responses governed by hormones and cell signaling (inherited plant strategy).
• Local electrical signals can propagate when cut or grazed, triggering defense chemistry (innovation: wounded grass emits electric potential to adjacent cells).
• Induced signaling: grazing triggers systemic chemical signals (like jasmonate) to grow new shoots (in place of neural response).
Grass (e.g. early Grasses, Poaceae).Digestive System:
• Autotroph – photosynthesis in leaves produces sugars (inherited).
• C₄ photosynthesis in many grasses – biochemical pathway that concentrates CO₂ in bundle sheath cells, improving efficiency in high heat/light (innovation ~ later evolution in grassesquizlet.com】. (46% of grass species are C】.)
• Extensive fibrous root system efficiently takes up water and nutrients from soil surface (innovation vs taproot for quickly exploiting rainfall).
Grass (e.g. early Grasses, Poaceae).Respiratory System:
• Stomata in linear leaves open/close to regulate gas exchange (inherited). Many grasses have stomata on both leaf surfaces and can handle intense sunlight for maximal CO₂ intake (inherited, optimized in open habitats).
• Kranz anatomy in C₄ grasses – wreath-like arrangement of cells for efficient CO₂ pumping (innovation aiding respiration in hot climates).
• High silica content reduces herbivore grazing (less respiration load due to fewer leaves being eaten – indirect benefit).
Grass (e.g. early Grasses, Poaceae).Circulatory System:
• Xylem vessels and phloem in vascular bundles run through leaves and stems (inherited vascular trait).
• Efficient transpiration stream: deep or extensive roots draw water; evaporation from leaves pulls continuous water flow (inherited).
• Narrow leaves reduce transpiration demand and ensure water reaches tip (adaptation to savanna environments – innovation in morphology).
Grass (e.g. early Grasses, Poaceae).Reproductive System:
• Wind-pollinated flowers – small, inconspicuous florets in inflorescences (spikelets) produce large amounts of pollen (innovation for open habitats】.
• Double fertilization with endosperm (inherited angiosperm trait) ensures each seed has food reserve (critical for grass seeds/g rains).
• Continuous meristems: grasses grow from base (intercalary meristems) allowing rapid regrowth after grazing or mowin】 (innovation for reproductive and vegetative regeneration).
Grass (e.g. early Grasses, Poaceae).Excretory System:
• No discrete excretory organs – wastes (like oxygen) diffuse out or are incorporated into tissues (inherited plant condition).
• Excess salts may be stored in vacuoles or old leaves which later die back (inherited strategy).
• Leaf shedding during drought can rid plant of accumulated toxins or conserve water (adaptive strategy).

Dinosaurs Extinction (K–Pg Event, 66 Mya.Nervous System:
• Selective survival: creatures with flexible behaviors fared better – mammals and birds could shelter/burrow and scavenge (those adaptable neural patterns survived】. Large non-avian dinosaurs with fixed behaviors perished.
• Post-impact, ecosystems favored small, smart generalists – mammalian brains allowed opportunistic feeding (innovation that aided survival) and rapid reproduction.
Dinosaurs Extinction (K–Pg Event, 66 Mya.Digestive System:
• Food chain collapse: herbivores died as plants died; survivors were detritivores or omnivores that could eat seeds, decaying matter, and small pre】. Mammals and birds with broad diets (insects, seeds, worms) persisted (inherited omnivory advantage).
• Dormancy/hibernation: some mammals may have entered torpor to survive lean times (innovation helping ride out famine). Crocodilians survived by fasting and living off stored energy (inherited cold-blooded strategy).
Dinosaurs Extinction (K–Pg Event, 66 Mya.Respiratory System:
• Atmospheric dust reduced sunlight – plant photosynthesis stalle】, oxygen levels may have dipped. Small animals with lower O₂ needs (and possibly the ability to lower metabolic rate) had an edge (innovation/inherited trait).
• Birds’ and mammals’ efficient lungs (air sacs in birds, diaphragm in mammals) let them sustain activity in low-light, cooler conditions (advantage).
Dinosaurs Extinction (K–Pg Event, 66 Mya.Circulatory System:
• Only small animals (<25 kg) survived on lan】; a small body means circulatory needs are lower and easier to maintain on scarce food (inherited advantage】. Larger animals couldn’t sustain their circulation without abundant food.
• Warm-blooded birds/mammals could keep organs perfused in cold “impact winter”, whereas ectothermic dinos got lethargic (advantage of endothermic circulation).
Dinosaurs Extinction (K–Pg Event, 66 Mya.Reproductive System:
• Surviving mammals carried unborn young internally – protected from harsh outside conditions (placental reproduction conferred some safety, innovation) – vs egg-laying dinosaurs whose eggs were exposed and failed to hatch. Bird eggs survived only in hardy lineages (e.g. ground-dwelling birds).
• Short generation time of survivors (small mammals) meant faster evolution post-event to fill niches (inherited trait: quick breeding cycles). This led to rapid adaptive radiation after extinction.
Dinosaurs Extinction (K–Pg Event, 66 Mya.Excretory System:
• Global darkness and drought meant limited drinking water and altered chemistry. Mammals’ efficient kidneys and ability to concentrate urine helped them survive dehydration (inherited).
• Many amphibians and large reptiles died; mammals and birds could move to find water or hibernate to conserve it (advantage).
• Waste recycling: burrowing mammals could re-eat fecal matter (coprophagy) to extract every nutrient (some rodents do this – possible survival strategy).

Afrotheres (1st placental split, e.g. Hy.Nervous System:
• Diverse clade – early Afrotheres (like tenrecs, elephant shrews) were small and nocturnal: strong olfactory and auditory processing (inherited small mammal traits).
• Some showed heterothermy (tenrecs can enter torpor) – neurological control of body temperature flexibility (innovation allowing survival in variable climates).
• Overall brain sizes follow body size; elephants later evolved very large brains with advanced memory and social cognition (innovation in one afrothere lineage).
Afrotheres (1st placental split, e.g. Hy.Digestive System:
• Early afrotheres mostly insectivorous (tenrecs, elephant shrews) – simple gut (inherited).
• Hyraxes and elephants (later Afrotheres) became herbivorous: hyraxes have multichambered stomachs (foregut fermentation) like ruminants (innovation convergent with ungulates), elephants are hindgut fermenters with an enormous cecum (innovation for bulk feeding).
• Low metabolic rate feeders: many Afrotheres (tenrecs, golden moles) can eat less per body weight due to lower metabolism, surviving lean conditions (inherited trait).
Afrotheres (1st placental split, e.g. Hy.Respiratory System:
• Standard mammalian lungs/diaphragm (inherited).
• Elephant shrews have high activity and correspondingly efficient lungs for their size (inherited mammal trait).
• Aquatic afrotheres (manatees) evolved dense lungs for buoyancy control (innovation in that subgroup), but generally Afrotheria as a whole has typical mammalian respiration.
Afrotheres (1st placental split, e.g. Hy.Circulatory System:
